###### 🌐 WebFetch `https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/`

`11:03:28`

```
Does FastAPI have native Server-Sent Events support? What is the import (e.g. fastapi.sse EventSourceResponse / ServerSentEvent), from which FastAPI version, and key features (keep-alive pings, Last-Event-ID, typed yields)? Show the minimal example code.
```

> Yes. FastAPI has native Server-Sent Events support, added in **FastAPI 0.135.0**. Import both classes from `fastapi.sse`:
> 
> ```python
> from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent
> ```
> 
> ## Minimal example
> 
> ```python
> from collections.abc import AsyncIterable
> 
> from fastapi import FastAPI
> from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse
> from pydantic import BaseModel
> 
> app = FastAPI()
> 
> 
> class Item(BaseModel):
>     name: str
>     description: str | None
> 
> 
> items = [
>     Item(name="Plumbus", description="A multi-purpose household device."),
>     Item(name="Portal Gun", description="A portal opening device."),
>     Item(name="Meeseeks Box", description="A box that summons a Meeseeks."),
> ]
> 
> 
> @app.get("/items/stream", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
> async def sse_items() -> AsyncIterable[Item]:
>     for item in items:
>         yield item
> ```
> 
> Use `yield` in a path operation function and set `response_class=EventSourceResponse`. Each yielded item is JSON-encoded into the `data:` field of an SSE event.
> 
> ## Key features
> 
> - **Typed yields:** Declaring `AsyncIterable[Item]` lets FastAPI validate, document (OpenAPI), and serialize data with Pydantic. The docs note that Pydantic serializes on the Rust side, so this is faster than omitting the return type.
> - **Sync or async functions:** Plain `def` functions with `Iterable[Item]` also work and don't block the event loop.
> - **`ServerSentEvent` for fields:** Set `event`, `id`, `retry`, or `comment` by yielding `ServerSentEvent` objects:
>   ```python
>   yield ServerSentEvent(data=item, event="item_update", id=str(i + 1), retry=5000)
>   ```
> - **Raw data:** `ServerSentEvent(raw_data="[DONE]")` sends data without JSON encoding. `data` and `raw_data` are mutually exclusive.
> - **`Last-Event-ID` resumption:** Read the header as a parameter to resume after a reconnect:
>   ```python
>   async def stream_items(last_event_id: Annotated[int | None, Header()] = None) -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
>   ```
> - **Any HTTP method:** SSE works with `POST`, which is useful for protocols like MCP.
> - **Keep-alive pings:** A `ping` comment is sent every 15 seconds when there are no messages, to keep proxies from closing the connection.
> - **Built-in headers:** `Cache-Control: no-cache` prevents caching, and `X-Accel-Buffering: no` prevents buffering in proxies such as Nginx.

###### 🌐 WebFetch `https://www.python-httpx.org/http2/`

`11:03:30`

```
How is HTTP/2 enabled in httpx (extra install name, client flag)? Is it enabled by default? Any caveats.
```

> **Enabling HTTP/2:**
> - **Install the extra:** `pip install httpx[http2]`
> - **Set the client flag:** `httpx.AsyncClient(http2=True)`. The flag is also available on `Client`.
> 
> **Enabled by default?** No. The docs say HTTP/2 support is "not enabled by default," since HTTP/1.1 is considered the more robust option for now. They note a future version may change this.
> 
> **Caveats:**
> - The server must also support HTTP/2. If it only supports HTTP/1.1, the client falls back to HTTP/1.1.
> - To check which protocol was used, inspect `response.http_version`.
> - The docs suggest HTTP/2 is most useful in async code with many concurrent requests.

Summarize: CPU-only run command, NVIDIA GPU run command (and nvidia container toolkit requirement), AMD ROCm image tag, Vulkan instructions (OLLAMA_VULKAN), and any statement about macOS / Apple GPU in Docker. Quote macOS-related sentences verbatim.

> **CPU-only:**
> ```shell
> docker run -d -v ollama:/root/.ollama -p 11434:11434 --name ollama ollama/ollama
> ```
> 
> **NVIDIA GPU:** Requires the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, installed via apt or yum/dnf. Then:
> 1. Run `sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker` and restart Docker.
> 2. Start the container:
> ```shell
> docker run -d --gpus=all -v ollama:/root/.ollama -p 11434:11434 --name ollama ollama/ollama
> ```
> On NVIDIA JetPack systems, set `JETSON_JETPACK=5` or `JETSON_JETPACK=6` in the container.
> 
> **AMD GPU (ROCm):** Use the `rocm` tag with the AMD devices passed through:
> ```shell
> docker run -d --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri -v ollama:/root/.ollama -p 11434:11434 --name ollama ollama/ollama:rocm
> ```
> 
> **Vulkan:** Vulkan is bundled in the `ollama/ollama` image and is enabled by default when the container can access GPU devices. Set `OLLAMA_VULKAN=0` to disable it, or set `GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<ids>` to select specific Vulkan devices.
> 
> **macOS / Apple GPU:** The page makes no statement about macOS or Apple GPUs in Docker, so there is nothing to quote.

###### 🌐 WebFetch `https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/gpu-support/`

`11:03:54`

```
Give the exact compose YAML for reserving NVIDIA GPUs (deploy.resources.reservations.devices with driver, count, capabilities) and the alternative 'gpus:' service attribute if documented. Any version requirements?
```

> The page doesn't document a `gpus:` service attribute. GPUs are reserved only through `deploy.resources.reservations.devices`:
> 
> ```yaml
> services:
>   test:
>     image: nvidia/cuda:12.9.0-base-ubuntu22.04
>     command: nvidia-smi
>     deploy:
>       resources:
>         reservations:
>           devices:
>             - driver: nvidia
>               count: 1
>               capabilities: [gpu]
> ```
> 
> - **`capabilities`** is required. The page warns: "You must set the `capabilities` field. Otherwise, it returns an error on service deployment."
> - **`count`** sets how many GPUs to reserve. If it's omitted or set to `all`, all host GPUs are used.
> - **`device_ids`** can target specific GPUs by ID, such as `['0', '3']`. It can't be combined with `count`.
> - **`driver`** is set to `nvidia` in the examples.
> 
> The page gives no specific Docker or Compose version requirements. It only says to install the GPU prerequisites described in the Docker resource constraints documentation, and that the Docker Daemon must be configured for GPU devices.

> The results don't mention Docker Desktop using libkrun. They cover Podman Desktop, Colima, and krunkit, which is the libkrun-based path on Mac that exists today.
> 
> - **Vulkan via Venus:** Mesa's Venus driver in the Linux guest forwards Vulkan calls over virtio-gpu to the host, where virglrenderer hands them to MoltenVK, which translates them to Metal ([Red Hat](https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/06/05/how-we-improved-ai-inference-macos-podman-containers)).
> - **Device access:** Containers see the GPU through `--device /dev/dri`, and a Podman test command runs `vulkaninfo` to confirm it ([Podman Desktop docs](https://podman-desktop.io/docs/podman/gpu)). The same docs note the virtualized GPU supports Vulkan compute shaders but not rendering or draw.
> - **Stock Mesa may not work:** One Colima report says the test image needs Venus support from a patched Mesa build, because stock Mesa fails under krunkit ([GitHub, oarbank #16](https://github.com/roeehrl/oarbank/issues/16)).
> - **Packaging problem:** A Podman issue reports the macOS installer bundled krunkit 1.1.1, which predates default GPU enablement, so GPU containers could not work with that package ([GitHub, podman #29918](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/issues/29918)).
> - **Performance:** Red Hat reports that libkrun GPU acceleration plus llama.cpp's Vulkan backend gave about a 40x improvement over the earlier macOS container path. A LocalAI issue cites community benchmarks at roughly 40% slower than native Metal on an M2 Max ([GitHub, LocalAI #12550](https://github.com/mudler/LocalAI/issues/12550)).

> **Setup:** Apple M2 Max (Mac Studio). The container VM had 8 CPUs and 64 GB RAM. Native runs used 8 threads. All tests used llama-bench on llama 7B Q4_0 (3.56 GiB, 6.74B params) with llama.cpp build b43d89e. Values are tokens/s.
> 
> | Configuration | pp512 | tg128 |
> |---|---|---|
> | Native Metal, GPU (ngl 99, fa 1) | 746.06 | 71.36 |
> | Container Vulkan/Venus, GPU (ngl 99) | 428.47 | 35.88 |
> | Container Vulkan, ngl 0 | 332.43 | 25.74 |
> | Container CPU-only | 135.06 | 28.59 |
> | Native Metal, CPU (ngl 0) | 139.60 | 23.11 |
> 
> **Ratios:**
> 
> - **Container GPU vs. native GPU:** pp is about 0.57x (roughly 43% slower). tg is about 0.50x (roughly half the speed).
> - **Container GPU vs. container CPU:** pp is about 3.2x faster. tg is about 1.25x faster.
> - **Native GPU vs. native CPU:** pp is about 5.3x faster. tg is about 3.1x faster.
> - **Container CPU vs. native CPU:** pp is about 0.97x, essentially equal. tg is about 1.24x in the container's favor, which the author did not highlight.
> - **Container Vulkan GPU vs. its own ngl 0 run:** pp is about 1.29x and tg about 1.39x. The author attributes the ngl 0 speed to Vulkan offloading large matmuls to the GPU.
> 
> **Other data in the thread (different models, briefly):**
> 
> - **Gemma 3 1B Q4_0, M1 MacBook Air (8 GB), commenter kth8:** Native GPU tg was 57 vs. 67 on CPU. The Podman Vulkan container reached 624 pp and 24 tg on GPU, and 476 pp and 65 tg on CPU.
> - **Llama 7B Q4_0, M2 Max and M4 Pro, author's follow-up:** The M2 Max GPU tg was about 72 tokens/s and the M4 Pro about 55. The M2 Max GPU pp was about 752 and the M4 Pro about 491. These numbers are approximate.

> Here's the workflow from the page, saved as `.github/workflows/playwright.yml`:
> 
> ```yaml
> name: Playwright Tests
> on:
>   push:
>     branches: [ main, master ]
>   pull_request:
>     branches: [ main, master ]
> jobs:
>   test:
>     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
>     steps:
>     - uses: actions/checkout@v6
>     - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
>       with:
>         node-version: lts/*
>     - name: Install dependencies
>       run: npm ci
>     - name: Install Playwright Browsers
>       run: npx playwright install --with-deps
>     - name: Run Playwright tests
>       run: npx playwright test
>     - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
>       if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
>       with:
>         name: playwright-report
>         path: playwright-report/
>         retention-days: 30
> ```
> 
> **Key points:**
> - **Actions:** `checkout@v6`, `setup-node@v6`, and `upload-artifact@v4`.
> - **Node version:** `lts/*`, which tracks the current LTS release.
> - **Browser install:** `npx playwright install --with-deps` also installs system dependencies.
> - **Artifact upload:** The HTML report is uploaded even when earlier steps fail, since the step runs unless the workflow was cancelled. It's kept for 30 days.
> - **Timeouts:** The page doesn't set a job-level `timeout-minutes`. It recommends setting `globalTimeout` in `playwright.config.ts` instead, so reporters still produce a report when a run times out.
> 
> **Not covered on this page:**
> - **Container image:** The page doesn't mention a recommended `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` image.
> - **`webServer` option:** The page doesn't document it. It only links to a "Web server" docs page that isn't included here.

###### 🌐 WebFetch `https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/`

`11:05:19`

```
Quote the depends_on long-syntax conditions (service_started, service_healthy, service_completed_successfully) and the 'profiles' attribute semantics (services without profiles always start; --profile flag; COMPOSE_PROFILES). Also the 'gpus' attribute if present and 'models' top-level attribute if present.
```

> **depends_on (long-syntax conditions)**
> 
> - `service_started`: "An equivalent of the short syntax described previously". Compose only checks that the dependency has started.
> - `service_healthy`: "Specifies that a dependency is expected to be "healthy"". Compose waits for the dependency's `healthcheck` to pass.
> - `service_completed_successfully`: "Specifies that a dependency is expected to run to successful completion before starting a dependent service." Compose waits for the dependency to exit successfully.
> 
> **profiles**
> 
> The page says: "If unassigned, the service is always started but if assigned, it is only started if the profile is activated." Services without profiles always start. Services with profiles start only when their profile is activated. The page doesn't cover the `--profile` flag or `COMPOSE_PROFILES`, so I can't describe those from this content.
> 
> **gpus**
> 
> "`gpus` specifies GPU devices to be allocated for container usage." It can be a list of device requests or the string `all` to allocate all available GPUs.
> 
> **models (top-level attribute)**
> 
> "`models` defines which AI models the service should use at runtime." Each referenced model must be defined under the top-level `models` element. Compose injects environment variables with connection details and model identifiers. The long syntax lets you set the variable names with `endpoint_var` and `model_var`.

> ## Facts
> 
> **(a) Ollama in Docker on Apple Silicon**
> - Docker Desktop passes GPUs to Linux containers only on Windows with WSL2 and NVIDIA. The docs say nothing about Mac GPU support. ([docs.docker.com/desktop/features/gpu](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/gpu/))
> - Docker Desktop's Mac VM managers are Docker VMM (the default since 4.86) and Apple Virtualization. It used libkrun from 4.35 to 4.85 and has dropped it. None of these is documented as giving containers a GPU. ([vmm](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/)) The newest version is 4.95.0 (2026-10-12), and its release notes have no Mac container GPU entry. ([release-notes](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/release-notes/))
> - Podman with libkrun/krunkit exposes Vulkan inside containers. The chain is Mesa Venus, then virtio-gpu, then MoltenVK, then Metal. Containers need `--device /dev/dri` and a **patched Mesa** in the image, and only Vulkan compute works. ([podman-desktop gpu](https://podman-desktop.io/docs/podman/gpu), [Red Hat](https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/06/05/how-we-improved-ai-inference-macos-podman-containers)) Colima 0.10+ has a `krunkit` VM type, but its GPU path goes through Docker Model Runner or Ramalama, not an Ollama container. Lima marks krunkit as experimental. ([Colima README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/abiosoft/colima/main/README.md), [Lima](https://lima-vm.io/docs/config/vmtype/krunkit/))
> - I found nothing about OrbStack GPU support.
> - The `ollama/ollama` image bundles Vulkan and turns it on when the container can reach GPU devices (`OLLAMA_VULKAN=0` turns it off). NVIDIA needs `--gpus=all` plus the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. AMD uses the `:rocm` tag. The docs say nothing about macOS. ([docs.ollama.com/docker](https://docs.ollama.com/docker.md))
> - Benchmark on an M2 Max with llama 7B Q4_0, in tokens/s ([llama.cpp #12985](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/12985)):
> 
>   | Setup | Generation | Prompt processing |
>   |---|---|---|
>   | Native Metal | 71.4 | 746 |
>   | Container, Venus GPU | 35.9 (0.50x) | 428 (0.57x) |
>   | Container, CPU only | 28.6 (0.40x) | 135 (0.18x) |
> 
>   With Gemma3 1B on an M1 Air, generation on CPU was close to or faster than on GPU. Red Hat claims Venus reaches 75-80% of native, and its "API remoting" preview is near native. ([Red Hat 2025-09](https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/09/18/reach-native-speed-macos-llamacpp-container-inference))
> - Ollama is at v0.40.5 (14 Oct 2026). Since v0.40.0, models that MLX supports run on MLX by default on Apple Silicon (native only). ([releases](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/releases))
> - The `ollama` PyPI package (0.6.3) is only "the official Python client". Its docs say "Ollama should be installed and running". ([pypi](https://pypi.org/pypi/ollama/json))
> - Compose features available: `depends_on` with `service_healthy` / `service_completed_successfully`, `profiles` (a service without a profile always starts), a `gpus` attribute, and a top-level `models` attribute for Docker Model Runner. ([compose services](https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/)) For NVIDIA, use `deploy.resources.reservations.devices` with `driver: nvidia`, `count`, `capabilities: [gpu]`; `capabilities` is required. ([gpu-support](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/gpu-support/))
> - Local machine: Apple M4 Pro, 48 GB RAM, 14 cores (`sysctl`), Docker Desktop 4.89.0 with engine 29.7.2 (`docker version`). **Ollama is not installed natively.** It is not on PATH, in `/opt/homebrew/bin`, `/usr/local/bin` or `/Applications`.
> 
> **(b) GitHub Actions on public repos**
> - Standard runners, free and unlimited for public repos ([docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners)):
> 
>   | Labels | Arch | vCPU | RAM | SSD |
>   |---|---|---|---|---|
>   | `ubuntu-latest` / `24.04` / `26.04` | x64 | 4 | 16 GB | 14 GB |
>   | `ubuntu-24.04-arm` | arm64 | 4 | 16 GB | 14 GB |
>   | `macos-latest` / `14` / `15` / `26` | M1 arm64 | 3 | 7 GB | 14 GB |
>   | `ubuntu-slim` | x64 | 1 | 5 GB | - |
> 
>   Standard runners have no GPU, and arm64 macOS runners do not support nested virtualization.
> - GitHub's Mac runners expose no Metal device, according to PyTorch CI. ([search summary](https://github.com/actions/runner-images/issues/9254))
> - Ollama CI patterns seen in other repos:
>   - **Install script with split binary and model caches:** warm restore takes under 5 s. ([coder/mux #531](https://github.com/coder/mux/pull/531))
>   - **No cache:** llama-stack found restoring the cache (~45 s) slower than pulling (~30 s), and later switched to a container image with the models already baked in. ([llama-stack](https://git.kvant.cloud/phoenix-oss/llama-stack/src/branch/main/.github/actions/setup-ollama/action.yml))
> - `actions/cache` gives 10 GB free per repo, with 7-day retention and LRU eviction. Going past 10 GB is paid. ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-11-20-github-actions-cache-size-can-now-exceed-10-gb-per-repository/))
> - CPU speed for tiny models: qwen3:0.6b ran at ~65 tok/s on 4 threads (one blog, CPU unknown). ([gadgetzamurai](https://gadgetzamurai.jp/?p=120659)) llama3.2:1b ran at ~9 tok/s on a 2-vCPU VPS. ([stackrecipes](https://stackrecipes.com/blog/local-llm-vps-ollama-benchmarks/)) qwen3:0.6b is about 523 MB. ([labuladong](https://labuladong.online/zh/ai-coding/basics/local-llm-ollama/))
> - Playwright's CI recipe: `actions/checkout@v6`, `setup-node@v6` with `lts/*`, `npx playwright install --with-deps`, and `upload-artifact@v4` with `if: !cancelled()`. ([playwright ci](https://playwright.dev/docs/ci-intro))
> 
> **(c) Frontend**
> - Next.js is at 16.4.2 (`npm view next version`); major 16 shipped in October 2025.
> - `output: 'export'` does not support: dynamic routes without `generateStaticParams`, route handlers that read the Request (only `GET` with `force-static` works), cookies, **rewrites**, redirects, headers, proxy, ISR, default image optimization, server actions, or intercepting routes. Using one of these "with `next dev` will result in an error". The official nginx recipe is `try_files $uri $uri.html $uri/ =404`. ([static-exports](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/static-exports))
> - The Next.js Vitest guide installs `vitest @vitejs/plugin-react jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/dom vite-tsconfig-paths` and sets `environment: 'jsdom'`. **Async Server Components are not supported**, so those should be covered by e2e tests. The guide does not mention MSW. ([vitest guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/testing/vitest))
> - Current npm versions: vitest 5.0.5, @testing-library/react 16.3.3, msw 3.0.3, @playwright/test 1.64.1.
> 
> **(d) Backend**
> - FastAPI is at 0.143.2 and needs Python 3.10+. ([pypi](https://pypi.org/pypi/fastapi/json))
> - FastAPI has **native SSE since 0.135.0** ([docs](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/)):
>   - `from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent`, with `response_class=EventSourceResponse` and `yield`.
>   - Typed `AsyncIterable[Model]` return values.
>   - A ping every 15 s.
>   - `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no` headers.
>   - `Last-Event-ID` resume support; POST works.
> - sse-starlette (3.5.0, BSD-3) is no longer needed.
> - httpx is at 0.28.1, last released December 2024, still marked Beta. HTTP/2 needs the `httpx[http2]` extra plus `http2=True`, and is off by default. ([http2](https://www.python-httpx.org/http2/))
> - selectolax 1.0.0 (MIT, Lexbor engine) has a README benchmark extracting from 754 top-domain home pages ([pypi](https://pypi.org/pypi/selectolax/json)):
> 
>   | Parser | Time |
>   |---|---|
>   | BeautifulSoup (html.parser) | 61.0 s |
>   | lxml | 9.1 s |
>   | html5_parser | 16.1 s |
>   | selectolax (Lexbor) | 2.4 s |
> 
>   That makes selectolax about 3.8x faster than lxml and about 25x faster than BS4.
> - trafilatura is at 2.3.1 (2026-10-06), **Apache-2.0**, Python 3.10+. ([pypi](https://pypi.org/pypi/trafilatura/json))
> 
> ## Implications for the design
> - **Ollama is not "just a pyproject dependency".** The Python package is only a client, so a server must run somewhere. Make it configurable with `OLLAMA_BASE_URL`.
> - **Two compose modes:**
>   - Default on Mac: the backend talks to native Ollama at `host.docker.internal:11434`. That uses Metal/MLX on the M4 Pro with 48 GB. Ollama must be installed natively first.
>   - `--profile bundled-ollama`: runs the `ollama/ollama` service on CPU, for Linux reviewers and CI. An optional `compose.gpu.yaml` override adds the NVIDIA `deploy.resources.reservations.devices` block.
> - **Do not plan on GPU inside Docker on Mac.** Podman/krunkit needs a patched Mesa that the Ollama image lacks (not verified). Expect a CPU container to generate at about 0.4x native speed and process prompts at about 0.2x.
> - **Compose plumbing:**
>   - A named volume `ollama:/root/.ollama`.
>   - A one-shot `ollama-pull` init service using the same image, with `OLLAMA_HOST=ollama:11434` and `ollama pull <models>`. The backend waits on it with `service_completed_successfully`.
>   - Health check with `["CMD","ollama","list"]`, which avoids depending on curl.
> - **Run evals and model comparisons natively, not in CI.** Commit the results as artifacts.
> - **CI plan:**
>   - BE and FE unit tests run with Ollama mocked.
>   - One integration and e2e job on `ubuntu-latest` with qwen3:0.6b-class models only, staying within the 14 GB disk.
>   - Pull the model directly; caching ~0.5 GB is probably not faster.
>   - Avoid macOS runners: no Metal, 3 vCPU and 7 GB.
> - **Frontend:**
>   - Client-side fetches to the relative path `/api/...`.
>   - An nginx container serves `out/` and proxies `/api/` to FastAPI, with `proxy_buffering off` for SSE.
>   - Use query params rather than `[id]` routes.
>   - Because rewrites are unsupported, dev needs either `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE` with FastAPI CORS, or `output: 'export'` applied only at build time.
> - **Backend:** native FastAPI SSE; `httpx[http2]` `AsyncClient` for fetching; selectolax to strip tags and nodes that carry no signal, then trafilatura for main text. Both licenses are permissive.
> 
> ## Unknowns / could not verify
> - OrbStack GPU status.
> - Whether the `ollama/ollama` image works under Podman krunkit/Venus.
> - Whether the Ollama image ships curl.
> - Measured tok/s for qwen3:0.6b on GitHub runners. The 4-vCPU figure above is from one blog with unknown hardware.
> - Ollama MLX speed against llama.cpp Metal for our candidate models.
> - API changes in MSW 3.x and Vitest 5.x compared with the Next.js guide.
> - The current Playwright Docker image tag.
> - Whether a conditional `output: 'export'` together with dev-only rewrites is officially supported.

**Partial or blocked:**
- Seeking Alpha: the listing page loaded, but an article returned 403.
- Forbes: the listing loaded, but an article returned 403.
- nasdaq.com: the request hung until the 60s timeout. That fits Akamai holding back unknown clients, and HTTP/1.1 hangs have been reported on Akamai hosts (https://users.rust-lang.org/t/http-request-with-redirects-runs-into-issues-reqwest/126516).

**Paywalls:**
- Reuters and CNN both added paywalls in October 2024. Reuters gives "a limited number" of free articles, then $1/week. CNN charges $3.99/month, with the homepage and breaking news left free. Sources: https://pressgazette.co.uk/?p=232735, https://www.mediaite.com/news/cnn-introduces-paywall-for-news-sites-will-cost-3-99-per-month-for-unlimited-access
- MarketWatch has had a paywall since 2020: https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/357191/marketwatch-adds-paywall-wsj-magazine-reduces.html
- Business Insider removed the paywall from much of its site but still has subscriber-only content: https://www.status.news/p/business-insider-paywall-strategy

**Bot protection:**
- One 2026 report says Reuters uses DataDome and returned a 1.5KB captcha page even to a stealth browser: https://akitaonrails.com/en/2026/02/18/web-scraping-in-2026-behind-the-m-akita-chronicles/
- Commercial scrapers for CNBC and AP use plain HTTP with no browser. The AP one routes through residential proxies by default. https://apify.com/xtracto/cnbc-scraper, https://apify.com/xtracto/apnews-scraper

**Yahoo EU consent.** yfinance handles the consent wall like this: GET `guce.yahoo.com/consent`, parse `csrfToken` and `sessionId`, then POST to `consent.yahoo.com/v2/collectConsent?sessionId=…` with `agree`, `consentUUID=default`, `originalDoneUrl` and `namespace=yahoo`. It also has a generic path: when the final host ends in `consent.yahoo.com`, it submits the first form on the page. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ranaroussi/yfinance/main/yfinance/data.py

**SEC EDGAR.** Requests must declare a User-Agent like `Company Name [redacted-email]`. The maximum rate is 10 requests per second. https://www.sec.gov/os/accessing-edgar-data

## Implications for the design

- **Fetcher:** `httpx` with HTTP/2 (the `httpx[http2]` extra), a consistent Chrome header set (UA, Accept, `Accept-Language: en-US`), redirects followed, `timeout=(5, 15)` so a held-back request becomes an error, and a byte cap.
- **Block detection:** return a typed `source_blocked` error rather than garbage. Signals: DataDome (`captcha-delivery.com`, `x-datadome` header), Cloudflare (`cf-mitigated: challenge`, "Just a moment"), PerimeterX ("px-captcha", "Press & Hold"), Akamai ("Access Denied", "Reference #"). Do not build evasion; suggest a mirror URL where one exists (Reuters/AP to Yahoo).
- **Extraction order:**
  1. JSON-LD `NewsArticle.articleBody`. If `isAccessibleForFree: false`, flag it as paywalled (Google's paywalled-content markup).
  2. A per-domain container selector.
  3. A generic pure-Python fallback such as trafilatura.
  4. Remove noise blocks and boilerplate paragraphs per domain.
- **Yahoo EU consent:** the Docker container's egress IP sets the jurisdiction. Either reuse the yfinance-style form submit (it auto-accepts consent for the user, so that is a decision to make) or fail with a clear error.
- **Press releases:** cut the forward-looking-statements and "About" boilerplate before sentiment scoring. It is long, generic legal text and drags the score toward neutral.
- **Tests:** CI should use saved HTML snapshots per source, because GitHub runner IPs are datacenter IPs and more likely to be blocked. Live per-source probes can run as a manual smoke test.
- **Live blogs** (Yahoo `/markets/live/`, CNBC live updates): join the updates and truncate.

## Unknowns / could not verify

- Whether any of these sites actually returns 401/403 to raw httpx from the user's EU IP. Nothing here tested that.
- JSON-LD presence, `articleBody` completeness, and all container selectors (scripts were stripped).
- Reuters' and CNN's current free-article limits. MarketWatch's bot vendor.
- Whether the Yahoo consent form fields still match yfinance's code.
- Benzinga's `__NEXT_DATA__` shape.

> 
> - **Akamai's detection goes beyond headers.** Akamai maintains a database of real browser TLS profiles and flags requests whose JA3 hash matches no known browser. One source concludes that any Python requests-based approach fails immediately against Akamai, even with perfect headers.
> - **Headers help only with simpler blocks.** A guide suggests setting browser-like headers, but warns that fake headers that do not match the rest of your request can make detection worse.
> - **Default user agents are a known giveaway.** Python Requests sends user agent strings like "python-requests/2.26.0" that explicitly announce the library name.
> - **Suggested workarounds are commercial.** Two sources recommend scraping APIs or headless browsers rather than plain requests. ZenRows and ScraperAPI are vendor pages, so treat their claims with caution.

###### 🌐 WebFetch `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ranaroussi/yfinance/main/y…`

`11:06:15`

```
Find any code handling Yahoo EU/GDPR consent (consent.yahoo.com, guce, collectConsent, csrfToken, sessionId, 'agree', GUCS cookie). Quote the relevant logic briefly: what form fields are posted and to which URL.
```

> The consent handling is in `yfinance`'s `data.py`-style module (`YfData` and `Auth`). There are two paths.
> 
> **1. Proactive CSRF consent flow (`_get_cookie_csrf`)**
> 
> - **GET** `https://guce.yahoo.com/consent`, then parse the `csrfToken` and `sessionId` hidden inputs from the HTML.
> - **POST** to `https://consent.yahoo.com/v2/collectConsent?sessionId={sessionId}` with form data:
>   - `'agree': ['agree', 'agree']`
>   - `'consentUUID': 'default'`
>   - `'sessionId'` and `'csrfToken'` (scraped values)
>   - `'originalDoneUrl': 'https://finance.yahoo.com/'`
>   - `'namespace': 'yahoo'`
> - **GET** `https://guce.yahoo.com/copyConsent?sessionId={sessionId}` with the same data.
> 
> **2. Reactive redirect handling (`get()` and `_accept_consent_form`)**
> 
> - `get()` checks whether the final response URL's hostname ends with `consent.yahoo.com`. If so, it calls `_accept_consent_form`.
> - `_accept_consent_form` takes the first `<form>` on the page and resolves its `action` URL against the response URL.
> - It copies all named inputs. Checkboxes and radios are included only if the name contains "agree" or "accept", or if they are checked.
> - If no agree/accept field exists, it adds `data["agree"] = "1"`.
> - It POSTs to the action URL with a `Referer` header set to the consent page URL and `allow_redirects=True`.
> 
> **Other notes**
> 
> - `GUCS` does not appear anywhere in this code.
> - `_save_cookie_curlCffi` discards any cookie key containing `consent` when more than one Yahoo cookie is present, so consent cookies are not cached as the primary session cookie.
> - Consent-related failures (`ChunkedEncodingError`) are caught and logged so the code can fall back to the other cookie strategy.

###### 🔎 WebSearch `benzinga.com scraping cloudflare 403 python requests article`

`11:06:41`

> I didn't find a Benzinga-specific article. The results are general guides on getting 403 errors from Cloudflare-protected sites with Python `requests`, so I can't confirm anything about Benzinga's setup.
> 
> The general picture from these guides:
> 
> - **Why it happens:** By default, it sends a `python-requests/2.x.x` User Agent, which is an obvious bot signal to Cloudflare. It's also missing the headers that every real browser sends by default, and sends a TLS fingerprint that Cloudflare recognizes as a raw HTTP client rather than Chrome or Firefox.
> - **Related error codes:** Cloudflare errors frequently include 403 (the most common), 401429, and 502. Rate limiting (error 1015) and geographic blocks (error 1009) are also common, and these are usually accompanied by a Cloudflare 403 Forbidden HTTP response status code.
> - **Workarounds:** Some guides recommend Cloudscraper, which is built on the Python Requests library and is specifically designed to bypass Cloudflare's anti-bot protection systems. Others say that if this error appears when web scraping using Cloudscraper, it implies that the target website implements advanced bot detection techniques that are beyond Cloudscraper's capabilities. Proxies and scraping APIs are the usual fallback, though these are vendor-written sources.

> - **Set a timeout regardless:** The Python Requests library has no timeout by default. Passing an explicit `timeout=(connect, read)` tuple at least turns a silent hang into a catchable exception.

> 
> **Rejected:**
> - WSJ, Barron's, Bloomberg, FT: hard or metered paywalls (from prior knowledge, not re-checked this session).
> - Reuters: metered paywall plus DataDome. Very likely to be pasted, so return a clear "blocked" error and point to the same wire story on Yahoo.
> - MarketWatch: Dow Jones paywall, and probably the same bot protection as its sister sites (not confirmed).
> - Seeking Alpha: articles return 403 (PerimeterX/HUMAN) and sit behind a login or premium gate.
> - Nasdaq.com: Akamai hangs the request, and most of its articles are syndicated from Motley Fool, Zacks or RTTNews.
> - Investopedia: mostly educational, few news URLs.
> - Business Insider: subscriber-only content and an unconfirmed fetch path.
> - TheStreet: 403 and a lower chance of being picked.
> 
> ## Implications for the design
> 
> - **Fetcher:** `httpx` with HTTP/2 (the `httpx[http2]` extra), a consistent Chrome header set (UA, Accept, `Accept-Language: en-US`), redirects followed, `timeout=(5, 15)` so a held-back request becomes an error, and a byte cap.
> - **Block detection:** return a typed `source_blocked` error rather than garbage. Signals: DataDome (`captcha-delivery.com`, `x-datadome` header), Cloudflare (`cf-mitigated: challenge`, "Just a moment"), PerimeterX ("px-captcha", "Press & Hold"), Akamai ("Access Denied", "Reference #"). Do not build evasion; suggest a mirror URL where one exists (Reuters/AP to Yahoo).
> - **Extraction order:**
>   1. JSON-LD `NewsArticle.articleBody`. If `isAccessibleForFree: false`, flag it as paywalled (Google's paywalled-content markup).
>   2. A per-domain container selector.
>   3. A generic pure-Python fallback such as trafilatura.
>   4. Remove noise blocks and boilerplate paragraphs per domain.
> - **Yahoo EU consent:** the Docker container's egress IP sets the jurisdiction. Either reuse the yfinance-style form submit (it auto-accepts consent for the user, so that is a decision to make) or fail with a clear error.
> - **Press releases:** cut the forward-looking-statements and "About" boilerplate before sentiment scoring. It is long, generic legal text and drags the score toward neutral.
> - **Tests:** CI should use saved HTML snapshots per source, because GitHub runner IPs are datacenter IPs and more likely to be blocked. Live per-source probes can run as a manual smoke test.
> - **Live blogs** (Yahoo `/markets/live/`, CNBC live updates): join the updates and truncate.
> 
> ## Unknowns / could not verify
> 
> - Whether any of these sites actually returns 401/403 to raw httpx from the user's EU IP. Nothing here tested that.
> - JSON-LD presence, `articleBody` completeness, and all container selectors (scripts were stripped).
> - Reuters' and CNN's current free-article limits. MarketWatch's bot vendor.
> - Whether the Yahoo consent form fields still match yfinance's code.
> - Benzinga's `__NEXT_DATA__` shape.

## Facts

**zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment**
- Ungated, MIT. The repo holds `sent_train.csv`, `sent_valid.csv` and `sent_dataset_meta.txt`. https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment
- Labels: 0 = Bearish, 1 = Bullish, 2 = Neutral. The text is finance tweets and headline-style lines. Nothing is published about how the labels were annotated. https://huggingface.co/datasets/zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment
- Real split sizes are train 9,543 (1,442 / 1,923 / 6,178) and validation 2,388 (347 / 475 / 1,566). Mean length is about 86 characters, max 227. The card's table says 9,938 / 2,486, which is stale. The meta file says N = 11,932, but its class counts add up to 11,931. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/statistics?dataset=zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment&config=default&split=train (same URL with split=validation), https://huggingface.co/datasets/zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment/raw/main/sent_dataset_meta.txt
- Parquet files, no token needed: `.../resolve/refs%2Fconvert%2Fparquet/default/train/0000.parquet` and `.../validation/0000.parquet` on the dataset repo. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/parquet?dataset=zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment
- No audit of its label noise was found. Related work says writer-tagged bullish/bearish labels on financial tweets are unreliable (Fin-SoMe). https://astro.paperswithcode.com/paper/issues-and-perspectives-from-10000-annotated

**takala/financial_phrasebank (FPB)**
- The main branch still contains `financial_phrasebank.py` and the viewer reports "Dataset scripts are no longer supported". The refs list shows branches `main` and `script` and `"converts":[]`. The `refs/convert/parquet` tree returns 404 and the datasets-server parquet endpoint returns 500. https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank/refs
- The `datasets` library dropped script loading in 4.0. The latest release is 5.1.0 (2026-10-05). https://discuss.huggingface.co/t/dataset-scripts-are-no-longer-supported/163891, https://pypi.org/project/datasets/
- The raw zip can still be fetched without a token (`gated:false`): `hf_hub_download("takala/financial_phrasebank", "data/FinancialPhraseBank-v1.0.zip", repo_type="dataset")`, 681,890 bytes. It contains `Sentences_{AllAgree,75Agree,66Agree,50Agree}.txt`, encoded iso-8859-1, one `sentence@label` per line (split with `rsplit("@",1)`). https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank/tree/main/data, https://huggingface.co/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank/raw/main/financial_phrasebank.py
- Config sizes: 50agree 4,846, 66agree 4,217, 75agree 3,453, allagree 2,264. AllAgree is about 13.4% negative / 61.4% neutral / 25.2% positive (≈303 / 1,391 / 570). Texts are single sentences, about 127 characters on average.
- Labels mean the expected influence on the stock price, from an investor's view. Each sentence had 5-8 annotators, all from Aalto.
- License is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. https://huggingface.co/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.04574
- Mirrors:
  - **atrost/financial_phrasebank**: ungated parquet of 50agree with the FinBERT split (train 3,100 / validation 776 / test 970; test is 125 neg / 565 neu / 280 pos). Labels 0 = neg, 1 = neu, 2 = pos. No license stated. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/parquet?dataset=atrost/financial_phrasebank
  - **ChanceFocus/flare-fpb**: ungated, 4,846 rows (so 50agree), card says MIT even though the source is NC-SA.
  - **TheFinAI/en-fpb**: gated, needs a login. https://huggingface.co/datasets/TheFinAI/en-fpb

**FiQA-2018 task 1**
- **pauri32/fiqa-2018**: ungated parquet with train 961 / validation 102 / test 150. Test is balanced 50 / 50 / 50 and splits into 81 posts and 69 headlines.
- Each row has a continuous `sentiment_score` (about -0.94 to 0.98), plus `target`, `aspects` and `format`.
- The label mapping is undocumented. The rows suggest 0 = pos, 1 = neu, 2 = neg. There is no license and no card. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/parquet?dataset=pauri32/fiqa-2018
- **TheFinAI/fiqa-sentiment-classification**: `gated:"auto"`, so it needs a token. https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/TheFinAI/fiqa-sentiment-classification

**SEntFiN 1.0**
- 10,753 headlines (2,847 with several entities), about 14,404 entity labels. Class split is roughly 35% positive / 26% negative / 38% neutral. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.12257, https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-9786449
- Raw CSV, no login: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pyRis/SEntFiN/main/SEntFiN.csv. Columns are `S No., Title, Decisions, Words`. `Decisions` is a Python-dict string such as `{'SpiceJet': 'neutral'}`.
- The repo is MIT-licensed. It is mostly Indian market news. Some labels look odd, for example "MMTC Q2 net loss" is labeled neutral. https://github.com/pyRis/SEntFiN
- The Kaggle copy needs a login.

**FinEntity**
- Ungated, ODC-BY. The single file is `FinEntity.json`, with a parquet conversion available.
- 979 news paragraphs of 108-581 characters. Each row lists entity spans (`start`/`end`) with Positive/Neutral/Negative labels. Some entities have conflicting labels. https://huggingface.co/datasets/yixuantt/FinEntity, https://github.com/yixuantt/FinEntity

**Longer-text candidates**
- **Jean-Baptiste/financial_news_sentiment**: MIT, ungated parquet. 1,779 rows of Canadian press releases (title plus opening text), with sentiment "manually validated".
  - Test split is 267 rows: label counts 12 / 156 / 99. The mapping is not documented; the rows suggest 0 = neg, 2 = pos.
  - Body mean is about 400 characters, max 1,304. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/statistics?dataset=Jean-Baptiste/financial_news_sentiment&config=default&split=test
- **NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment**: 100k web/news chunks of 63 to about 5,870 characters, ODC-By. The labels come from LLMs (majority vote, then GPT-5.1 active learning), not from people. https://huggingface.co/datasets/NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment
- **Economic News Article Tone (WSJ/WaPo)**: no license found. The sentometrics copy keeps only the relevance labels. https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/sentometrics/html/usnews.html
- No full-article financial sentiment dataset with human labels and a permissive license was found.

## Implications for the design

- **Loaders**: do not use `load_dataset` for FPB. Download the zip with `hf_hub_download` and parse it in our own code. For everything else, read the parquet or CSV files directly. No HF token is needed anywhere if TheFinAI and Kaggle copies are avoided.
- **Label mapping**: positive → Bullish, negative → Bearish. Keep a separate mapping per dataset, because the label ids differ between datasets.
- **Committing data to the public repo**:
  - Twitter (MIT): safe to commit the sampled IDs and text.
  - FinEntity and NOSIBLE (ODC-BY): safe to commit with attribution.
  - FPB (NC-SA) and FiQA (no license): do not commit. Download them when the eval runs.
- **Precision math**: the 95% margin on precision is about ±0.07 at 100 predicted positives and about ±0.04 at 300. Each directional class needs at least 300 gold items in the final eval.
- **Recommended sets**:
  - **Dev (prompt tuning)**: a seeded, stratified 300 from the Twitter train split (100 Bearish / 100 Bullish / 100 Neutral). That is about 1-10 minutes per model and prompt pair.
  - **Holdout (final ranking of the top 2-3 configs only)**:
    - (a) The full Twitter validation split (2,388 at its natural class mix, so precision reflects real prevalence). About 8-80 minutes per config.
    - (b) FPB AllAgree, all 2,264. These are the cleanest labels and use investor-impact semantics, so precision is least distorted by label noise.
  - **Cross-domain / longer text**:
    - FinEntity paragraphs where every entity has the same label (needs filtering, likely about 600).
    - All 267 rows of the Jean-Baptiste test split. Note it has only 12 Bearish examples.
    - Optionally, about 500 single-entity SEntFiN headlines.
- **Article-level gap**: the scraped inputs will be full articles, so either hand-label 50-100 of them (a user decision) or measure agreement with NOSIBLE as a silver check, not as accuracy. Also report how predictions shift with input length.
- **Neutral**: treat Neutral as "no signal". Report Bullish and Bearish precision separately, plus coverage and p50/p95 latency.

## Unknowns / could not verify

- How the Twitter dataset was annotated, and its actual noise rate.
- The class split of FPB 50agree and 75agree. The allagree counts are reconstructed from published percentages, not counted directly.
- FinEntity's entity class split. The paper PDF could not be parsed.
- Whether pyRis/SEntFiN is the authors' official release, and whether its MIT license covers the data.
- The Jean-Baptiste and pauri32 label mappings, which are inferred from sample rows.
- Licenses for FiQA-2018 and the Appen tone dataset.
- The exact contents of SEntFiN v1.1 on Kaggle. The page needs a login.

> The search didn't turn up a direct audit of label noise in the zeroshot dataset itself. The closest evidence concerns related financial-tweet data and how models trained on this dataset are described.
> 
> - **Writer-labeled bullish/bearish tags are unreliable.** A study of StockTwits tweets found that the reliability of writer-labeled data is sometimes poor. Its example is a tweet tagged bullish that lacks enough content. A related paper on 10,000 expert-annotated tweets (Fin-SoMe) concluded that writer-labeled market sentiment may be a misleading label.
> - **Bullish/bearish confusion.** In one model's confusion matrix, only 5.1% of Bullish labels are misclassified as Bearish, and 12.5% of Bearish labels are misclassified as Bullish. That is a different model and dataset, so it doesn't measure zeroshot's noise directly.
> - **Models trained on the dataset.** Community fine-tunes list zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment as their training data and report accuracy around 0.821 for a DistilBERT model and 0.843 for a BERT-Large model. These are accuracy figures, not label-quality audits.
> 
> My conclusion is that the evidence supports the general concern about bullish/bearish tag noise in financial tweets. I could not confirm a specific error rate for the zeroshot dataset. Searching for the dataset's Hugging Face card or its annotation description would be the next step.

Users report the error Dataset scripts are no longer supported, but found GAIA.py, and it also appears with `trust_remote_code=True`. Maintainers point to Parquet conversion as the fix. For example, one OpenSLR dataset was converted to Parquet, which makes it work with datasets>=4.0.
> 
> The main workarounds are:
> - **Pin an older version:** downgrading the datasets library to version 3.6.0 or earlier avoids the error.
> - **Load a converted copy:** Some repos have a Parquet branch. One user loaded the Parquet files from the refs/convert/parquet branch with the generic `parquet` loader.
> - **Use a builder class directly:** One forum answer notes that support for building datasets locally would continue, so a custom builder can be run with `download_and_prepare()` and `as_dataset()`.
> 
> One source gives a different version threshold. A Patho-Bench issue says datasets >= 4.5.0 dropped support, but the other reports and the 4.0.0 timing point to 4.0.0 as the release that removed it. I'd treat 4.0.0 as the version to check against, but I didn't confirm that against the official release notes, which I couldn't retrieve.

> ## Facts
> 
> **zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment**
> - Ungated, MIT. The repo holds `sent_train.csv`, `sent_valid.csv` and `sent_dataset_meta.txt`. https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment
> - Labels: 0 = Bearish, 1 = Bullish, 2 = Neutral. The text is finance tweets and headline-style lines. Nothing is published about how the labels were annotated. https://huggingface.co/datasets/zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment
> - Real split sizes are train 9,543 (1,442 / 1,923 / 6,178) and validation 2,388 (347 / 475 / 1,566). Mean length is about 86 characters, max 227. The card's table says 9,938 / 2,486, which is stale. The meta file says N = 11,932, but its class counts add up to 11,931. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/statistics?dataset=zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment&config=default&split=train (same URL with split=validation), https://huggingface.co/datasets/zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment/raw/main/sent_dataset_meta.txt
> - Parquet files, no token needed: `.../resolve/refs%2Fconvert%2Fparquet/default/train/0000.parquet` and `.../validation/0000.parquet` on the dataset repo. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/parquet?dataset=zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment
> - No audit of its label noise was found. Related work says writer-tagged bullish/bearish labels on financial tweets are unreliable (Fin-SoMe). https://astro.paperswithcode.com/paper/issues-and-perspectives-from-10000-annotated
> 
> **takala/financial_phrasebank (FPB)**
> - The main branch still contains `financial_phrasebank.py` and the viewer reports "Dataset scripts are no longer supported". The refs list shows branches `main` and `script` and `"converts":[]`. The `refs/convert/parquet` tree returns 404 and the datasets-server parquet endpoint returns 500. https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank/refs
> - The `datasets` library dropped script loading in 4.0. The latest release is 5.1.0 (2026-10-05). https://discuss.huggingface.co/t/dataset-scripts-are-no-longer-supported/163891, https://pypi.org/project/datasets/
> - The raw zip can still be fetched without a token (`gated:false`): `hf_hub_download("takala/financial_phrasebank", "data/FinancialPhraseBank-v1.0.zip", repo_type="dataset")`, 681,890 bytes. It contains `Sentences_{AllAgree,75Agree,66Agree,50Agree}.txt`, encoded iso-8859-1, one `sentence@label` per line (split with `rsplit("@",1)`). https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank/tree/main/data, https://huggingface.co/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank/raw/main/financial_phrasebank.py
> - Config sizes: 50agree 4,846, 66agree 4,217, 75agree 3,453, allagree 2,264. AllAgree is about 13.4% negative / 61.4% neutral / 25.2% positive (≈303 / 1,391 / 570). Texts are single sentences, about 127 characters on average.
> - Labels mean the expected influence on the stock price, from an investor's view. Each sentence had 5-8 annotators, all from Aalto.
> - License is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. https://huggingface.co/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.04574
> - Mirrors:
>   - **atrost/financial_phrasebank**: ungated parquet of 50agree with the FinBERT split (train 3,100 / validation 776 / test 970; test is 125 neg / 565 neu / 280 pos). Labels 0 = neg, 1 = neu, 2 = pos. No license stated. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/parquet?dataset=atrost/financial_phrasebank
>   - **ChanceFocus/flare-fpb**: ungated, 4,846 rows (so 50agree), card says MIT even though the source is NC-SA.
>   - **TheFinAI/en-fpb**: gated, needs a login. https://huggingface.co/datasets/TheFinAI/en-fpb
> 
> **FiQA-2018 task 1**
> - **pauri32/fiqa-2018**: ungated parquet with train 961 / validation 102 / test 150. Test is balanced 50 / 50 / 50 and splits into 81 posts and 69 headlines.
> - Each row has a continuous `sentiment_score` (about -0.94 to 0.98), plus `target`, `aspects` and `format`.
> - The label mapping is undocumented. The rows suggest 0 = pos, 1 = neu, 2 = neg. There is no license and no card. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/parquet?dataset=pauri32/fiqa-2018
> - **TheFinAI/fiqa-sentiment-classification**: `gated:"auto"`, so it needs a token. https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/TheFinAI/fiqa-sentiment-classification
> 
> **SEntFiN 1.0**
> - 10,753 headlines (2,847 with several entities), about 14,404 entity labels. Class split is roughly 35% positive / 26% negative / 38% neutral. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.12257, https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-9786449
> - Raw CSV, no login: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pyRis/SEntFiN/main/SEntFiN.csv. Columns are `S No., Title, Decisions, Words`. `Decisions` is a Python-dict string such as `{'SpiceJet': 'neutral'}`.
> - The repo is MIT-licensed. It is mostly Indian market news. Some labels look odd, for example "MMTC Q2 net loss" is labeled neutral. https://github.com/pyRis/SEntFiN
> - The Kaggle copy needs a login.
> 
> **FinEntity**
> - Ungated, ODC-BY. The single file is `FinEntity.json`, with a parquet conversion available.
> - 979 news paragraphs of 108-581 characters. Each row lists entity spans (`start`/`end`) with Positive/Neutral/Negative labels. Some entities have conflicting labels. https://huggingface.co/datasets/yixuantt/FinEntity, https://github.com/yixuantt/FinEntity
> 
> **Longer-text candidates**
> - **Jean-Baptiste/financial_news_sentiment**: MIT, ungated parquet. 1,779 rows of Canadian press releases (title plus opening text), with sentiment "manually validated".
>   - Test split is 267 rows: label counts 12 / 156 / 99. The mapping is not documented; the rows suggest 0 = neg, 2 = pos.
>   - Body mean is about 400 characters, max 1,304. https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/statistics?dataset=Jean-Baptiste/financial_news_sentiment&config=default&split=test
> - **NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment**: 100k web/news chunks of 63 to about 5,870 characters, ODC-By. The labels come from LLMs (majority vote, then GPT-5.1 active learning), not from people. https://huggingface.co/datasets/NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment
> - **Economic News Article Tone (WSJ/WaPo)**: no license found. The sentometrics copy keeps only the relevance labels. https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/sentometrics/html/usnews.html
> - No full-article financial sentiment dataset with human labels and a permissive license was found.
> 
> ## Implications for the design
> 
> - **Loaders**: do not use `load_dataset` for FPB. Download the zip with `hf_hub_download` and parse it in our own code. For everything else, read the parquet or CSV files directly. No HF token is needed anywhere if TheFinAI and Kaggle copies are avoided.
> - **Label mapping**: positive → Bullish, negative → Bearish. Keep a separate mapping per dataset, because the label ids differ between datasets.
> - **Committing data to the public repo**:
>   - Twitter (MIT): safe to commit the sampled IDs and text.
>   - FinEntity and NOSIBLE (ODC-BY): safe to commit with attribution.
>   - FPB (NC-SA) and FiQA (no license): do not commit. Download them when the eval runs.
> - **Precision math**: the 95% margin on precision is about ±0.07 at 100 predicted positives and about ±0.04 at 300. Each directional class needs at least 300 gold items in the final eval.
> - **Recommended sets**:
>   - **Dev (prompt tuning)**: a seeded, stratified 300 from the Twitter train split (100 Bearish / 100 Bullish / 100 Neutral). That is about 1-10 minutes per model and prompt pair.
>   - **Holdout (final ranking of the top 2-3 configs only)**:
>     - (a) The full Twitter validation split (2,388 at its natural class mix, so precision reflects real prevalence). About 8-80 minutes per config.
>     - (b) FPB AllAgree, all 2,264. These are the cleanest labels and use investor-impact semantics, so precision is least distorted by label noise.
>   - **Cross-domain / longer text**:
>     - FinEntity paragraphs where every entity has the same label (needs filtering, likely about 600).
>     - All 267 rows of the Jean-Baptiste test split. Note it has only 12 Bearish examples.
>     - Optionally, about 500 single-entity SEntFiN headlines.
> - **Article-level gap**: the scraped inputs will be full articles, so either hand-label 50-100 of them (a user decision) or measure agreement with NOSIBLE as a silver check, not as accuracy. Also report how predictions shift with input length.
> - **Neutral**: treat Neutral as "no signal". Report Bullish and Bearish precision separately, plus coverage and p50/p95 latency.
> 
> ## Unknowns / could not verify
> 
> - How the Twitter dataset was annotated, and its actual noise rate.
> - The class split of FPB 50agree and 75agree. The allagree counts are reconstructed from published percentages, not counted directly.
> - FinEntity's entity class split. The paper PDF could not be parsed.
> - Whether pyRis/SEntFiN is the authors' official release, and whether its MIT license covers the data.
> - The Jean-Baptiste and pauri32 label mappings, which are inferred from sample rows.
> - Licenses for FiQA-2018 and the Appen tone dataset.
> - The exact contents of SEntFiN v1.1 on Kaggle. The page needs a login.

## Implications for the design

1. **Export after the session ends.** The JSONL is still growing. Export after the final turn (ideally after `/exit`), and well before the 90-day cleanup.
2. **Use a repo-local `uv` script**, `scripts/export_transcript.py`, writing to `.context/transcript/`:
   - **`raw/`:** filtered copies of the main JSONL, `subagents/**`, the workflow `.js` scripts, `journal.jsonl`, `*.meta.json` and the plan file.
   - **Record types to drop:** `api-request-shape`, `api request blob`, `api-request` (keep only `params.model`, the beta flags and the thinking config in `meta.json`), `file-history-snapshot` and `atis-latch`.
   - **Attachments to drop:** `instructions` (CLAUDE.md), `session context` (the email), `credential_org`, `remote_session_change`, `environment`, `opened_file_in_ide`, `deferred_tools_delta` / `skill_listing` / `mcp_instructions_delta` (they list private skills and MCP servers), and hook stdout (Vercel and [redacted] plugins).
   - **Other edits:** strip thinking `signature` blobs; replace `~` with `~`; redact the email; leave out `tool-results/` or scan it before including.
   - **Rendering:** render the filtered JSONL with `uvx claude-code-log --depth agent` to HTML and with `--format md`, so subagents and the workflow tree are included. Optionally keep `/export` plain text as a backup.
   - **`meta.json`:**
     - harness: `Claude Code 2.1.301`, entrypoint `cli`
     - model: `claude-opus-5-5` (Opus 5.5); subagent alias `opus`
     - effort: `xhigh` per record; adaptive thinking
     - `ultracode:true`; plan mode from the `permission-mode` records
     - skills from `Skill` tool_use / `commandName`
     - workflows: one entry per `wf_*`, with script name and agent labels/models from `journal.jsonl` and the meta files

> **claude-code-log: Report**

> - **Latest version:** 1.7.0, released Oct 5, 2026. The project has 17 prior releases, starting with 0.1.0 in June 2025.

> - **Output formats:** HTML (per-session and combined project pages, plus a master index) and Markdown (`--format md`). The page doesn't mention JSON output.
> - **Subagent/sidechain transcripts:** Not stated. The page mentions Task (agent delegation) calls as signals kept at the `low` detail level, but doesn't say whether subagent transcripts are rendered.
> - **Token usage display:** Yes. It shows token counts per message and session totals in HTML, and token usage appears in the TUI's session list and expanded rows.
> - **Thinking blocks:** Listed as a supported message type, described as Claude's internal reasoning. The page doesn't describe how they're displayed or whether they can be hidden or collapsed.
> - **Exporting a single session:**
>   - Pass a file path: `claude-code-log transcript.jsonl`, optionally with `-o <file>` and `--format md`.
>   - Use `--provider agy|codex --session-id <id>` for experimental single-session exports from Antigravity CLI or Codex CLI.
>   - In the TUI, press `h` for HTML or `m` for Markdown.
> - **Homepage/repo:** https://github.com/daaain/claude-code-log (issues are tracked there too).
> - **Maintenance status:** The page doesn't state this directly. Its cadence (1.5.0 in July, 1.6.0 in August, 1.7.0 in October 2026) and the presence of a changelog suggest active development. It has one listed maintainer.

> The search didn't turn up official documentation for a built-in `/export` command that writes Markdown transcripts with subagents included. The results are third-party guides and tools, so treat them as secondhand.
>

>

> - `--depth` (session, user, assistant, agent, tool, hook) controls how much is rendered.
> - `--detail` is deprecated and maps to the depth levels. It will be removed in 2.0.
> - `--no-recaps` drops recap summaries.
> - `--compact` merges repeated Markdown headings.

###### 🌐 WebFetch `https://ccusage.com/guide/session-reports`

`11:04:44`

```
How to get a report for one specific session id (flag name, e.g. --id), JSON output flag, fields in session JSON, whether subagent JSONL files are included, deduplication behavior, offline pricing.
```

> **Single session lookup:** Use the `--id` flag, or `-i` for short. For example, `ccusage claude session --id <session-id>`. Codex accepts the full `sessionId`, the JSONL filename with or without its extension, the trailing UUID, or a `codex://threads/<uuid>` URI. Shortened UUIDs are rejected, and ambiguous UUIDs are reported as errors.
> 
> **JSON output:** Add `--json`, as in `ccusage codex session --id <session-id> --json`.
> 
> **Session JSON fields:** Each entry in `sessions` includes:
> - `sessionId`
> - `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cacheCreationTokens`, `cacheReadTokens`, `totalTokens`
> - `totalCost`
> - `firstActivity`, `lastActivity`
> - `modelsUsed`
> - `modelBreakdowns`, each with `model`, `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, and `totalCost`
> 
> The top-level `totals` object contains `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, and `totalCost`.
> 
> **Subagent JSONL files:** The page doesn't say whether they're included.
> 
> **Deduplication:** The page doesn't describe any deduplication behavior.
> 
> **Offline pricing:** Use `--offline` or `-O` to rely on cached pricing data without network access.

## Context

VeriTrade prescreen (`.context/prescreen-brief-kristiyan-dimitrov.md`): a Python API that takes a public
financial-news URL, fetches + extracts the article, and returns an LLM summary + Bullish/Bearish/Neutral
sentiment with low latency, plus a basic frontend, README (design + latency trade-offs, run/test

  - Group 1 (split): fast "decision" model on a dedicated signal endpoint + separate summary endpoint.
  - Group 2 (combined): one endpoint, one low-tier ("haiku-grade") model.

  - Evals on public labelled sentiment datasets; prompt tuned per model; optimise precision over recall.

> - **Selection metric:** F0.5, averaged over the bullish and bearish classes. It weights precision twice as much as recall, and "always say neutral" can't game it because recall still counts.
> - **Hard limit:** the share of bullish-to-bearish flips (or the reverse) must stay under a small cap, e.g. 2%. These are reported separately because they're the worst error.
> - **Accuracy vs speed:** the winner is the best F0.5 among setups that fit a latency budget. We set that budget in round 2, once we know your hardware.
> 
> The alternatives are bullish/bearish precision with a minimum recall (e.g. at least 30%), or plain macro-F1 (the research doc's default, which doesn't favour precision).

## Verdicts

1. **PARTLY (most details right).** clef-flash exists. The page calls it "a 9B decision model from Cloudflare", fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-9B, Apache 2.0, needs Ollama 0.35.1 or later.

   - Context window is inconsistent: the tags list 256K, the page highlights say 64K, and Cloudflare's hosted version is now 24K.
   - `clef` (27B, Qwen3.8-27B base) exists, with local tags at 18–20 GB and also `clef:cloud`.

2. **CONFIRMED, with corrections.** `POST /v1/systemone` "Returns one JSON response; streaming, video, tools, and generation controls are not supported."

   - The response has **no timing fields**. The Go struct only has `model`, `answers` and `usage`, plus an undocumented `prompt_eval_cached_count`.

## `/v1/systemone` examples (from docs.ollama.com/api/systemone.md and openapi.yaml)

```bash
curl http://localhost:11434/v1/systemone \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "nimble",
    "state": "Our checkout has returned 500 errors since 9am.",
    "questions": {
      "label": {
        "type": "choice",
        "instructions": "Which label fits this ticket?",
        "criteria": {
          "billing": "Payments and refunds",
          "bug": "Software errors",
          "account": "Login and account access"
        }
      }
    }
  }'
```

```yaml
model: nimble
answers:
  label:
    type: choice
    choice: bug
    probabilities: {billing: 0.0125, bug: 0.9781, account: 0.0093}
    confidence: 0.8906
usage: {input_tokens: 174, output_tokens: 1}
```

**Question shapes:**
- **choice**: each option in `criteria` maps to a description string or `null` (null means a bare label). Ties follow the model's option order.
- **noul**: `criteria` is optional and only takes `"true"` and `"false"`. The answer is a probability of true between 0 and 1, not a boolean.
- **score**: `criteria` is an array of 2–10 descriptions, lowest first. The answer has `score` (a fractional weighted average), `legend`, `probabilities` and `confidence`.
- **confidence** for choice and score is 1 − H(p)/ln(N), which measures how concentrated the distribution is. The docs say it is not calibrated correctness.

**Other limits:**
- Locally, text plus schema must be 64 KiB or less, and the whole request 32 MiB or less. Input is "never truncated" but must fit the loaded context. The v0.40.4 notes do say the MLX runner now "clips long states", which conflicts with that.
- Nimble and Tev need two token positions for scoring.
- The code mentions a server-side `runner` request field that the docs don't.

## What changes the 3-class sentiment endpoint design

- **Batching is per text, not across texts.** The 64-question limit is many questions about one shared `state`. For N headlines, send N concurrent requests rather than packing them into one state, because `usage` counts the shared context again for each question.
- **Use one `choice` question** with `bullish`/`bearish`/`neutral` and a description for each. Put `neutral` first so ties fall to it.
- **Use `probabilities`, not `confidence`, for thresholds.** None of the sources has a sentiment benchmark for any of these models, so you'll need to evaluate on your own labelled set.
- **Measure latency on the client.** The response has no timing fields. Set `keep_alive: -1` so the model stays loaded between requests.
- **Linux `ollama/ollama` container:** only GGUF tags apply. laya, kev and strands-decider are MLX-only.
  - Usable candidates: `tev1:0.8b-q8_0` (834 MB), `tev1:4b-q4_K_M` (2.8 GB), `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` (5.6 GB), `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` (11 GB), and possibly `d1:3b` (3.7 GB, not confirmed as a decision model).
  - Pin version 0.40.4 or later. That release added "native decision model support" in llama.cpp, and the server has an error for old Clef GGUF downloads ("downloaded in a format that is no longer supported… run 'ollama pull'"). So re-pull the models.
- **Keep inputs short.** Effective context is about 2K tokens for tev1, 8,192 for nimble, 512 for laya and 4K for strands-decider, whatever the tag list says.
- **Licences:** avoid `nimble-v3` for commercial use (CC BY-NC). clef-flash, nimble and laya are Apache 2.0. tev1's page doesn't state a licence for the weights.
- **Published latency is from other hardware.** Cloudflare's hosted clef-flash measured 38.8 ms median, and nimble-v3 on llama.cpp Q4_K_M measured 168 ms median on an M5 Max (MLX 88–103 ms). Expect slower on a Linux GPU, and much slower on CPU.
- **Fallback path:** a regular LLM on `/api/chat` with `logprobs` and `top_logprobs` (20 or fewer) over a one-token label. The docs don't say how that combines with a `format` enum or `think`, so test it yourself.

Cloudflare's original Oct 1 post and the Oct 9 follow-up don't mention Ollama at all. I didn't use secondary blogs except to find the Cloudflare URLs.

Sources: [eesel.ai](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/cloudflare-clef), [infoq](https://infoq.com/news/2026/10/clef-decision-models), [developersdigest](https://www.developersdigest.tech/blog/cloudflare-clef-decision-models-2026). These came from search results; only the primary URLs above back the verdicts.

> 
> I can't reproduce the page verbatim because of the quote-length limit, so this summarizes it. The page doesn't document `options`, `stream`, or timing fields like `total_duration`. It says streaming, video, tools, and generation controls are not supported.
> 
> **Endpoint:** `POST /v1/systemone`, on `http://localhost:11434` (local) or `https://ollama.com` (cloud). Cloud requests need a bearer API key. Requires Ollama v0.35.0+, or v0.40.5+ for cloud models.
> 
> ## Request fields
> 
> - **`model`** (required, string): A System One model such as `nimble`, or `clef:cloud` for cloud.
> - **`state`** (required): A nonempty string, or a JSON object or array. It isn't parsed as chat messages.
> - **`questions`** (required): An object of 1 to 64 named questions about the shared state. Answers aren't passed between questions, so this is the batching mechanism.
> - **`images`** (optional): Base64-encoded images shared by all questions. Requires a vision model such as Clef. URLs and data URLs aren't supported.
> - **`keep_alive`** (optional): A duration string or seconds. Zero unloads after the request, and a negative value keeps the model loaded. Defaults to 5m.
> 
> ## Question types
> 
> - **`choice`**: `instructions` plus `criteria`, a map of option keys to descriptions or `null`. Requires 2 to 255 options, and keys can't be blank. Ties follow the model's option order.
> - **`noul`**: A two-outcome (false/true) question. `instructions` is required. `criteria` is optional, with `true` and `false` descriptions, and defaults apply if omitted.
> - **`score`**: `instructions` plus `criteria`, an ordered array of 2 to 10 descriptions from lowest to highest. The scale runs from 0 to the number of criteria minus 1.
> 
> ## Response
> 
> Top-level fields: `model`, `answers` (keyed by question name), and `usage`.
> 
> - **Choice answer:** `type`, `choice` (highest-probability key), `probabilities` (normalized, summing to 1), and `confidence`.
> - **Noul answer:** `type` and `noul`, a number from 0 to 1 giving the probability of true. It isn't a Boolean.
> - **Score answer:** `type`, `score` (a probability-weighted average from 0 to the number of criteria minus 1, not rounded), `legend` (index strings mapped to descriptions), `probabilities` (keyed by index strings), and `confidence`.
> - **`confidence`:** Computed as 1 − H(p)/ln(N), where N is the candidate count. It measures distribution concentration and isn't calibrated correctness.
> - **`usage`:** `input_tokens` (includes image positions and recounts shared context for each separately scored question) and `output_tokens` (internal scoring tokens, not JSON length).
> 
> ## Limits
> 
> **Local:**
> - Text and schema, excluding images, must be 64 KiB or less.
> - The whole request must be 32 MiB or less.
> - The full input must fit the loaded context window. Input is never truncated.
> - Nimble and Tev need two token positions for scoring.
> 
> **Cloud:**
> - Requires a paid plan or purchased usage credits.
> - Up to 64 questions per request.
> - Question names are up to 100 ASCII letters, digits, `_`, `.`, or `-`.
> - Up to 4 images, each at most 4 MiB and 16 megapixels, 8 MiB total.
> - The request must be 13 MiB or less, and input must fit the 65,536-token context window.
> 
> ## Errors
> 
> - **400:** Invalid request, unsupported model or runner, or prompt over the context or token limit.
> - **401:** Cloud model without sign-in or with an invalid key. Local responses include a `signin_url`.
> - **402:** Cloud model not included in the Free plan, or a failed payment.
> - **404:** Model not found. Download a local model first.
> - **413:** Size limits exceeded.
> - **500:** Model loading, rendering, or scoring failed.
> 
> ## Examples
> 
> The page's curl example sends model `nimble`, a support-ticket `state`, and a `label` choice question with options `billing`, `bug`, and `account`. The sample response returns `bug` as the choice, with a confidence of 0.8906, and usage of 174 input and 1 output tokens. For the exact JSON, see https://docs.ollama.com/llms.txt, which links to the full OpenAPI spec.

> I can't reproduce every code example verbatim. The source limits quotes to 125 characters, and full curl commands and JSON responses exceed that. Here is a summary, with short excerpts where useful.
> 
> **Supported models and requirements**
> - Decision models: Nimble and Tev1 (text), plus Clef and Clef Flash, which can also judge images.
> - Start Ollama "v0.35.0 or later" to use the decision models. Clef image judging requires v0.35.1 or later.
> - Local requests need no API key.
> - Cloud Clef requires a local server at v0.40.5 or later, signed in to ollama.com, or a direct call with an API key.
> - The page doesn't address MLX vs. llama.cpp/GGUF runners, Linux or Docker support, or Python and JavaScript client libraries.
> 
> **CLI usage (`ollama run`)**
> - Ask a yes/no question: `ollama run nimble --ask "..."`, with the input piped in or given as a file.
> - Add `--choice label="description"` to pick a label.
> - Add `--level` repeatedly, ordered from lowest to highest, to score on a scale.
> - Repeat `--ask` to ask several questions at once.
> - Reference JSON fields in backticks, and use `--format json` for the full response.
> - Judge images with `ollama run clef ./receipt.png --ask "..."`.
> - Without a state, the interactive prompt takes your first message as the state. Later lines are yes/no questions. `/clear` starts over.
> 
> **Declaring questions (API)**
> 
> Questions go in a `questions` object, each with a `type`, `instructions`, and `criteria`:
> - `choice`: 2–26 named options, each with a description. Returns the most likely option, all probabilities, and a confidence value.
> - `noul`: descriptions for `"false"` and `"true"`. Returns the probability of `true`.
> - `score`: 2–10 descriptions ordered from lowest to highest. Returns a probability-weighted average of zero-based levels, so with three levels the result ranges from 0 to 2.
> 
> **Images**
> - Send base64-encoded PNG, JPEG, or WebP files in `images`. URLs and data URLs are rejected.
> - Images are shared by all questions. `state` is still required.
> 
> **Limits and billing (cloud)**
> - Up to 64 questions per request.
> - Up to 4 images, each at most 4 MiB and 16 megapixels, 8 MiB total.
> - Input is capped at 65,536 tokens. Billing is per input token.
> 
> **Batching and latency**
> - The page doesn't give batching or latency guidance. It does show that multiple questions can share one request.
> 
> **Calibration and interpretation**
> - `confidence` for `choice` and `score` measures how strongly the model favors one answer. It does not guarantee correctness.
> - Results "can vary with the model and configuration."
> - The page says nothing about option order, tie-breaking, or prompt tips.

> - **Scoring tokens:** Nimble and Tev require two token positions for scoring.

> **Note:** I can't reproduce the full logprobs text verbatim. I've quoted only short fragments (well under 125 characters each) and paraphrased the rest.
> 
> ## Request parameters
> 
> - **`logprobs`** (boolean): Controls whether log probabilities of the output tokens are returned. The spec describes it as "Whether to return log probabilities of the output tokens."
> - **`top_logprobs`** (integer): Sets how many of the most likely tokens are returned at each token position. It applies only when `logprobs` is enabled. The spec gives no maximum (cap) value.
> 
> ## Response shape
> 
> The top-level response has a **`logprobs`** field: an array of `Logprob` objects, populated when logprobs are enabled.
> 
> Each `Logprob` object contains:
> 
> - **`token`** (string): The text representation of the token.
> - **`logprob`** (number): The log probability of this token.
> - **`bytes`** (array of integers): The raw byte representation of the token.
> - **`top_logprobs`** (array of `TokenLogprob`): The most likely alternative tokens at this position, with their log probabilities.
> 
> Each `TokenLogprob` object contains **`token`**, **`logprob`**, and **`bytes`**, with the same meanings as above. It describes a single alternative token.
> 
> ## Example code blocks
> 
> The spec includes no logprobs example. Its code samples cover Default, Non-streaming, Structured outputs, Tool calling, Thinking, and Images.
> 
> ## Interaction with `format` or `think`
> 
> The spec doesn't mention logprobs in connection with either field. The `format` field (JSON or a JSON schema) and the `think` field (`ThinkValue`) are documented without any reference to logprobs.
> 
> ## All request fields
> 
> 1. **`model`** (string, required): Model name.
> 2. **`messages`** (array, required): Chat history as message objects, each with a role and content.
> 3. **`tools`** (array): Optional function tool definitions the model may call.
> 4. **`format`** (string `"json"` or object): Response format, either `json` or a JSON schema.
> 5. **`options`** (object): Runtime generation options, such as seed, temperature, top_k, top_p, min_p, stop, num_ctx, and num_predict.
> 6. **`stream`** (boolean, default `true`): Whether to stream the response.
> 7. **`think`** (boolean, string, or null): Controls thinking output. Supported values depend on the model.
> 8. **`keep_alive`** (string or number): How long the model stays loaded, for example `5m` or `0`.
> 9. **`logprobs`** (boolean): Whether to return output token log probabilities.
> 10. **`top_logprobs`** (integer): Number of most likely tokens to return per position when logprobs are enabled.
