# 01 - Design decisions

Every decision below was settled with Kris in a `/grill-me` interview (2026-10-16 to 2026-10-18) before any code
was written. Background facts came from read-only research agents (local machine, Ollama library, Docker/CI, news
sources, datasets, transcript format) and were re-verified against primary sources where they were surprising
(the Ollama decision-model API). The full conversation is in `.context/transcript/`.

Guiding principle (Kris, R2): **this is a PoC - balance the level of rigor per aspect**, no exhaustive sweeps.

## Round 1

| # | Question | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Where does the Ollama server run? | Native Ollama on the host is the documented default on macOS; a `bundled` compose profile runs `ollama/ollama` (CPU) for Linux/CI; `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` switches; benchmarks are labelled `native-metal` / `docker-cpu` | Docker Desktop cannot pass Apple's GPU into Linux containers (~0.2x prompt-eval, ~0.4x generation vs native); reviewers on Macs will have Ollama anyway |
| Q2 | What does "precision" mean, how is a winner picked? | Positives are directional calls (bullish/bearish); neutral is the safe default. Selection metric F0.5 macro over {bullish, bearish}; bullish<->bearish inversions capped at 2%; winner = best F0.5 inside the latency budget, else the Pareto knee | A wrong call costs a trade, a missed call costs little; F0.5 cannot be gamed by "always neutral" |
| Q3 | Sentiment output contract | 3-class `sentiment` + `abstained`; compare two precision knobs for generative models (label-token logprob threshold vs ordinal -2..+2 \|score\| threshold) and keep the better one; decision models threshold their native class probabilities | Ollama emits logprobs, but only for non-streaming calls; the ordinal knob also works when streaming |
| Q4 | What does the quick signal read? | `scope=lede` (headline + opening paragraphs) by default, `scope=full` available; both evaluated for accuracy and speed | Lede matches headline-level datasets and decision-model context limits; prompt length drives latency |
| Q5 | Article-level gold set | 90 real articles (10 sources x 3 classes x 3), labelled by Opus subagents, no human check | Public datasets are sentences/headlines; real requests are full articles |
| Q6 | Public datasets and splits | Dev: stratified 300 from Twitter Financial News train. Holdout: full Twitter validation + Financial PhraseBank AllAgree (downloaded at eval time, never committed, CC BY-NC-SA) + FinEntity single-label paragraphs | Twitter FNS already uses Bearish/Bullish/Neutral and has official splits; FPB is the cleanest cross-domain check |
| Q7 | Prompt tuning method | Automated grid per model, then one manual error-analysis pass, freeze, run holdout once. Optional backlog starts with a DSPy-style optimizer loop | Reproducible and explainable within a PoC budget |
| Q8 | API surface | `/api/signal`, `/api/summary`, `/api/analyze`, `/api/models`, `/api/health`; model allowlist; per-URL fetch cache with single-flight; result cache; timing breakdown in every response; SSE **and** JSON variants for `/summary` and `/analyze` | Streaming improves perceived latency; both variants make the comparison measurable |
| Q9 | How the UI is served | Reopened in round 2 (R1) | - |
| Q10 | Extraction | Full parser x extractor comparison matrix, switchable from the UI, results published | Extraction quality and speed both feed end-to-end latency |
| Q11 | Fixtures and publisher rights | Skeleton fixtures (real DOM structure, synthetic text) + scheduled live smoke; article texts never committed (URL + hash + labels only) | Respect each publisher's content rights in a public repo |
| Q12 | CI | Everything on GitHub Actions, including e2e with a real tiny model | Free for public repos |
| Q13 | Transcript | Redacted raw JSONL + rendered Markdown/HTML + `meta.json` under `.context/transcript/`, stripped of anything not suitable for a public repo | The brief asks for the AI log; Kris wants reviewers to read it |
| Q14 | Git workflow | Milestone commits straight to `main`, no feature branches; repo-local author Kristiyan Dimitrov; public repo `cleverjobs/veritrade-analytics` | Solo PoC |
| Q15 | Tooling | Python 3.13 uv workspace (`backend`, `evals`), ruff + mypy; Node 24 + pnpm, Next.js 16 strict TS, ESLint + Prettier, Vitest + RTL + MSW, Playwright | Conventional, fast |
| Q16 | Native Ollama install | `brew install ollama` + `brew services` | Metal acceleration for evals and the native path |
| Q17 | Model roster | See R2 and the follow-ups | - |
| Q18 | Top-10 sources | Yahoo Finance, CNBC, AP News, Investing.com, Motley Fool, Benzinga, PR Newswire, GlobeNewswire, SEC EDGAR 8-K EX-99.1, CNN Business; backups Fortune, Business Wire, Guardian, BBC; the live probe decides | Reviewer likelihood x accessibility; the brief names earnings reports, EDGAR is their primary source |
| Q19 | Fetch identity | Standard browser header set, no evasion (no captcha solving, proxies or TLS impersonation); typed `source_blocked` / `paywalled` / `consent_required` errors with hints; `SEC_USER_AGENT` for EDGAR | Neither end of the spectrum |
| Q20 | Yahoo EU consent wall | Submit "reject all" and cache the cookie; fall back to `consent_required` | Gets the article without granting tracking consent on anyone's behalf |

## Round 2

| # | Question | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | UI serving topology | FastAPI serves the static Next.js export from the same origin (multi-stage Docker build); dev uses `pnpm dev` + CORS for localhost | No proxy hop on the latency path, no nginx, no Node at runtime; the brief requires a Python backend anyway |
| R2 | Decision models | `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` + `nimble:9b-q4_K_M`, with `qwen3.5:0.8b` as the generative baseline | PoC balance; clef-flash by request, nimble best published accuracy among the rest |
| R3 | Streaming `/analyze` | Typed SSE events `meta` -> `sentiment` -> `summary_delta*` -> `done`; JSON field order (sentiment-first vs summary-first) is an eval dimension | Sentiment arrives after a handful of output tokens when it is generated first |
| R4 | Extraction matrix + reference | 4 parsers x 4 own strategies + trafilatura (default, precision), readability-lxml, newspaper4k, justext, strip-tags; reference bodies produced by Opus, kept local (gitignored) | Comparable quality metric without publishing article text |
| R5 | Article-set procedure | Opus discovery via RSS/sections (last ~60 days, fetchable by our fetcher); two independent Opus labellers + adjudicator, ambiguous articles replaced; agreement reported; split 30 dev / 60 test | Stand-in for a human check |
| R6 | Summary evaluation | Deterministic checks (numbers grounded in source, entity named, length) + key-fact coverage via a local embedding model + Opus-as-judge on finalists | Cheap reproducible signal plus a strong judge where it matters |
| R7 | Latency budgets (native, warm, excl. fetch) | `/signal` lede p50 <= 500 ms; `/summary` and `/analyze` TTFT <= 1.5 s, complete p50 <= 4 s; unrealistic budgets are surfaced, not silently moved | Concrete selection gate |
| R8 | Bundled models | Per-endpoint winners if they total <= ~10 GB, else the best finalist that fits; all other Docker containers stopped during setup | Docker Desktop VM has 15.6 GiB |
| R9 | Transcript scope | Only this build session (main + subagents + workflows) | No other relevant sessions |
| R10 | Docs layout | `.context/docs/design/NN-*.md`, backlog in `90-optional-backlog.md`, eval reports in `evals/results/` | Book-order reading |

## Follow-ups

- Generative roster trimmed: summary {`qwen3.5:2b`, `qwen3.5:4b`}; combined {`qwen3.5:4b`, `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507`,
  `ministral-3:3b`}; `qwen3.5:9b` only as a holdout quality ceiling; Gemma 4 dropped (open think+format bug).
- Lean prompt grid: 2 rubric styles x few-shot {0, 4} x field order where relevant (<= 8 configs per model).
- Stopped Docker containers stay stopped; the restart command is handed back at the end.
- `tev1:0.8b-q8_0` is used only in CI to exercise the real decision-model path in containers; it is not evaluated.

## Build-time findings that adjusted the plan

Measured during P1/P2, recorded here so the deviations are traceable. Inputs for the Ollama probe were synthetic
(`evals/results/ollama_probe.json`, native Metal, warm, n=5).

- **Sources** (`02-source-probe.md`): AP News, Investing.com, Benzinga and Business Wire refuse a plain client at
  their CDN (Cloudflare / Akamai), so all four backups were promoted. Final 10: Yahoo Finance, CNBC, Motley Fool,
  PR Newswire, GlobeNewswire, SEC EDGAR EX-99.1, CNN Business, Fortune, Guardian Business, BBC Business.
- **R7 sanity gate passed**: each endpoint has at least one candidate inside its budget, so no budget moved.
  - `/signal`: `qwen3.5:0.8b` answers in 190 ms at ~510 prompt tokens. The 9B decision models take 1.3-1.5 s
    at the same size, so they are reported against the budget rather than the budget relaxed for them.
  - `/summary`: `qwen3.5:2b` shows first text at 0.93 s and finishes at 2.2 s on ~1.6k-token articles;
    `qwen3.5:4b` misses the 1.5 s TTFT budget at that size (2.4 s).
  - `/analyze`: `ministral-3:3b` reaches the score at 1.47 s and finishes at 3.5 s on ~1.75k tokens; the 4B
    qwen models miss TTFT at full-article size.
- **Logprobs**: Ollama 0.40.6 also returns logprobs on streamed chunks (undocumented). The knob comparison stays
  on non-streaming `/signal`; `/analyze` keeps the ordinal knob. Logprob-weighted streaming confidence goes to
  the backlog.
- **Field order**: `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507` ignores schema property order (always entity, score, summary) and
  ignores `think:false` when a schema is set, so the field-order dimension runs on `qwen3.5:4b` and
  `ministral-3:3b` only.
- **Fetch cap** raised from 5 MB to 10 MB: CNN article pages are 5.7-6.6 MB decompressed.
- **Sampling penalties zeroed**: the qwen3.5 Modelfiles ship `presence_penalty 1.5`, which still applies under
  greedy decoding. Few-shot answers end in `neutral` / `0`, so the penalty pushed generated labels away from
  neutral (26 of 60 dev tweets disagreed with the logprob argmax; 0 of 60 with the penalty off). Every chat call
  now pins `presence_penalty 0`, `frequency_penalty 0`, `repeat_penalty 1`; `num_predict` still bounds runaway
  output.
- **Length-cut generations are salvaged**: a summary or analyze output that hits `num_predict` returns its fields
  with the summary cut to the last full sentence and `truncated: true`, instead of a 502 after a doubled-budget
  retry.
- **Summary length is enforced in serving** (R6 follow-up): no candidate reached the 0.8 deterministic pass rate
  on the dev articles, mostly on the 60-word cap. Rather than relax the gate, the service caps every summary at
  3 sentences / 60 words at a sentence boundary, and the frozen prompts ask for 2-3 sentences of at most 50 words
  that name the primary entity first.
- **Key-fact coverage threshold 0.60** (R6): a hand spot-check of 45 key facts on 10 dev articles agreed best
  at a cosine of 0.60 (33/45); 0.75 marked no false "covered" but missed 20 stated facts. 0.60 is primary and
  0.75 is reported as a conservative bound; the Opus judge remains the selection signal.

# 02 - Source probe

Question (Q18, Q19): which of the 14 candidate publishers can a plain Python client fetch, with no evasion,
and what do the extractors need to know about each one? The answer is measured, not assumed:
`scripts/probe_sources.py` fetched every candidate live on 2026-10-18 and its output decided
`backend/src/veritrade/data/sources.toml`.

## Method

- **Client**: `httpx 0.28.1` `AsyncClient`, HTTP/2, the Chrome 155 desktop header set from
  `veritrade.fetch.headers` (UA, Accept, `Accept-Language: en-US`, client hints, `Sec-Fetch-*`,
  `Upgrade-Insecure-Requests`, `Priority`), `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br` because `brotli` is installed.
  `sec.gov` gets the declared `SEC_USER_AGENT` and no Chrome hints. No cookies are pre-seeded, no TLS
  impersonation, headless browser, proxy or captcha solving (Q19).
- **Redirects**: followed by hand (max 5), exactly as the serving fetcher will; a hop to Yahoo's consent hosts is
  answered once with reject-all (`veritrade.fetch.consent`) and the original URL retried.
- **Politeness**: one request at a time per registrable domain with at least 1 s between them; EDGAR at 5 req/s
  (half its 10 req/s fair-access ceiling). Reported fetch times exclude these waits.
- **Discovery**: each source's `feeds` (RSS/Atom, non-English `dc:language` items skipped) or `sections`
  (HTML pages and sitemaps), filtered by `article_pattern`; the 3 newest matches are probed. EDGAR resolves the
  8-K Atom feed to filing indexes and then to the EX-99.1 exhibit, preferring index descriptions that say press
  release, earnings or results. When a source refuses its own hubs, links to it are harvested from the other
  sources' captured pages (AP).
- **Per article** (all in `evals/data/source_probe.json`, metadata only): status, final URL, redirects, bytes,
  network ms, `detect.classify` outcome and time, JSON-LD types / `articleBody` words / `isAccessibleForFree` /
  `hasPart` selectors, framework JSON markers, ranked body-container candidates with paragraph and word counts
  under both parsers, noise blocks inside the best container (selectors only) and press-release boilerplate
  labels (label and position only). Raw HTML goes to `evals/data/private/probe/<source>/<n>.html` (gitignored).
- **Profile check**: every `[sources.<key>.profile]` is applied with selectolax (Lexbor) and lxml `cssselect`;
  it passes when both parsers keep the same paragraphs in the same order (non-whitespace characters within 1%)
  and the body has at least 120 words. `--reanalyze` reruns all analysis on the saved HTML without network,
  which is how the profiles were tuned.

## Results

Vantage: residential ISP in Bulgaria (EU), macOS, Sunday 2026-10-18. Fetch ms is network time per article
(median, max of 3); size is the median HTML size.

| Source | Discovery used | OK | Fetch ms | Size | JSON-LD NewsArticle / articleBody | `isAccessibleForFree` | Blocks, consent | Profile |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yahoo Finance | `/topic/stock-market-news/` page (RSS now 404) | 3/3 | 477 (575) | 682 KB | 3 / 0 | absent | none; no consent redirect | 3/3 |
| CNBC | RSS `id/100003114` | 3/3 | 161 (221) | 838 KB | 3 / 0 | absent | none | 3/3 |
| Motley Fool | RSS `foolwatch` | 3/3 | 202 (235) | 372 KB | 3 / 0 | absent | none | 3/3 |
| PR Newswire | RSS financial services | 3/3 | 34 (43) | 219 KB | 3 / 0 | absent | none | 3/3 |
| GlobeNewswire | RSS public companies | 3/3 | 552 (662) | 74 KB | 3 / 0 | true | none | 3/3 |
| SEC 8-K EX-99.1 | Atom, 25 indexes, 2 releases + 1 statement | 3/3 | 135 (538) | 19 KB | 0 / 0 | absent | none (declared UA) | 3/3 |
| CNN Business | `edition.cnn.com/business` page (no RSS) | 3/3 | 35 (50) | 5.7 MB | 3 / 3 | false, full text served | none; www redirects to edition for EU | 3/3 |
| Fortune | RSS | 3/3 | 367 (495) | 431 KB | 3 / 0 | "False", full text served | none | 3/3 |
| Guardian Business | RSS `uk/business` | 3/3 | 116 (169) | 412 KB | 3 / 0 | true | none | 3/3 |
| BBC Business | RSS | 3/3 | 26 (62) | 394 KB | 3 / 0 | absent | none | 3/3 |
| AP News | hub + news sitemap both 403; 3 links harvested | 0/3 | - | - | - | - | Cloudflare managed challenge (403, `cf-mitigated: challenge`) on every path | - |
| Investing.com | RSS works | 0/3 | - | - | - | - | Cloudflare 403 with a 3-byte body on every HTML page | - |
| Benzinga | Google News sitemap works | 0/3 | - | - | - | - | Cloudflare "Sorry, you have been blocked" 403 on every HTML page | - |
| Business Wire | MRSS feed works | 0/3 | - | - | - | - | Akamai 403 "Page Unavailable" on releases; `/newsroom` serves an Akamai interactive challenge with HTTP 200 | - |

Every response came over HTTP/2 and no article URL redirected. One PR Newswire release took 6.8 s on a cache
miss during an earlier run, close to the 8 s fetch deadline.

## Decision

Final 10 (`status = "primary"`, `rank` in `sources.toml`), plan order with backups swapped in for the
rejected sources:

1. Yahoo Finance
2. CNBC
3. The Motley Fool
4. PR Newswire
5. GlobeNewswire
6. SEC EDGAR 8-K EX-99.1
7. CNN Business
8. Fortune (replaces AP News)
9. The Guardian Business (replaces Investing.com)
10. BBC Business (replaces Benzinga)

The mix is 7 news outlets, 2 press-release wires and 1 regulatory filing source. **No backups remain**: the
fourth backup, Business Wire, is blocked too. If a primary degrades, rerun the probe with `--only` on the
candidates and promote from there.

Rejected (`status = "rejected"`, `reason` in `sources.toml`): AP News, Investing.com, Benzinga, Business Wire,
all refused at the CDN (Cloudflare or Akamai) before any content is served. These outlets are syndicated
widely, so `detect.py` answers a block with a hint that points at the syndicated copy (usually Yahoo Finance).

## Yahoo EU consent

- From this IP, `finance.yahoo.com`, `yahoo.com/news`, `uk.finance.yahoo.com` and `de.yahoo.com` served content
  directly with no consent redirect. The pages carry `"gdpr":true` and a client-side CMP
  (`consent.cmp.oath.com`), so in October 2026 the server-side wall no longer stands in front of articles.
- The server-side flow still exists at `guce.yahoo.com/consent` -> `consent.yahoo.com/v2/collectConsent`, so the
  probe exercises it on every run (`yahoo_consent_check` in the JSON): `consent.reject_all` posted the
  reject-all form in 857 ms and the jar received `A1`, `A1S`, `CFC`, `EuConsent`, `GUC`. Decoding the TCF v2
  string in `EuConsent` gives **0 of 24 purposes consented**, which confirms that reject-all was recorded and
  accept-all was never sent. A second pass with the same jar skips the form (about 120 ms, no POST).
- Serving contract: when a redirect lands on a consent host, the fetcher calls `reject_all` with its SSRF
  guard and retries the original URL once; if that lands on the wall again, `detect.classify` raises
  `consent_required` with a hint.

## Block, consent and paywall detection

`detect.classify(status, headers, html, final_url)` is pure and string-based, so it runs on every fetch.

| Signal | Raised as |
|---|---|
| Final URL on `consent.yahoo.com` / `guce.yahoo.com`, or a Yahoo consent form in the page | `consent_required` |
| HTTP 401, 403, 429 (retryable), 451 | `source_blocked`, naming the CDN edge from `server` / `cf-ray` |
| Cloudflare: `cf-mitigated: challenge`, "Just a moment...", `_cf_chl_opt`, `/cdn-cgi/challenge-platform/h/`, "Attention Required! \| Cloudflare" | `source_blocked` |
| DataDome `captcha-delivery.com` or `x-dd-b`; PerimeterX `px-captcha` or "Press & Hold"; Akamai "Access Denied" + "Reference #", `sec-if-cpt-container`, `errors.edgesuite.net`; Imperva `_Incapsula_Resource` | `source_blocked`, including when served with HTTP 200 |
| JSON-LD `isAccessibleForFree` false (bool or string) and both the JSON-LD `articleBody` and the visible `<p>` text under 200 words | `paywalled` |

Design points the probe forced:

- Cloudflare's passive `/cdn-cgi/challenge-platform/scripts/jsd/main.js` beacon sits on normal pages, so only
  the interactive `/h/` path counts. `x-datadome` alone is ignored because DataDome sets it on allowed responses.
- Markers are only searched in the first 64 KB: interstitials are a few KB, and it keeps 6 MB CNN pages cheap.
  Over all 42 captured pages `classify` takes at most 1.7 ms (CNN, 5.8 MB) and under 1 ms everywhere else
  (median of 5 runs).
- CNN and Fortune declare `isAccessibleForFree: false` yet serve the whole article (their walls are
  client-side), which is why a not-free flag alone is never treated as a paywall.
- Hints are keyed by host suffix: Reuters, AP, Business Wire and Benzinga blocks point to the syndicated copy on
  Yahoo Finance; WSJ, Barron's, FT and Bloomberg paywalls point to free sources.

## What the extractors get

Profile semantics (documented at the top of `sources.toml`): remove `drop` selectors, take `body` matches in
document order, ignore paragraphs under `min_words`, then cut at the first paragraph after the lede that starts
with a `stop_markers` prefix. All selectors use only tag, class, id, attribute and descendant parts; GlobeNewswire
also uses a selector list for `p, li`. All 30 primary pages pass the two-parser check.

Findings that are not visible in the selectors:

- **JSON-LD `articleBody` exists only on CNN** (3/3). Everywhere else the cascade has to fall through to the
  profile or density strategy. No source ships `__NEXT_DATA__`; Fool and Fortune use the Next.js flight stream
  and Yahoo SvelteKit, neither worth parsing for the body.
- **Text joining differs between parsers**: selectolax `text(separator=" ")` splits words at inline tags (drop
  caps become "R ogue", "Fla. ,"), while lxml `text_content()` glues text across `<br>` ("WangEmail"). Joining
  text nodes without a separator, with spaces only at `<br>` and block boundaries, gives the same text on both.
- **Press releases** end with an "About <issuer>" heading, forward-looking statements and contacts as plain
  paragraphs, so they are cut with stop markers, not selectors. The "About" check only applies after the lede.
- **SEC exhibits** arrive wrapped in the EDGAR SGML envelope, with no `h1`, JSON-LD or containers, and start with
  "Exhibit 99.1" and the issuer name. Some filer agents emit `div`/`span` text without `<p>`, which this profile
  cannot read; the cascade must fall back to density there. EX-99.1 is sometimes a financial statement (11.6k
  words in one sample), which `scope=lede` and the token cap absorb.
- **Yahoo** stories are mostly partner copy (Motley Fool, Insider Monkey, 24/7 Wall St, named in `providerId`)
  and partner promos survive inside the body; the second half of the text sits in a hidden "Story continues"
  block that must be kept.
- **CNBC** has editor-written Key Points (`div.RenderKeyPoints-list li`) outside the body, a ready-made lede.
- **CNN** pages are 5.7 MB, so DOM parsing is the slow step there; the JSON-LD strategy avoids it.

## Caveats

- One vantage point. Bot management depends on IP reputation: GitHub Actions runners use US datacenter IPs that
  Cloudflare and Akamai treat more strictly, and US visitors see different geo behaviour (no Yahoo consent at
  all, `www.cnn.com`, `bbc.com`). CI therefore runs on skeleton fixtures; the weekly live smoke is informational.
- Three articles per source on a Sunday: the wires were dominated by non-US issuers, and only 2 of the 25 newest
  8-K filing indexes had an EX-99.1 described as a press release.
- Blocking decisions drift over time and with request rate; the probe stayed at or under 1 request per second per
  domain. The Business Wire `/newsroom` challenge was seen while exploring and is not in the final JSON, because
  discovery uses its MRSS feed.
- AP's article URLs were harvested from other publishers' pages because its own hubs and sitemaps are blocked.
- A Chrome TLS fingerprint might get past Cloudflare for AP, Benzinga and Investing.com. That is evasion, which
  Q19 rules out.

## Reproduce

```bash
uv run python scripts/probe_sources.py --vantage "EU (Bulgaria) residential ISP"   # live, about 2 minutes
uv run python scripts/probe_sources.py --only cnbc,bbc                               # re-probe some sources
uv run python scripts/probe_sources.py --reanalyze                                   # re-score saved HTML offline
```

# Model selection

Generated by `uv run python -m veritrade_evals select` from committed results; numbers only.

## Rules

- **signal**: Candidates: the frozen /signal configs at the default lede scope. Filters: dev300 inversion rate <= 2% at the frozen operating point (n=300); the articles dev set must not fail the cap, meaning the 95% CI of its inversion rate reaches down to 2% (the freeze's clear-failure rule: at n=30 one inversion is about 5% of the calls); warm native p50 excluding fetch <= 500 ms at lede. Rank: dev300 F0.5 macro (primary, n=300), then articles dev F0.5, then lower latency.
- **analyze**: Candidates: the frozen /analyze configs (full scope, ordinal |score| >= t, sentiment-first). Filters: the same inversion rules as /signal; streamed TTFT p50 <= 1.5 s and complete p50 <= 4 s (warm, native, excluding fetch). Rank: dev300 F0.5 macro, then articles dev F0.5, then lower latency.
- **summary**: Candidates: the frozen /summary models. Filter: deterministic pass rate >= 0.8 on the dev articles; streamed TTFT p50 <= 1.5 s and complete p50 <= 4 s. Rank: Opus judge faithfulness, then judge coverage, then key-fact coverage (key-fact coverage leads while the judge is pending).
- **winner**: The best-ranked candidate inside every filter. When no accuracy-eligible candidate meets its latency budget, the Pareto knee (metrics.knee) of quality against budget utilisation (the worst measured metric divided by its limit) among the measured candidates, with the reason stated.
- **bundle**: R8: the per-endpoint winners when their model files total <= 10 GB (decimal), else the combination of accuracy-eligible candidates that fits with the fewest rank steps away from the winners (ties: signal, then summary, then analyze keeps its better pick; then the smaller total).

## Notes from the error-analysis read

Hand-written after reading the tables above; counts and my own descriptions only, no dataset text. These are
tweets, not articles: the thresholds and latencies here are a starting point for the article dev set, not a
substitute for it.

**A decoding fix came out of this grid.** The qwen3.5 Modelfiles ship `presence_penalty 1.5`, and the client
only pinned temperature and seed, so "greedy" qwen3.5 output was pushed away from any token in the recent
context. With four shots whose last answer is neutral (or score 0), the generated qwen3.5:0.8b label disagreed
with its own first-token argmax on 84/300 (v2) and 62/300 (v4) tweets, and v2-ordinal emitted -2 for 104/300.
`FIXED_OPTIONS` now neutralises the penalties; every number on this page comes from the greedy re-run. The
label-logprob cells were identical before and after (logprobs are reported before the penalty is applied), and
seven cells re-run to replace contended timings reproduced their predictions exactly, so the cache and decoding
are deterministic.

**Decision models lead on precision.** clef-flash v4 (plain question, bare labels) reaches F0.5 0.874 at
min_p 0.80 with no inversions, answering 73% of tweets and calling 33% directional against a 35% directional
prior. nimble over-calls: with no threshold it calls 65-74% of tweets directional, and it only becomes precise
at min_p 0.97-0.98, where it answers about a quarter of the tweets (F0.5 0.843 for v1). The served
`directional_tau` rule runs at min_p 0, so for these peaked models it only removes their abstention: it loses
to the plain rule by 0.046 (clef-flash) and 0.303 (nimble) F0.5, both significant, and is not served for them.

**qwen3.5:0.8b is neutral-leaning, which caps the served label policy.** Its first-token argmax is neutral on
most directional tweets (0.3-7% signal rate across label configs), so a min_p threshold can only remove calls:
the plain rule (v2-label, no abstention) misses 162 of 200 directional tweets at F0.5 0.512. The served
`directional_tau` rule calls the likelier directional class when neutral leads and that class reaches tau;
at tau 0.28 it gives F0.5 0.730 [0.651, 0.795] with precision 0.91 / 0.92 and no inversions (+0.218
[+0.141, +0.307] paired). It is the largest single lever found here, it is now the model's best config, and it
is frozen (min_p 0, directional_tau 0.28).

**Knob verdict for qwen3.5:0.8b.** As served (argmax + min_p on label tokens vs |score| >= t on the ordinal
schema), the best label config beats the best ordinal config by +0.059 F0.5 [-0.068, +0.187]: not significant
at n=300. With the `directional_tau` rule the logprob knob wins clearly. The ordinal schema cannot borrow that
rule: this tokenizer fuses the space and the minus sign (" -") while the bare-space alternative keeps about a
quarter of the mass, so the sign is unobservable for negative scores. `score_sign_probabilities` used to read
those as bearish 1.0 (and miss the " -" mass behind positive scores). It now returns None for every negative
score in these cells (48, 32, 17 and 8 of 300), and serving falls back to the ordinal policy there.

**Prompt dimensions.**
- Rubric A (definitions) beats rubric B (impact questions) for every generative model. B's "is the change
  clear and material" framing makes the small models answer neutral: qwen3.5:0.8b v3-label calls 0.3% of
  tweets directional, and ministral drops from 0.660 to 0.440.
- Four synthetic shots help qwen3.5:0.8b on the label schema (0.365 to 0.512) but hurt every /analyze model:
  qwen3.5:4b 0.752 to 0.655, ministral 0.660 to 0.494, and qwen3-instruct v2 breaks the inversion cap. Shots
  also roughly double qwen3.5:4b's time to score.
- For the decision models the spread across prompts is small (clef 0.83-0.87, nimble 0.81-0.84). Bare labels
  with the short question are also the fastest variant (clef 468 vs 710 ms, nimble 751 vs 975 ms).

**Where the calls go wrong.**
- Inversions are nearly absent: one bullish tweet called bearish across all six best configs.
- Wrong calls are mostly gold-neutral tweets called directional (1-8 per model). Relative to its size, the
  earnings and guidance bucket holds the most of them (13 across the six models in 46 tweets, against 14 in
  128 for the catch-all bucket), which fits mixed results (a beat alongside a cut outlook) being the hard case.
- The real loss is recall: 34 (clef-flash) to 162 (qwen3.5:0.8b) directional tweets missed.
- The biggest miss bucket for every generative model is the price-move tweet: 33-44 of 57 directional ones
  missed, against 10 for clef-flash. The rubrics ask for economic impact, not tone, and the small models read
  a reported share-price move as not material, while the dataset labels such moves as directional. Whether to
  close that gap is a product question: on articles the impact reading is the intended behaviour.
- Analyst actions (upgrades, price targets) are handled well by the larger models (qwen3.5:4b catches 21 of
  22, clef-flash 19 of 22, with no wrong calls).
- 20 directional tweets get no correct call from any model; they are the first place to look for label noise
  or genuinely ambiguous items.

**Follow-ups after the grid (analyze).** Two cells per model, each paired against v1 on the same tweets
and never eligible as the best config.
- v5 = v1 with the summary rule tightened after the summary eval (2 to 3 sentences, at most 50 words, entity
  first). Only the summary line changes, yet the score moves: ministral +0.025 [+0.002, +0.052], qwen3-instruct
  -0.011 [-0.047, +0.023], qwen3.5:4b -0.021 [-0.054, +0.007]. On the article dev set qwen3.5:4b loses more
  (0.800 vs 0.880, gap -0.080 [-0.178, -0.014]: two more bullish articles missed), so the freeze keeps v1 for
  qwen3.5:4b /analyze and serves v5 to ministral and qwen3-instruct.
- `v1-summary-first` (the field-order check) is never better: ministral -0.017 [-0.088, +0.059], qwen3.5:4b
  -0.061 [-0.122, +0.003], and its time to the score is 1.0-1.5 s against 0.15-0.6 s, because the whole
  summary decodes first. Every /analyze model stays sentiment-first.

**The one manual revision.** Few-shot is dropped for /analyze (every frozen /analyze prompt is zero-shot).
The price-move / analyst-action sentence was not added: on the article dev set the /analyze models miss 0-1
of the 5 directional price-move headlines and no headline falls in the analyst-action bucket, so the tweet
misses do not carry over (see `evals/results/articles_dev/summary.md`). qwen3.5:0.8b keeps its four shots: they
help the label schema (0.365 to 0.512 plain).

**Timing provenance.** Wall times are per call at client concurrency 1, warm. Concurrent load on the shared
machine (mostly the Docker Desktop VM saturating the CPU) inflated some tails, so clef-flash v2 and nimble v2/v3
were re-run at 19:28-19:47 and all eight qwen3.5:0.8b cells at 20:11-20:25, each with identical predictions.
The tables show the re-run timings. The qwen3.5:0.8b re-run still shared the machine (load about 30): on a
quiet machine earlier the same calls measured p50 155-200 ms with p95 near 210-300 ms, against 209-276 ms and
up to 1.06 s here. nimble v3's tail is also somewhat elevated. The analyze follow-ups (v5, summary-first)
ran later at concurrency 1 on an Ollama shared with two other eval runs, so their timings are indicative only.

```

## Notes

Hand-written after reading the tables above; counts and my own descriptions only, no article text. With 10
articles per class, read these as a check that the dev300 operating points transfer, not as a ranking.

**Every served rule holds.** No served rule clearly fails (no inversion CI above the 2% cap, no coverage
collapse), so every dev300 threshold is frozen as tuned and nothing was re-picked on the articles.

**/signal.**
- clef-flash v4 at p >= 0.80 scores F0.5 0.848 on the lede and 0.907 on the full body, close to its dev300
  0.874. It makes one inversion in 20 calls on the lede and none on the full body.
- nimble v1 at p >= 0.97 answers far more articles than tweets (coverage 60-67% against 26% on dev300) at
  F0.5 0.88-0.90: articles state their news more plainly than tweets, so the peaked model is sure more often.
- qwen3.5:0.8b with `directional_tau` 0.28 scores 0.685 on the lede against 0.595 for the plain rule (a tie
  at n=30); on the full body the tau rule wins clearly (+0.229 [+0.022, +0.560]). It still misses about half
  the directional articles, so it remains the fast, low-recall option.
- Lede vs full is a tie for all three models; the lede (the /signal default) is two to three times faster.

**/analyze.**
- Articles are easier than tweets for every generative model: qwen3.5:4b v1 0.880, qwen3-instruct 0.798 and
  ministral 0.741, against 0.75 / 0.66 / 0.66 on dev300.
- The tightened summary rule (v5) changes no ministral call, costs qwen3-instruct one (a tie), and costs
  qwen3.5:4b two bullish and one bearish article plus one false alarm (-0.080 [-0.178, -0.014]). It therefore
  keeps v1 for /analyze; its /summary endpoint still gets the tightened summary prompt.
- Summary-first is a tie on the articles (qwen3.5:4b -0.013, ministral +0.058) and never wins on dev300,
  while its time to the score is two to three times longer. Every model stays sentiment-first.
- The wrong calls are mostly neutral articles called directional (3-5 of the 10 per model, mostly bullish).
  Price-move headlines are not the problem they were on tweets (0-1 of the 5 directional ones missed per
  model), so the price-move / analyst-action rubric sentence was not added.

# Extraction matrix

Generated by `uv run python -m veritrade_evals.extraction_bench report` from local measurements; no article text is stored here.

- Data: the 90 committed articles (all splits) from 10 sources; stored HTML through the serving `veritrade.extract.registry.extract`; third-party extractors bring their own parser (parser column `(built-in)`).
- Quality: macro means over articles against the Opus gold body. Tokens are lowercased `\w+` runs; P/R/F1 are bag-of-words with multiplicity; a failed extraction scores 0. Leakage is the share of extracted tokens outside every 5-token window that also occurs in the gold body (successful extractions only). 95% CIs: bootstrap over articles (B=1000).
- Time: wall ms of one `extract` call (parse + extract), median of 5 runs per article after a warm-up, then p50/p95 over articles, failures included.
- Tokens: chars / 4 of the uncapped `full` input (title + body) at p50; lede = the `/signal` lede input at the decision model's budget.
- Install: decimal MB of the RECORD files a row adds to the backend core (its closure without any parser or extractor); own strategies add 0 beyond their parser.
- Signal: `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` v4 (grid best), served sentiment at p >= 0.8; agreement = share of articles whose verdict on the row's lede equals the verdict on the gold lede, title held at the gold headline; a failed extraction is a miss.
- Machine: Apple M4 Pro, 48 GB, Python 3.13.12; Ollama had a model resident in 90/90 per-article samples (another eval was running), mean 1-min load average 6.1.

## Notes

- The gold body is a subset of the `strip-tags` lines (selectolax blocks) chosen by Opus, so `strip-tags` recall is about 1 by construction and own strategies share the gold's text joining; scores are bag-of-words and the leakage only needs 5 tokens in order, so segmentation is moot.
- The gold packets folded the page outside the span the served `selectolax/cascade` found (Opus could open the full page), so the gold leans toward the cascade; read own vs third-party gaps as upper bounds.
- The globenewswire, prnewswire and yahoo profiles were tightened after a first measurement with these articles in view, so their scores, and the overall means they feed, are optimistic; `.context/docs/design/03-extraction.md` keeps the first-run numbers.
- Timings come from one process on a shared workstation; see the environment block in matrix.json for load average and Ollama residency during the run.
- The `jsonld` strategy reads JSON-LD from the raw HTML and never builds the tree, so its 4 rows differ only by timing noise.

# Summary evaluation

Decision R6: deterministic checks, key-fact coverage by a local embedding model, and Claude Opus as a
blind judge. Summaries come from the serving adapters (`/api/summary`, `/api/analyze`) with the default
`selectolax` + `cascade` extraction and `full` scope, run on the stored HTML of the Opus article set.
Written by `uv run python -m veritrade_evals.summary_eval report`; no article or summary text is committed.
Every check scores the served summary: serving caps it at 3 sentences and 60 words
(`cap_summary` in `veritrade.inference.adapters`), and `score` applies the same cap to cached generations.

- **Halluc.** (`hallucinationRate`): share of summaries with any unsupported detail, minor slips included.
- **Material** (`materialErrorRate`): share at faithfulness <= 3: a material error.

## Definitions

- **Pass**: <= 60 words, <= 3 sentences (serving sentence splitter), every number
  grounded, entity named, not truncated. Rates are over all articles; a candidate that produced no summary
  fails every check. Length holds by construction for served summaries; **Capped** is the share the cap
  had to shorten (whole leading sentences kept; an overlong first sentence ends in an ellipsis).
- **Numbers**: every number in the summary appears in the gold title or body. Thousands separators, `%`,
  currency symbols and units are ignored and 1.50 equals 1.5; number words up to twenty in the article
  ground their digits; Q1-Q4 / H1-H2 match the same token, `third quarter` / `first half`, `September
  quarter` or `July to September` (calendar quarters); `FY27` matches 2027; `80K` matches 80,000 (K/M/B
  abbreviations); a clock time on the hour (`5:00 p.m.`) matches the bare hour (`5PM`). Derived figures
  (a percentage change the model computed) count as unsupported: the prompt asks for verbatim numbers.
- **Entity**: the gold entity appears (case-insensitive, whole words); or its short name, without legal
  suffixes (Inc, Corp, Ltd, plc, Holdings, Group, ...) and trailing descriptors (Entertainment,
  Technologies, Industries, ...), as a phrase or as all its words anywhere (`UK ... economy`); or its first
  word when the name has several words and that word has 4+ letters and is not generic (American, United,
  Bank, ...); or the gold ticker (case-sensitive, also without an exchange suffix such as `.HK`).
- **Truncated**: the output hit `num_predict` and the serving path cut it to its last full sentence.
- **Key facts**: each of the 3-5 Opus key facts and each summary sentence is embedded with
  `qwen3-embedding:0.6b`; a fact is covered when its best cosine is >= 0.60, the threshold
  that agreed best with hand labels in the spot check. Mean share per article. **Key facts (strict)** uses
  0.75, where every flagged fact was really stated: a conservative lower bound.
- **Faithful / Cover**: Opus judge scores 1-5 (`evals/opus_prompts/50-judge.md`), candidates anonymised and
  shuffled per article. **Halluc.** and **Material** are defined at the top: a minor slip such as a
  loosely worded detail counts towards the first only. **Leads**: share the judge found leading with the
  market-moving fact.

```

# 03 - Extraction

Question (Q10, R4): which parser and extractor recover a financial news body best and fastest, and does the
choice change what the `/signal` model decides? The answer is measured on the 90-article evaluation set with
the same `extract` function the API calls, not assumed from library benchmarks. Numbers come from
`evals/results/extraction/matrix.json` (summary tables in `evals/results/extraction/summary.md`). They are from
the second measurement, taken after the changes listed in "Changes after the first measurement". That section
also keeps the first-run numbers.

## Setup

- **Articles**: the 90 committed articles, 10 sources with 9 each (Yahoo 10, BBC 8), fetched on
  2026-10-18. The stored HTML and the gold bodies stay in `evals/data/private/`; only ids, sources
  and numbers are committed. All splits are used. The extraction code and source profiles were committed (M2)
  before the set existed (M3), and none of the 90 URLs is among the probe pages the profiles were first tuned
  on (`02-source-probe.md`). After the first measurement, however, the GlobeNewswire, PR Newswire and Yahoo
  profiles were tightened with this same set in view (see Caveats). For those three sources the set is no
  longer held out.
- **Gold body**: Opus chose line ranges from the page's visible-text lines (`evals/opus_prompts/20-gold.md`).
  The lines are the selectolax block walk (the `strip-tags` output), with very long blocks split into
  sentence chunks. The gold excludes the headline, dek, key-points boxes, captions, promos, financial tables and
  press-release boilerplate (About, forward-looking statements, contacts).
- **Rows (22)**: 4 parsers (`selectolax`, `lxml`, `bs4`, `bs4-lxml`) x 4 own strategies (`cascade`, `jsonld`,
  `profile`, `density`), plus 6 extractors that bring their own parser: `trafilatura` (default and
  `favor_precision`), `readability-lxml`, `newspaper4k`, `jusText` and the `strip-tags` baseline. Every row
  calls `veritrade.extract.registry.extract(html, final_url, parser=..., extractor=...)`. An extraction under
  40 words raises `ExtractionEmpty`, as in the API.

## Metrics

- **Tokens**: maximal runs of Python `\w` characters in the lowercased text; an extraction's text is its
  paragraphs joined by blank lines.
- **Precision, recall, F1**: bag of words with multiplicity. With `c(t)` the count of token `t`,
  `common = sum over t of min(c_extracted(t), c_gold(t))`, `P = common / |extracted|`,
  `R = common / |gold|`, `F1 = 2PR / (P + R)`. Each is a macro mean over the 90 articles, and a failed
  extraction scores 0 on all three. 95% CIs are percentile bootstraps over articles (B = 1000, same resamples
  for every row).
- **Leakage**: the share of extracted tokens that lie in no 5-token window also present, in order, in the
  gold token sequence. It is a mean over successful extractions, since a failure sends nothing. Bag-of-words
  `1 - P` is reported too. The two differ on purpose: `1 - P` credits a promo or caption that reuses the
  story's names and common words, and it penalises body text repeated twice. Order-aware coverage asks
  whether the text is part of the story. On this set the two agree within about 1 point per row, except
  `readability` (34.4% against 30.7%), where order-aware coverage flags more of the output.
- **Failure rate**: `ExtractionEmpty` or any exception, recorded by type name.
- **Time**: wall ms around one `extract` call, covering parse, strategy, JSON-LD scan and title. Each
  (row, article) gets one untimed warm-up, which is the output that gets scored, then 5 timed calls. The
  article's time is the median of the 5, and p50 / p95 are taken over the 90 articles, failures included. Rows
  are interleaved per article, so machine-load drift hits every row alike.
- **Tokens to the LLM**: `chars / 4`, the service's estimate, of `build_input(article, "full", uncapped)`
  (`TITLE:` line plus body), at p50. Served inputs are further capped at the model's `max_input_tokens`
  (2000 to 6000). The lede size is `build_input(article, "lede", 2000)`.
- **Install MB**: decimal MB of the files in each distribution's RECORD, summed over the row's dependency
  closure minus the backend core. The core is the closure of the backend's requirements with every parser and
  extractor package removed, so it is what a row adds to the app. Own strategies add nothing beyond their
  parser.
- **Downstream signal**: the `/signal` decision model `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` with its grid-best config `v4`
  (plain instructions, bare criteria) and the probability policy at the grid's operating point,
  `p >= 0.8` (abstentions become neutral, as served). The input is the serving lede,
  `build_input(article, "lede", 2000)`, built from each row's paragraphs. The title is held at the gold
  headline so that only the body varies. The reference is the same lede built from the gold body.
  Agreement is the share of the 90 articles whose verdict matches the gold-lede verdict, and a failed
  extraction counts as a miss. Calls go through the grid runner's `call_once` at concurrency 1. The
  prediction cache keys each record by (row, article) and reuses an answer when the input hash repeats.
  There were 2,070 records (1,980 rows x articles plus 90 gold ledes). The 348 failed extractions need no
  call, and the other 1,722 collapse to 375 distinct ledes. The re-measurement reused every cached answer
  and called the model only for the 9 ledes that were new.

## Results

### Quality: the parser does not matter

For every own strategy the four parsers give the same scores (F1 spread 0.0000). The shared block walker joins
text identically on every backend (`02-source-probe.md`), so the parser is purely a speed and footprint
choice. Own strategies below use `selectolax`.

| `cascade` (served) | 0.959 [0.942, 0.973] | 0.945 | 0.981 | 5.3% | 0.0% | 718 |
| `density` | 0.953 [0.936, 0.967] | 0.936 | 0.977 | 6.1% | 0.0% | 704 |
| `profile` | 0.927 [0.888, 0.961] | 0.915 | 0.947 | 5.2% | 3.3% | 723 |

### Speed and footprint

`bs4` is small because `beautifulsoup4` and `soupsieve` are pure Python, and it is the slowest parser for the
same reason. The `jsonld` rows never build a tree, so all four cost 0.2 ms. They fail on 81 of 90 pages,
because only CNN ships an `articleBody`. Every row, including the unchanged third-party ones, is faster than
in the first run (cascade p50 1.6 ms and p95 3.3 ms then), mostly because the machine was less loaded (see
Caveats).

### Per source

Column notes:

- "Directional lost" means a bullish or bearish gold verdict became neutral.
- "Added" is the reverse.
- "No verdict" is a failed extraction, which counts as a miss.

The cascade's 2 disagreements are both SEC exhibits near the 0.8 threshold:

- In one, the gold lede is bearish at 0.92 and the cascade lede leans bearish at 0.75, below the threshold,
  so it is served as neutral.
- In the other, the gold lede leans bearish at 0.79, just under the threshold (served neutral), while the
  cascade lede reads bullish at 0.88. That is the one case in which the top class itself changes. The
  cascade fell back to `density` on that exhibit, and 21 of the 40 tokens in its lede are header lines that
  the gold leaves out.

The first run's third disagreement was a PR Newswire release on which the model abstained. It is gone: after
the PR Newswire profile change, that release's cascade lede is one the model had already scored, and the
verdict agrees.

## Findings

1. **The parser is a speed and footprint choice, not a quality one.** All four give identical bodies.
   `selectolax` is the fastest (parse p50 0.6 ms against 1.3 for `lxml` and 11.4 for `bs4`) and adds 7.5 MB.
2. **`cascade` and `density` are tied on quality, and `cascade` is faster at the tail.**
   - F1 is 0.959 for `cascade` against 0.953 for `density`. The paired gap, `density` minus `cascade`, is
     -0.006 [-0.013, +0.001], which is inside the noise.
   - `density` leaks less on Yahoo (10.3% against 14.9%) and does worse on Motley Fool and Fortune.
   - The cascade's p95 is 2.4 ms against 11.6, because a JSON-LD hit (CNN, 5.7 MB pages) returns before any
     tree is built.
3. **The cascade's fallback earns its place on SEC.** The SEC profile fails on the 3 exhibits whose filer
   agent emits no `<p>` (profile alone: F1 0.59, 3 failures). The cascade falls through to `density` and
   reaches 0.91 with no failure.
4. **What the served cascade still leaks, it mostly leaks at the end of the story, on the same three
   sources.**
   - Leakage is 14.9% on Yahoo, 13.3% on PR Newswire and 13.1% on GlobeNewswire (first run: 24.1%, 22.3%,
     31.2%), and at most 6.6% elsewhere.
   - Counting a paragraph as leaked when most of its tokens are, 597 of the Yahoo, 469 of the GlobeNewswire
     and 249 of the PR Newswire leaked tokens sit after the last gold paragraph.
   - What is left:
     - Yahoo partner tails with no stable opening phrase (StockStory's closing pair).
     - One PR Newswire release (66% leaked) whose "About" heading falls inside the protected lede.
     - One short GlobeNewswire release that still leaks half its tokens.
   - This costs the `full` scope (`/summary`, `/analyze`) tokens, not the lede.
5. **Every third-party extractor trails the own strategies here, and each has a source it breaks on.**
   - `trafilatura` now extracts all 9 SEC exhibits (the EDGAR envelope is unwrapped, see below). It returns
     the whole exhibit, though: SEC F1 0.62 with 52% leakage. 5,644 of the 8,169 leaked tokens come after
     the last gold paragraph, and 98% sit in prose paragraphs, not tables. Its weak sources are the three
     wires (GlobeNewswire 0.62, PR Newswire 0.55, SEC 0.62).
   - `readability` picks the same 21-word block on every Motley Fool page, before our adapter touches the
     output, and the wrong block on Fortune (F1 0.08).
   - `newspaper4k` is the slowest (p50 72 ms) and not deterministic: on one Yahoo page it returned two
     different bodies across repeated calls in one process.
   - `jusText` keeps boilerplate (27% leakage).
6. **Extraction quality barely moves the lede signal until the extraction is wrong.**
   - Every extractor that finds the story agrees with the gold-lede verdict on 94 to 99% of the pages it
     extracts, even though its lede is byte-identical to the gold lede on only 21 to 64% of the 90 pages.
   - What costs agreement is failing outright (`readability` on Motley Fool, `jsonld` off CNN) or putting
     page chrome in the lede. `strip-tags` loses 14 of 63 directional calls, because navigation text pushes
     the story out of the 200-token lede and the model abstains.
   - With SEC now extracted, `trafilatura-precision` agrees on 98.9% (first run 90.0%, all 9 misses were SEC
     failures). Most of its SEC leakage comes after the story, past the lede, and its one miss is an SEC
     exhibit.
   - No row turns a served bullish verdict into a bearish one or back: bad extraction makes the model
     abstain, it does not make it invert.
7. **Tokens**: competent extractors send 704 to 822 tokens of `full` input (p50), against 2,116 for
   `strip-tags`. Ledes are 119 to 128 tokens for every extractor that finds the story.

## What we serve and why

The default stays **`selectolax` + `cascade`** (already the `registry.extract` default):

- **Quality**: best or tied F1 (0.959 [0.942, 0.973]), zero failures on the 90 pages, and 97.8% [94.4%, 100%]
  agreement with the gold-lede verdict, with no inversion.
- **Speed**: the lowest tail of any row that finds bodies, p50 1.2 ms and p95 2.4 ms. That is noise
  against the 500 ms `/signal` budget.
- **Footprint and provenance**: 7.5 MB, no third-party extractor needed at runtime, and the winning method
  (`jsonld`, `profile` or `density`) is reported in every response's meta.

`density` is not promoted: it trails by a gap inside the noise, its p95 is about five times higher, and the
cascade already falls back to it where profiles fail. The other 21 rows stay selectable from the UI and the
API (Q10) so the comparison can be repeated on any URL. If a source-agnostic default were ever needed,
`trafilatura-precision` is now the candidate. It has no failures and the best signal agreement (98.9%), but it
leaks 17.7% (51 to 59% on the three wire sources), costs 60.8 MB and takes about 14 times the cascade's p50.

## Changes after the first measurement

The first run filed two requests for the extraction code. Both were applied, and then the set was
re-measured: a fresh `measure`, `signal` for the 9 ledes that were new, and `report`. The four parsers still
agree on every own strategy, and the skeleton tests cover the new rules on all four.

1. **EDGAR envelope** (`veritrade.extract.third_party.unwrap_edgar`).
   - Third-party adapters now get the `<TEXT>` body of an EDGAR SGML document; any other page passes
     unchanged.
   - It is unit-tested with the synthetic envelope from the first run's repro
     (`backend/tests/unit/extract/test_third_party.py`).
   - The own strategies already read the envelope and are unaffected. The other third-party rows see the
     inner page too, and their SEC F1 moves by 0.01 at most.
2. **Profile tails** (`[sources.*.profile]` in `backend/src/veritrade/data/sources.toml`, plus one engine
   option).
   - **`max_link_density`** (new; set on Yahoo to 0.5).
     - A body paragraph whose link text exceeds that share of its visible characters is dropped before
       triage, without ending the body.
     - It removes Yahoo's related-story promos and partner link lists without the hashed `yf-*` classes. On
       this set it dropped 18 leaked paragraphs and no gold paragraph.
     - `Node.link_density` counts characters the way the block walker does, so all parsers agree.
   - **Yahoo**: stop markers for partner sign-offs ("More Top Reads From", "This article by Simply Wall St",
     "For updates and corrections").
     - A drop for the trailing list in the read-more block was tried and rejected. It added 0.013 F1 on
       Yahoo, but it needs either the hashed class or a bare `ul` drop that would also remove story lists.
   - **PR Newswire**:
     - The body selector adds `li`, because bulleted highlights are story text: recall went from 0.903 to
       0.966.
     - `p.prntac` is dropped (centred deks and logo lines).
     - New stop markers: "Forward-looking", "For further information" and "Conference Call".
   - **GlobeNewswire**: drops the attachment block (`#gnw_attachments_section-header`,
     `#gnw_attachments_section-items`) and adds the same three stop markers.
   - **All sources**: `GENERIC_STOPS` gains "Forward-Looking Information".
   - **Fixtures**: the Yahoo, PR Newswire and GlobeNewswire skeleton fixtures gained synthetic structural
     elements, so these rules run on real publisher DOM in the four-parser skeleton tests:
     - a link-only promo and a partner tail (Yahoo)
     - a dek and a bullet list (PR Newswire)
     - an attachment block (GlobeNewswire)

   The fixture vocabulary was regenerated by the capture script's own writer.

| scope (`selectolax/cascade`) | F1 first run | F1 now | leakage first run | leakage now | recall first run / now |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| all 90 articles | 0.929 [0.900, 0.957] | 0.959 [0.942, 0.973] | 9.0% | 5.3% | 0.975 / 0.981 |
| GlobeNewswire | 0.780 | 0.918 | 31.2% | 13.1% | 1.000 / 1.000 |
| PR Newswire | 0.814 | 0.910 | 22.3% | 13.3% | 0.903 / 0.966 |
| Yahoo Finance | 0.848 | 0.904 | 24.1% | 14.9% | 0.996 / 0.995 |
| the other 7 sources | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged |

| row | SEC failures | SEC F1 | overall F1 | signal agreement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `trafilatura` | 9 -> 0 | 0.00 -> 0.62 | 0.797 -> 0.859 | 87.8% -> 96.7% |
| `trafilatura-precision` | 9 -> 0 | 0.00 -> 0.62 | 0.802 -> 0.864 | 90.0% -> 98.9% |

`density` rose too, from 0.932 to 0.953, because it cuts its block run at the same profile stop markers and
triage. `profile` rose from 0.897 to 0.927.

## Caveats

- **Three profiles were tuned on this set.**
  - The GlobeNewswire, PR Newswire and Yahoo changes were made after the first measurement. They were
    chosen from counts taken on these same 90 articles: selector matches, stop-marker candidates and
    per-paragraph link shares, with no text printed. The same pages were then used to check them.
  - So the gains on those three sources are in-sample. For an unseen page, the first-run scores (F1 0.780,
    0.814, 0.848) are the honest estimate, and the new ones (0.918, 0.910, 0.904) are optimistic. The same
    holds for the overall cascade F1: 0.929 is the honest figure and 0.959 the optimistic one.
  - The rules are generic in form: a link-share cap, attachment-block ids and release stop phrases. Still,
    "Conference Call" and "For further information" would cut a release whose story continues after a call
    notice or a contact line. Stop markers never cut the lede.
  - No other source's profile changed. The EDGAR unwrap fixes a bug rather than tuning a score.
- **The gold leans toward the own strategies, and toward the cascade in particular.**
  - Opus picked from the same selectolax block lines that the own strategies walk, so their text matches the
    gold token for token. Third-party extractors join text their own way and lose a little even on the right
    blocks.
  - The gold packets folded the page outside the span the served cascade found. Opus could open the full
    page, but the default view was anchored on the cascade.
  - So the gap between own and third-party extractors is an upper bound. The ranking among third-party
    extractors, and the failures listed above, do not depend on it.
- **One annotator, small n.** Opus made one gold body per page and no human checked them. There are 9 pages
  per source, so per-source numbers rest on 9 pages, and one signal disagreement moves agreement by 1.1 points.
- **Timings come from a shared workstation.**
  - The machine is an Apple M4 Pro with 14 cores and 48 GB.
  - During the second run, the mean 1-minute load average was 6.1 (max 7.3), and Ollama had a model
    resident in all 90 per-article samples. During the first run, the load average was 24.6 (max 43.7).
  - Medians of 5 and per-article interleaving keep rows comparable within one run. Compare rows within a
    run, not across runs.
  - Absolute milliseconds are pessimistic. This is not the latency suite.
- **The signal check is narrow.** It uses one decision model at one operating point, and agreement is with
  that model's own verdict on the gold lede, not with the labels: the test split's labels stay reserved for
  the one-shot holdout. It covers the lede only, so tail leakage (finding 4) is not exercised.
- **The title is held fixed in the signal check.** The served title, from the JSON-LD headline, `og:title` or
  `<title>`, equals the gold headline in 85 to 90% of the extracted articles, depending on the row (87% for
  the cascade and for `trafilatura`).
- **Install sizes are macOS arm64 wheels.** Linux wheels differ, and runtime `__pycache__` is not counted.
- **Versions**: `selectolax` 1.0.1, `lxml` 6.1.3, `beautifulsoup4` 4.15.0, `trafilatura` 2.3.1,
  `readability-lxml` 0.8.4.1, `newspaper4k` 0.9.6, `justext` 3.0.2, and Ollama 0.40.6.

## Reproduce

```bash
uv run python -m veritrade_evals.extraction_bench list              # the 22 rows
uv run python -m veritrade_evals.extraction_bench measure --fresh   # timing + quality, CPU only (~5 min)
uv run python -m veritrade_evals.extraction_bench signal            # lede verdicts via native Ollama, concurrency 1
uv run python -m veritrade_evals.extraction_bench report            # evals/results/extraction/{matrix.json,summary.md}
```

`measure` and `signal` need the private article files (`articles verify` passes). `measure` resumes when run
without `--fresh`. `signal` calls the model only for ledes it has not seen. It reads the operating point from
`evals/results/grid/signal__clef-flash_9b-q8_0.json`, so re-run it after the grid's best config changes.

# policy      probability | label-logprob | ordinal  (streaming and /analyze always use ordinal)

# Default: the app uses native Ollama on the host (Metal on macOS; on Linux start it with OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0).
#   docker compose up -d
# Bundled: CPU Ollama in a container, models pulled on first start (Linux, CI, no native install).
#   docker compose --profile bundled --env-file deploy/bundled.env up -d
# Either way the UI and API answer on http://localhost:8000 (VT_PORT changes the host port).
name: veritrade

services:
  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/app.Dockerfile
    image: veritrade-app:local
    ports:
      - "${VT_PORT:-8000}:8000"
    environment:
      VT_OLLAMA_BASE_URL: ${VT_OLLAMA_BASE_URL:-http://host.docker.internal:11434}
      VT_OLLAMA_BACKEND_LABEL: ${VT_OLLAMA_BACKEND_LABEL:-native-metal}
      # Empty values keep the models.toml allowlist and defaults.
      VT_MODELS: ${VT_MODELS:-}
      VT_DEFAULT_MODEL_SIGNAL: ${VT_DEFAULT_MODEL_SIGNAL:-}
      VT_DEFAULT_MODEL_SUMMARY: ${VT_DEFAULT_MODEL_SUMMARY:-}
      VT_DEFAULT_MODEL_ANALYZE: ${VT_DEFAULT_MODEL_ANALYZE:-}
      # Passed through only when set on the host; otherwise the app's public contact default applies.
      SEC_USER_AGENT:
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
    depends_on:
      ollama-pull:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
        required: false

  ollama:
    profiles: [bundled]
    image: ollama/ollama:${OLLAMA_IMAGE_TAG:-0.40.6}
    # Unlimited by default; OLLAMA_CPUS=4 mimics a GitHub runner and spares a busy host.
    cpus: ${OLLAMA_CPUS:-0}
    volumes:
      # OLLAMA_MODEL_DIR swaps the named volume for a host directory (CI caches it between runs).
      - ${OLLAMA_MODEL_DIR:-ollama-models}:/root/.ollama/models
    environment:
      OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE: 30m
      OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS: "2"
      OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION: "1"
      OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE: q8_0
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "ollama", "list"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 10s
      retries: 30

  ollama-pull:
    profiles: [bundled]
    image: ollama/ollama:${OLLAMA_IMAGE_TAG:-0.40.6}
    depends_on:
      ollama:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      OLLAMA_HOST: http://ollama:11434
      VT_PULL_MODELS: ${VT_PULL_MODELS:-qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0}
    volumes:
      - ./docker/ollama-pull.sh:/ollama-pull.sh:ro
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "/ollama-pull.sh"]
    restart: "no"

volumes:
  ollama-models:
---

ci.yml
live-smoke.yml

bundled.env
ci-models.txt
models-eval.txt

app.Dockerfile
e2e/
