# 01 - Design decisions

Every decision below was settled with Kris in a `/grill-me` interview (2026-10-16 to 2026-10-18) before any code
was written. Background facts came from read-only research agents (local machine, Ollama library, Docker/CI, news
sources, datasets, transcript format) and were re-verified against primary sources where they were surprising
(the Ollama decision-model API). The full conversation is in `.context/transcript/`.

Guiding principle (Kris, R2): **this is a PoC - balance the level of rigor per aspect**, no exhaustive sweeps.

## Round 1

| # | Question | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Where does the Ollama server run? | Native Ollama on the host is the documented default on macOS; a `bundled` compose profile runs `ollama/ollama` (CPU) for Linux/CI; `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` switches; benchmarks are labelled `native-metal` / `docker-cpu` | Docker Desktop cannot pass Apple's GPU into Linux containers (~0.2x prompt-eval, ~0.4x generation vs native); reviewers on Macs will have Ollama anyway |
| Q2 | What does "precision" mean, how is a winner picked? | Positives are directional calls (bullish/bearish); neutral is the safe default. Selection metric F0.5 macro over {bullish, bearish}; bullish<->bearish inversions capped at 2%; winner = best F0.5 inside the latency budget, else the Pareto knee | A wrong call costs a trade, a missed call costs little; F0.5 cannot be gamed by "always neutral" |
| Q3 | Sentiment output contract | 3-class `sentiment` + `abstained`; compare two precision knobs for generative models (label-token logprob threshold vs ordinal -2..+2 \|score\| threshold) and keep the better one; decision models threshold their native class probabilities | Ollama emits logprobs, but only for non-streaming calls; the ordinal knob also works when streaming |
| Q4 | What does the quick signal read? | `scope=lede` (headline + opening paragraphs) by default, `scope=full` available; both evaluated for accuracy and speed | Lede matches headline-level datasets and decision-model context limits; prompt length drives latency |
| Q5 | Article-level gold set | 90 real articles (10 sources x 3 classes x 3), labelled by Opus subagents, no human check | Public datasets are sentences/headlines; real requests are full articles |
| Q6 | Public datasets and splits | Dev: stratified 300 from Twitter Financial News train. Holdout: full Twitter validation + Financial PhraseBank AllAgree (downloaded at eval time, never committed, CC BY-NC-SA) + FinEntity single-label paragraphs | Twitter FNS already uses Bearish/Bullish/Neutral and has official splits; FPB is the cleanest cross-domain check |
| Q7 | Prompt tuning method | Automated grid per model, then one manual error-analysis pass, freeze, run holdout once. Optional backlog starts with a DSPy-style optimizer loop | Reproducible and explainable within a PoC budget |
| Q8 | API surface | `/api/signal`, `/api/summary`, `/api/analyze`, `/api/models`, `/api/health`; model allowlist; per-URL fetch cache with single-flight; result cache; timing breakdown in every response; SSE **and** JSON variants for `/summary` and `/analyze` | Streaming improves perceived latency; both variants make the comparison measurable |
| Q9 | How the UI is served | Reopened in round 2 (R1) | - |
| Q10 | Extraction | Full parser x extractor comparison matrix, switchable from the UI, results published | Extraction quality and speed both feed end-to-end latency |
| Q11 | Fixtures and publisher rights | Skeleton fixtures (real DOM structure, synthetic text) + scheduled live smoke; article texts never committed (URL + hash + labels only) | Respect each publisher's content rights in a public repo |
| Q12 | CI | Everything on GitHub Actions, including e2e with a real tiny model | Free for public repos |
| Q13 | Transcript | Redacted raw JSONL + rendered Markdown/HTML + `meta.json` under `.context/transcript/`, stripped of anything not suitable for a public repo | The brief asks for the AI log; Kris wants reviewers to read it |
| Q14 | Git workflow | Milestone commits straight to `main`, no feature branches; repo-local author Kristiyan Dimitrov; public repo `cleverjobs/veritrade-analytics` | Solo PoC |
| Q15 | Tooling | Python 3.13 uv workspace (`backend`, `evals`), ruff + mypy; Node 24 + pnpm, Next.js 16 strict TS, ESLint + Prettier, Vitest + RTL + MSW, Playwright | Conventional, fast |
| Q16 | Native Ollama install | `brew install ollama` + `brew services` | Metal acceleration for evals and the native path |
| Q17 | Model roster | See R2 and the follow-ups | - |
| Q18 | Top-10 sources | Yahoo Finance, CNBC, AP News, Investing.com, Motley Fool, Benzinga, PR Newswire, GlobeNewswire, SEC EDGAR 8-K EX-99.1, CNN Business; backups Fortune, Business Wire, Guardian, BBC; the live probe decides | Reviewer likelihood x accessibility; the brief names earnings reports, EDGAR is their primary source |
| Q19 | Fetch identity | Standard browser header set, no evasion (no captcha solving, proxies or TLS impersonation); typed `source_blocked` / `paywalled` / `consent_required` errors with hints; `SEC_USER_AGENT` for EDGAR | Neither end of the spectrum |
| Q20 | Yahoo EU consent wall | Submit "reject all" and cache the cookie; fall back to `consent_required` | Gets the article without granting tracking consent on anyone's behalf |

## Round 2

| # | Question | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | UI serving topology | FastAPI serves the static Next.js export from the same origin (multi-stage Docker build); dev uses `pnpm dev` + CORS for localhost | No proxy hop on the latency path, no nginx, no Node at runtime; the brief requires a Python backend anyway |
| R2 | Decision models | `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` + `nimble:9b-q4_K_M`, with `qwen3.5:0.8b` as the generative baseline | PoC balance; clef-flash by request, nimble best published accuracy among the rest |
| R3 | Streaming `/analyze` | Typed SSE events `meta` -> `sentiment` -> `summary_delta*` -> `done`; JSON field order (sentiment-first vs summary-first) is an eval dimension | Sentiment arrives after a handful of output tokens when it is generated first |
| R4 | Extraction matrix + reference | 4 parsers x 4 own strategies + trafilatura (default, precision), readability-lxml, newspaper4k, justext, strip-tags; reference bodies produced by Opus, kept local (gitignored) | Comparable quality metric without publishing article text |
| R5 | Article-set procedure | Opus discovery via RSS/sections (last ~60 days, fetchable by our fetcher); two independent Opus labellers + adjudicator, ambiguous articles replaced; agreement reported; split 30 dev / 60 test | Stand-in for a human check |
| R6 | Summary evaluation | Deterministic checks (numbers grounded in source, entity named, length) + key-fact coverage via a local embedding model + Opus-as-judge on finalists | Cheap reproducible signal plus a strong judge where it matters |
| R7 | Latency budgets (native, warm, excl. fetch) | `/signal` lede p50 <= 500 ms; `/summary` and `/analyze` TTFT <= 1.5 s, complete p50 <= 4 s; unrealistic budgets are surfaced, not silently moved | Concrete selection gate |
| R8 | Bundled models | Per-endpoint winners if they total <= ~10 GB, else the best finalist that fits; all other Docker containers stopped during setup | Docker Desktop VM has 15.6 GiB |
| R9 | Transcript scope | Only this build session (main + subagents + workflows) | No other relevant sessions |
| R10 | Docs layout | `.context/docs/design/NN-*.md`, backlog in `90-optional-backlog.md`, eval reports in `evals/results/` | Book-order reading |

## Follow-ups

- Generative roster trimmed: summary {`qwen3.5:2b`, `qwen3.5:4b`}; combined {`qwen3.5:4b`, `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507`,
  `ministral-3:3b`}; `qwen3.5:9b` only as a holdout quality ceiling; Gemma 4 dropped (open think+format bug).
- Lean prompt grid: 2 rubric styles x few-shot {0, 4} x field order where relevant (<= 8 configs per model).
- Stopped Docker containers stay stopped; the restart command is handed back at the end.
- `tev1:0.8b-q8_0` is used only in CI to exercise the real decision-model path in containers; it is not evaluated.

## Build-time findings that adjusted the plan

Measured during P1/P2, recorded here so the deviations are traceable. Inputs for the Ollama probe were synthetic
(`evals/results/ollama_probe.json`, native Metal, warm, n=5).

- **Sources** (`02-source-probe.md`): AP News, Investing.com, Benzinga and Business Wire refuse a plain client at
  their CDN (Cloudflare / Akamai), so all four backups were promoted. Final 10: Yahoo Finance, CNBC, Motley Fool,
  PR Newswire, GlobeNewswire, SEC EDGAR EX-99.1, CNN Business, Fortune, Guardian Business, BBC Business.
- **R7 sanity gate passed**: each endpoint has at least one candidate inside its budget, so no budget moved.
  - `/signal`: `qwen3.5:0.8b` answers in 190 ms at ~510 prompt tokens. The 9B decision models take 1.3-1.5 s
    at the same size, so they are reported against the budget rather than the budget relaxed for them.
  - `/summary`: `qwen3.5:2b` shows first text at 0.93 s and finishes at 2.2 s on ~1.6k-token articles;
    `qwen3.5:4b` misses the 1.5 s TTFT budget at that size (2.4 s).
  - `/analyze`: `ministral-3:3b` reaches the score at 1.47 s and finishes at 3.5 s on ~1.75k tokens; the 4B
    qwen models miss TTFT at full-article size.
- **Logprobs**: Ollama 0.40.6 also returns logprobs on streamed chunks (undocumented). The knob comparison stays
  on non-streaming `/signal`; `/analyze` keeps the ordinal knob. Logprob-weighted streaming confidence goes to
  the backlog.
- **Field order**: `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507` ignores schema property order (always entity, score, summary) and
  ignores `think:false` when a schema is set, so the field-order dimension runs on `qwen3.5:4b` and
  `ministral-3:3b` only.
- **Fetch cap** raised from 5 MB to 10 MB: CNN article pages are 5.7-6.6 MB decompressed.
- **Sampling penalties zeroed**: the qwen3.5 Modelfiles ship `presence_penalty 1.5`, which still applies under
  greedy decoding. Few-shot answers end in `neutral` / `0`, so the penalty pushed generated labels away from
  neutral (26 of 60 dev tweets disagreed with the logprob argmax; 0 of 60 with the penalty off). Every chat call
  now pins `presence_penalty 0`, `frequency_penalty 0`, `repeat_penalty 1`; `num_predict` still bounds runaway
  output.
- **Length-cut generations are salvaged**: a summary or analyze output that hits `num_predict` returns its fields
  with the summary cut to the last full sentence and `truncated: true`, instead of a 502 after a doubled-budget
  retry.
- **Summary length is enforced in serving** (R6 follow-up): no candidate reached the 0.8 deterministic pass rate
  on the dev articles, mostly on the 60-word cap. Rather than relax the gate, the service caps every summary at
  3 sentences / 60 words at a sentence boundary, and the frozen prompts ask for 2-3 sentences of at most 50 words
  that name the primary entity first.
- **Key-fact coverage threshold 0.60** (R6): a hand spot-check of 45 key facts on 10 dev articles agreed best
  at a cosine of 0.60 (33/45); 0.75 marked no false "covered" but missed 20 stated facts. 0.60 is primary and
  0.75 is reported as a conservative bound; the Opus judge remains the selection signal.
- **Docker-cpu pass 1 was biased by Ollama's prompt cache**: the pass ran the bundled app over HTTP (n=10 warm per
  cell), and each JSON cell re-sent prompts its SSE twin had just evaluated on the same articles, so its prompt eval
  read 118-171 ms. `container_reload` in `evals/src/veritrade_evals/latency.py` now stops the model inside the
  bundled container (`docker exec ... ollama stop`) before every warm phase, mirroring the native suite's unload.
- **Docker-cpu pass 2 was invalidated by host contention**: unrelated workloads on the same Mac pushed the load
  average to 50-64 (6.89 at the native preflight, [`preflight.json`](../../../evals/results/latency/preflight.json)),
  `qwen3.5:0.8b` decode went from about 31 ms to about 2.8 s per token, and 4 `/analyze` requests timed out. The
  bundled Ollama runs llama.cpp with 14 threads on a 14-vCPU Docker VM over a 14-core host, and its spin-barrier
  threads stall whenever the host takes cores. The samples of both passes were discarded and are not committed.
  - Pass 1's valid streaming rows, indicative only (native-metal p50 from
    [`latency.md`](../../../evals/results/latency/latency.md) in brackets): `/signal` 0.8b lede p50 2,657 ms (178);
    `/summary` 4B SSE TTFT 8,768 ms (1,128), complete 14,405 ms (2,199); `/analyze` 4B SSE time to signal
    8,644 ms (1,098), TTFT 9,147 ms (1,292), complete 12,106 ms (2,584). CPU-only Docker is roughly 5-15x slower
    than Metal on this machine, which is why native Ollama is the macOS default (Q1) and the bundled profile is for
    Linux and CI.
<!-- PENDING:docker-cpu one line: date and load average of the quiet-host re-run and its per-endpoint docker-cpu p50 / TTFT against native, linking evals/results/latency/latency.md -->
- **`OLLAMA_CPUS` is a quota, not a thread count**: compose's `cpus:` caps CPU time but does not lower llama.cpp's
  thread count, so a quota below the visible core count can make CPU inference slower, not just capped. A `cpuset`
  or `num_thread` is the fix ([90-optional-backlog.md](90-optional-backlog.md)).

`uv run python -m veritrade_evals select` applied the Q2 / R6 / R7 rules to the committed results, and

[`selection.md`](../../../evals/results/selection/selection.md); latency is native-metal, warm, excluding fetch
([`latency.md`](../../../evals/results/latency/latency.md)). Every endpoint had an accuracy-eligible candidate inside
its budget, so no Pareto knee was needed.

| Endpoint | Winner, frozen config | Rule that picked it | Accuracy (dev) | Latency p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/signal` | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0`, v2-label, label logprobs with `directional_tau` 0.28, lede | Best dev300 F0.5 among candidates with dev300 inversions <= 2%, an articles-dev inversion CI reaching 2%, and lede p50 <= 500 ms | dev300 F0.5 0.730 [0.651, 0.795]; articles 0.685 | 178 ms |
| `/summary` | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M`, prompt v2 | Deterministic pass rate >= 0.8 and both stream budgets, then Opus judge faithfulness | Faithfulness 4.40 vs 3.97 for `qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M`, paired gap 0.43 [0.07, 0.77] ([summary eval](../../../evals/results/summary/summary.md)) | TTFT 1,128 ms, complete 2,199 ms |
| `/analyze` | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M`, v1, ordinal \|s\| >= 1, sentiment-first | As `/signal`, with TTFT p50 <= 1.5 s and complete p50 <= 4 s | dev300 F0.5 0.752 [0.664, 0.834]; articles 0.880 | Signal 1,098 ms, TTFT 1,292 ms, complete 2,584 ms |

- **Bundle (R8)**: the winners alone, `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` and `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M`, are 4.34 GB of model files

  needed.
- **The `/signal` trade-off**: `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` has the best dev300 F0.5 (0.874 [0.811, 0.937]) but misses the

# 04 - Evaluation

How the models, prompts and thresholds behind `/signal`, `/summary` and `/analyze` were chosen, and how well they
do. The reasons behind each choice are in [`01-decisions.md`](01-decisions.md); the fetch and extraction path every
eval runs through is in [`02-source-probe.md`](02-source-probe.md) and [`03-extraction.md`](03-extraction.md).
Every number links to the committed result file it comes from. Rigor is balanced per aspect, as for the rest of this
PoC (R2): the signal metric, the splits and the one-time holdout are strict; the prompt grid is deliberately lean;
the article labels and summary judgements come from Claude Opus subagents with no human check.

```
dev300 grid (prompt x policy x threshold per model) -> one error-analysis pass -> articles dev check (transfer only,
never re-tuned) -> freeze -> summary eval on the frozen prompts -> latency suite -> select -> holdout, run once
```

## 1. Objective and metrics

A wrong directional call costs a trade, a missed one costs little (Q2). So the positives are directional calls, and
neutral or an abstention is the safe default. Definitions follow
[`metrics.py`](../../../evals/src/veritrade_evals/metrics.py):

- **Directional call**: an answered (not abstained) bullish or bearish prediction. An abstention is served as neutral
  with `abstained: true`. **Coverage** is the share of rows answered, **signal rate** the share with a directional
  call, **accuracy** the share whose served label (abstention -> neutral) equals gold.
- **Precision / recall** per class c in {bullish, bearish}: correct c calls / c calls and correct c calls / gold c
  rows. A class with no calls scores 0, not NaN, so "always neutral" scores F0.5 0.
- **F0.5 macro** (the selection metric): the mean of the two per-class F-beta scores at beta = 0.5, which weights
  precision above recall. Neutral is not a positive class.
- **Inversion rate**: bullish<->bearish flips (a directional call on a gold-directional row with the opposite label)
  over all directional calls. The cap is **2%**.
- **Operating point**: thresholds are swept over 0 and every distinct confidence value (the only points where calls
  change); the chosen point is the **max F0.5 among points with inversion <= 2%**, ties to higher coverage, then a
  lower threshold. A config with no point under the cap is "cap missed" and cannot be selected.
- **Prevalence weights** (dev300 only): each row weighs train prior / sample prior of its class, so rates estimate
  the real tweet mix; confusion and error counts stay raw. Articles and holdout sets are unweighted.
- **CIs**: 95% percentile bootstrap (B = 1,000, seed 20261018), resampled within each gold class, on the headline
  metrics only (F0.5 macro, inversion, coverage, signal rate, accuracy). Gaps between two configs on the same rows use
  a paired bootstrap. The threshold is not re-chosen per resample, so a CI at a tuned operating point is optimistic.

## 2. Datasets and splits

From the split headers in [`evals/data/splits/`](../../../evals/data/splits/) and [`stats.json`](../../../evals/data/articles/stats.json):

| split | source | role | n | bullish / bearish / neutral | weighting |
|---|---|---|--:|---|---|
| `dev300` | Twitter Financial News Sentiment (FNS), train | tuning: prompt grid, thresholds | 300 | 100 / 100 / 100 | train prior 20.2% / 15.1% / 64.7% |
| articles dev | Opus-labelled articles (section 3) | transfer check, error analysis, summary eval | 30 | 10 / 10 / 10 | none |
| articles test | Opus-labelled articles | holdout | 60 | 20 / 20 / 20 | none |
| `tfns_val` | Twitter FNS, validation | holdout, in-domain tweets | 2,388 | 475 / 347 / 1,566 | none (natural prior) |
| `fpb_allagree` | Financial PhraseBank, Sentences_AllAgree | holdout, cross-domain sentences | 2,259 | 570 / 303 / 1,386 | none |
| `finentity_single` | FinEntity, rows with one distinct label | holdout, cross-domain paragraphs | 851 | 181 / 180 / 490 | none |

- **dev300** comes from Twitter FNS train after dropping 69 rows whose normalised text is also in validation, 70
  duplicates and 4 rows with conflicting labels; then 100 per class with seed 20261018. Class weights are 0.605
  (bullish), 0.453 (bearish) and 1.942 (neutral). FPB and FinEntity positive / negative / neutral map to bullish /
  bearish / neutral; FPB collapses exact duplicates and drops sentences seen with two labels; FinEntity keeps rows
  with at least one entity annotation and exactly one distinct label.
- **Committed**: per split, the ids, the sha1 of the normalised text (NFKC, casefold, URLs and whitespace runs
  dropped), the labels, the selection rule and the dataset revision;
  [`datasets.lock.json`](../../../evals/data/datasets.lock.json) pins each dataset commit, file sha256 and licence. A
  split fails to load on a revision mismatch, a missing id, text-hash drift or label drift.
- **Never committed**: dataset text (FPB is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0), downloaded at eval time into the gitignored
  `evals/data/private/`, along with article HTML, gold bodies, headlines, predictions, summaries and judge packets.

## 3. The Opus-labelled article set

Public datasets hold sentences and headlines; the service reads whole articles (Q5, R5). The set has 90 real articles
from the 10 sources in [`02-source-probe.md`](02-source-probe.md), 3 classes x 3 per source, published 2026-08-19 to
2026-10-18. One seeded article per (source, class) cell goes to dev: **30 dev / 60 test**. Two quota adjustments keep
the 30/30/30 balance (Yahoo 4 bearish, BBC 2 bearish). Every Opus step ran as a Claude Code subagent pinned to Claude Opus
5.5, so no API key or paid service was used. Prompts and runbook: [`evals/opus_prompts/`](../../../evals/opus_prompts/00-README.md).

1. **Discover** (one agent per source): candidates from RSS and section pages, fetched by the deterministic
   `articles` CLI through the serving fetcher; agents never fetch anything themselves.
2. **Gold**: Opus picks the body as line ranges of the page, writes 3-5 key facts in its own words, and gives a
   provisional label.
3. **Label A / label B**: two independent agents apply the service's rubric (economic impact on the primary entity,
   not tone; neutral when in doubt), never seeing each other's output or the provisional label.
4. **Adjudicate**: one agent reviews every article where the labels differ or either labeller flagged ambiguity, and
   either keeps it (its label is final) or replaces it as genuinely ambiguous.
5. **Refill and finalize**: short cells repeat steps 1-4; `finalize` picks per cell, agreed articles first; `verify`
   re-checks the set.

| pool statistic | value |
|---|--:|
| articles with a usable gold body | 298 |
| labelled by both labellers | 157 |
| labels agree | 151 (raw agreement 96.2%) |
| Cohen's kappa (A vs B) | 0.943 |
| sent to adjudication (6 disagreements, 43 agreed but flagged ambiguous) | 49 (31.2%) |
| replaced by the adjudicator | 24 of 49 (49.0%) |
| adjudicated articles kept in the final 90 | 5 |

In the final 90, A and B agree on every label (kappa 1.0), by construction since agreed articles are picked first, so
the pool agreement is the meaningful figure. The committed [`articles.jsonl`](../../../evals/data/articles/articles.jsonl)
holds ids, URLs, sources, dates, both labels, the adjudication, entity and ticker, and rationales and key facts in
Opus's words; the CLI rejects any that share 10 consecutive words with the article, so no article text is committed.
**Caveats**: Opus-only labels with no human check; replacing ambiguous articles makes the set cleaner than real
traffic; with 10 articles per class on dev, a gap needs about 0.2 F0.5 to clear zero.

## 4. Models, prompts and confidence policies

**Roster** (R2 and its follow-ups). The split architecture serves `/signal` + `/summary`; the combined one `/analyze`.

| endpoint | models | kind |
|---|---|---|
| `/signal` | `clef-flash:9b-q8_0`, `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` | decision models (native class probabilities) |
| `/signal` | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | generative baseline (label and ordinal schemas) |
| `/summary` | `qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M`, `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | generative |
| `/analyze` | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M`, `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M`, `ministral-3:3b` | generative, one call -> score + entity + summary |
| `/analyze` (holdout only) | `qwen3.5:9b-q4_K_M` | quality ceiling, untuned (prompt v1, \|s\| >= 1) |

**Lean prompt grid** on dev300: 33 cells ([`grid/manifest.json`](../../../evals/results/grid/manifest.json)), all on
native Metal, Ollama 0.40.6, greedy (temperature 0, seed 0, sampling penalties neutralised; see the build-time
findings in `01-decisions.md`).

- Generative `/signal` and `/analyze`: rubric A (definitions) or B (impact questions) x 0 or 4 synthetic shots =
  v1-v4; for `qwen3.5:0.8b` each runs on both the label and the ordinal schema.
- Decision models: rubric or plain one-line question x described or bare criteria = v1-v4.
- `/analyze` follow-ups, paired against v1: v5 (the tightened summary rule) and `v1-summary-first` (the field-order
  check, on `qwen3.5:4b` and `ministral` only).

**Confidence policies** ([`confidence.py`](../../../backend/src/veritrade/inference/confidence.py)):

- **probability** (decision models): argmax of the native class probabilities; abstain when it is below `min_p`.
- **label-logprob** (generative `/signal`): first label-token probabilities, renormalised over the tokens the grammar
  accepts, with the same `min_p` rule. With **`directional_tau`**, a neutral argmax still yields the likelier
  directional class when that class holds p >= tau; below tau the row is a served neutral, not an abstention. On a
  first-token label collision the adapter re-asks with the ordinal schema.
- **ordinal** (`/analyze`, streams, fallback): a score from -2 to 2, directional only when \|score\| >= t. It is read
  mid-stream as soon as it closes and needs no logprobs (Q3); logprob-weighted streaming confidence is on the backlog.

**Scope and field order.** `/signal` reads `lede` by default (headline plus opening paragraphs, body capped at 200
tokens); `lede` and `full` are both scored on articles. `/analyze` reads `full` and emits the sentiment field first,
so the score streams after a handful of tokens (R3).

**Error analysis and freeze.** One hand-written read of the grid counts
([`grid/notes.md`](../../../evals/results/grid/notes.md)) drove the changes listed in section 5. The `freeze`
command then wrote [`frozen.json`](../../../evals/results/frozen.json) and
[`models.toml`](../../../backend/src/veritrade/data/models.toml):

| endpoint | model | frozen prompt | policy | threshold | field order |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/signal` | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | `v2@ff82e957` (rubric A, 4 shots, label schema) | label-logprob + `directional_tau` | min_p 0, tau 0.28 (ordinal \|s\| >= 1 fallback) | - |
| `/signal` | `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` | `v4@fcc93f1b` (plain question, bare labels) | probability | min_p 0.80 | - |
| `/signal` | `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` | `v1@a1e34f63` (rubric, described criteria) | probability | min_p 0.97 | - |
| `/summary` | `qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M`, `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | `v2@84ce3858` (tightened summary rule) | - | - | - |
| `/analyze` | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | `v1@7daf4f28` | ordinal | \|s\| >= 1 | sentiment-first |
| `/analyze` | `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M` | `v5@e2b57fc6` | ordinal | \|s\| >= 1 | sentiment-first |
| `/analyze` | `ministral-3:3b` | `v5@e2b57fc6` | ordinal | \|s\| >= 1 | sentiment-first |

Freeze rules: `/signal` keeps the dev300 best rule unless it clearly fails on the articles. `/analyze` takes v5
unless the whole paired 95% CI of its gap against v1 is below zero on dev300 or the articles, which rejected v5 for
`qwen3.5:4b` (articles -0.080 [-0.178, -0.014]). Summary-first needed a dev300 win without an articles loss; it never
got one.

## 5. Accuracy on dev

Frozen configs only. Articles use the dev300 threshold unchanged and the serving extraction (`selectolax` +
`cascade`). Sources: [`grid/summary.md`](../../../evals/results/grid/summary.md),
[`articles_dev/summary.md`](../../../evals/results/articles_dev/summary.md).

**`/signal`** (dev300 weighted; articles lede is the served default):

| model | dev300 F0.5 [95% CI] | P bull / P bear | inversion | coverage | signal rate | articles lede F0.5 [95% CI] | inv. | articles full F0.5 [95% CI] | inv. |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|---|--:|---|--:|
| `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | 0.730 [0.651, 0.795] | 0.914 / 0.918 | 0.0% | 100.0% | 15.4% | 0.685 [0.473, 0.833] | 1/14 | 0.635 [0.329, 0.817] | 0/10 |
| `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` | 0.874 [0.811, 0.937] | 0.867 / 0.905 | 0.0% | 72.9% | 33.2% | 0.848 [0.708, 0.963] | 1/20 | 0.907 [0.820, 0.989] | 0/20 |
| `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` | 0.843 [0.773, 0.901] | 0.948 / 0.891 | 0.0% | 26.3% | 24.2% | 0.895 [0.771, 0.976] | 0/17 | 0.880 [0.761, 0.976] | 0/19 |

**`/analyze`** (full scope, sentiment-first, \|s\| >= 1, coverage 100% for all):

| model | config | dev300 F0.5 [95% CI] | P bull / P bear | inversion | signal rate | articles F0.5 [95% CI] | inv. |
|---|---|---|---|--:|--:|---|--:|
| `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | v1 | 0.752 [0.664, 0.834] | 0.877 / 0.821 | 0.0% | 21.4% | 0.880 [0.791, 0.989] | 0/22 |
| `ministral-3:3b` | v5 | 0.685 [0.589, 0.772] | 0.837 / 0.768 | 1.0% | 20.0% | 0.741 [0.611, 0.858] | 0/19 |
| `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M` | v5 | 0.647 [0.553, 0.741] | 0.702 / 0.752 | 0.0% | 23.1% | 0.779 [0.646, 0.879] | 1/22 |

No served rule clearly fails on the articles (whole inversion CI above 2%, or whole coverage CI below half the dev300
coverage), so every dev300 threshold stands. What the error analysis found
([`grid/notes.md`](../../../evals/results/grid/notes.md),
[`error_patterns.json`](../../../evals/results/grid/error_patterns.json)):

- **Inversions are nearly absent**: across the six best configs one tweet is inverted, by `ministral`. Wrong calls
  are mostly gold-neutral tweets called directional (1-8 per model). The real loss is recall: 34 (`clef-flash`) to
  162 (`qwen3.5:0.8b`) directional tweets missed; for every generative model the largest miss bucket is price-move
  tweets, which the impact rubric reads as immaterial.
- **`directional_tau` is the largest single lever**: `qwen3.5:0.8b` parks most of its mass on neutral, and the tau
  rule lifts its F0.5 by +0.218 [+0.141, +0.307] (paired). It loses for the peaked decision models (-0.046 and
  -0.303), so they keep the plain rule.
- **Other changes**: rubric A beats B for every generative model; shots help `qwen3.5:0.8b` on the label schema but
  hurt every `/analyze` model, so all frozen `/analyze` prompts are zero-shot; summary-first never wins and delays
  the score (2-3x on articles). The price-move rubric sentence was not added: articles do not show the tweet miss
  (0-1 of 5 directional price-move headlines missed).
- **Knob comparison**: without tau, the logprob knob beats the ordinal one on `qwen3.5:0.8b` by +0.059 [-0.068,
  +0.187], not significant; with tau it wins clearly. The ordinal schema cannot use tau, because this tokenizer fuses
  `" -"` and hides the sign of negative scores.

## 6. Summary evaluation

Decision R6, run by `veritrade_evals.summary_eval` on the stored HTML of the 30 dev articles through the serving
adapters (full scope, frozen prompts). Serving caps every summary at **3 sentences / 60 words** at a sentence
boundary, and the checks score the capped text.

- **Deterministic checks** (pass-rate gate >= 0.8): length, sentence count, every number grounded in the gold article
  (format-tolerant; a derived figure counts as unsupported), gold entity named, not truncated.
- **Key-fact coverage**: each Opus key fact and each summary sentence is embedded with `qwen3-embedding:0.6b`; a fact
  is covered at a best cosine **>= 0.60** (primary), with 0.75 as the strict bound. In the hand-labelled spot check
  of 45 facts on 10 summaries ([`spotcheck.dev.json`](../../../evals/results/summary/spotcheck.dev.json)), 0.60
  matched 33 of 45 flags with 5 false "covered" and 0.55 matched 34 with 6, a near tie; 0.75 had no false "covered"
  but missed 20 stated facts (see the build-time findings in `01-decisions.md`).
- **Opus judges**, blind: per article the candidate summaries are anonymised as `S1..Sn` and shuffled
  ([`50-judge.md`](../../../evals/opus_prompts/50-judge.md)); each gets faithfulness 1-5, coverage 1-5, a list of
  hallucinations, and whether it leads with the market-moving fact. **Material error rate** = share at
  faithfulness <= 3.

Dev articles, n = 30 per row ([`summary/summary.md`](../../../evals/results/summary/summary.md)); length and sentence
count pass 100% by construction; CIs resample articles within their sentiment label.

| endpoint | model | pass | numbers | entity | key facts 0.60 / 0.75 | faithful [95% CI] | cover | halluc. flag | material [95% CI] | leads |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|---|---|--:|--:|---|--:|
| summary | `qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M` | 90% | 97% | 93% | 52% / 24% | 3.97 [3.67, 4.23] | 4.30 | 67% | 30% [17%, 47%] | 90% |
| summary | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | 90% | 93% | 97% | 47% / 23% | 4.40 [4.17, 4.60] | 4.57 | 50% | 10% [0%, 20%] | 100% |
| analyze | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | 93% | 97% | 97% | 57% / 29% | 4.47 [4.20, 4.70] | 4.63 | 40% | 10% [0%, 20%] | 100% |
| analyze | `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M` | 90% | 90% | 100% | 56% / 25% | 4.73 [4.53, 4.93] | 4.43 | 20% | 7% [0%, 17%] | 83% |
| analyze | `ministral-3:3b` | 77% | 80% | 97% | 45% / 19% | 3.77 [3.37, 4.20] | 4.27 | 63% | 40% [23%, 57%] | 80% |

**Hallucination flag vs material error.** The flag rate counts any summary with at least one entry in the judge's
hallucination list, including minor slips that still allow faithfulness 4 (a loosely worded or small unsupported
detail "a trader would shrug off"). The material error rate counts only faithfulness <= 3: a wrong key number, an
unsupported claim that matters, a misattribution, or worse. So `qwen3.5:4b` on `/summary` is flagged on half the
articles but has a material error on 10% [0%, 20%]; the material rate is the one to read as risk. The deterministic
number check agrees in direction: 1-3 unsupported numbers across 30 summaries for the qwen models, 8 for `ministral`.

## 7. Selection

Rules: [`selection/selection.md`](../../../evals/results/selection/selection.md). Accuracy filters come first (dev300
inversion <= 2%, articles dev not clearly over the cap, summary pass rate >= 0.8), then the native warm latency
budgets of R7 (measured in `05-latency.md`). Survivors rank on dev300 F0.5 then articles dev F0.5 (`/signal`,
`/analyze`) or on judge faithfulness then coverage (`/summary`). Budgets are reported, never moved; when nothing meets
one, the Pareto knee is used with the reason stated.

| endpoint | winner | deciding numbers | others |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/signal` | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` (v2-label, tau 0.28) | only candidate inside the 500 ms lede budget: p50 178 ms, dev300 F0.5 0.730 | `clef-flash` 0.874 at 659 ms; `nimble` 0.843 at 1,061 ms |
| `/summary` | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` (v2) | faithfulness 4.40 vs 3.97, paired +0.43 [0.07, 0.77]; TTFT p50 1,128 ms, complete 2,199 ms | `qwen3.5:2b` faster (484 / 1,272 ms), more material errors (30%) |
| `/analyze` | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` (v1) | dev300 F0.5 0.752; TTFT p50 1,292 ms (limit 1,500), complete 2,584 ms | `ministral` 0.685; `qwen3-instruct` 0.647, though its summary faithfulness is best (4.73 vs 4.47, paired gap 0.27 [-0.07, 0.60], not significant) |

Bundled models (R8): `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` + `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M`, 4.34 GB against the 10 GB cap.

**The `/signal` trade-off.** `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` has the best dev300 F0.5 (0.874) but misses the 500 ms lede budget
(p50 659 ms), and its 10.58 GB file alone exceeds the 10 GB bundle cap. `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` (0.843, 1,061 ms) misses
the budget too. The selected `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` scores 0.730 at 178 ms: high dev300 precision (0.91 / 0.92), low
recall (it misses about half the directional articles on dev). The budget was not moved to fit the 9B models; both
stay on the allowlist and can be chosen per request with the `model` parameter on native Ollama.

## 8. Holdout

Protocol of `uv run python -m veritrade_evals holdout {plan,run,analyze}` ([`holdout.py`](../../../evals/src/veritrade_evals/holdout.py)):

- Frozen rules at their frozen thresholds and prompts, no re-tuning, natural class priors (unweighted); a prompt that
  drifted since the freeze fails the run. `gap` = holdout F0.5 minus the dev F0.5 of the same rule (articles dev at
  the same scope for articles; dev300 for the tweet and cross-domain sets).
- 22 cells: the three `/signal` finalists on the test articles (lede and full) and `tfns_val`; the three `/analyze`
  finalists on the test articles (full) and `tfns_val`; the two winners also on `fpb_allagree` and
  `finentity_single`; the `qwen3.5:9b` ceiling on the test articles and both cross-domain sets. Then summaries from
  the `/summary` and `/analyze` winners on the 60 test articles go to the blind Opus judges.
- **Run once**: [`holdout_runs.json`](../../../evals/results/holdout_runs.json) is a guard keyed by the sha256 of
  `frozen.json`, recording the selection sha256, git sha, and start and completion times. An interrupted run resumes
  from its caches; a completed config refuses a second run unless `--force --reason` is passed, which is logged in
  the guard and must be disclosed. It also refuses a provisional selection (one made before the latency suite)
  without `--allow-provisional`; this selection was not provisional.
- `holdout analyze` only re-scores the cached predictions and never calls a model; the tables below come from the
  `evals/results/holdout/holdout.md` it writes.

## 9. Threats to validity

- **One labeller family**: article labels, gold bodies, key facts and summary judges are all Claude Opus. Labellers
  were independent and judges blind, but a shared bias would not show, and no human checked any label.
- **Small n**: with 30 dev and 60 test articles, CIs span 0.2-0.5 F0.5; article results check that rules transfer,
  they do not rank models.
- **Tuned on tweets**: thresholds and prompts were tuned on 300 tweets and only checked on articles; CIs at a tuned
  threshold exclude the threshold choice, and `directional_tau` is one more tuned parameter.
- **Class mix**: the article sets are balanced while real traffic is likely neutral-heavy (64.7% in Twitter FNS
  train), so per-call precision in production is likely below the article figure. dev300 reweights; articles do not.
- **Cleaner than reality**: 10 fetchable sources, a 60-day window, 24 ambiguous articles replaced; for three sources
  the extraction profiles were tuned with this set in view (caveats in `03-extraction.md`).
- **Contamination**: the public datasets may be in the models' pretraining data; the articles are recent, which
  limits but does not rule out overlap.
- **Precision first, by design**: the selected `/signal` model misses about half the directional articles; a miss is
  cheap under Q2, but users will see many neutrals.
- **Indicative parts**: grid and articles timings ran on a shared machine (selection uses the dedicated native-metal
  suite; Docker CPU is in `05-latency.md`), and the error-analysis keyword buckets are a first-match heuristic.

# 05 - Latency

Question (R7): how fast does each endpoint answer, where does the time go, and which trade-offs shaped the
served defaults? This chapter builds on [00-overview.md](00-overview.md) (endpoints, split / combined),
[01-decisions.md](01-decisions.md) (R7, Q1), [03-extraction.md](03-extraction.md) and [04-evals.md](04-evals.md)
(candidates, selection). Native numbers: [latency.json](../../../evals/results/latency/latency.json), table in
[latency.md](../../../evals/results/latency/latency.md), session `20261018T200825Z`. As a PoC (R2), the suite
measures one machine at one concurrency, in depth; what it leaves out is under "Levers".

## Budgets

Set before any measurement (R7), for native Metal, warm models, excluding fetch: **`/signal` lede p50 <= 500 ms;
`/summary` and `/analyze` TTFT p50 <= 1,500 ms and complete p50 <= 4,000 ms**. A missed budget is reported,
never moved. `/signal` at full scope has no budget (n/a); JSON variants are checked on completion only. The
selection rule (01, Q2) takes the most accurate candidate inside the budget, so these numbers and
[selection.md](../../../evals/results/selection/selection.md) decide the served defaults.

## Method

From [latency.py](../../../evals/src/veritrade_evals/latency.py) and the method block of `latency.md`:

- **App**: the real FastAPI app (`create_app`) in process over an ASGI transport, with a local fetcher serving
  the stored HTML of the 30 dev articles from memory, so the network stays out. Parser `selectolax`, extractor
  `cascade` (the serving default), `no_cache=true` so neither cache can answer.
- **Concurrency 1**, models grouped so each loads once, every other model unloaded first. **Cold**, n=3 per
  cell: the first 3 dev articles, the model unloaded before each request.
- **Warm**, n=30 per cell, one per dev article. Before each cell's warm phase the model is unloaded, then warmed
  on a synthetic page that is not a dev article: Ollama reuses a cached prompt prefix, so warming on a measured
  article, or a JSON cell re-sending its SSE twin's prompts, would make prompt eval look free.
- **Clocks** server side from request receipt (the in-process client agreed within 3 ms). TTFT is the first
  `summary_delta` event; time to signal is the `sentiment` event (for JSON, the total). **Stages**: parse,
  extract, inference wall, load, prompt eval, eval. Decision models answer through `/v1/systemone`, which
  reports wall time and input tokens only, hence their `-` columns.
- **Machine** ([preflight.json](../../../evals/results/latency/preflight.json)): Apple M4 Pro, 14 cores, 48 GB,
  macOS 26.6.2, Ollama 0.40.6 as a brew service with `OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1`, `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=30m`,
  `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0`, `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=3`. No Docker container ran; 1-minute load average
  6.89; the preflight warned that swap held 23,200 of 25,600 MB (free memory 70%). **Output**: 528 samples (16
  cells x 33), 0 errors, ids and numbers only in the
  [raw JSONL](../../../evals/results/latency/raw/20261018T200825Z.jsonl).

### What meets and what misses

- **Every generative candidate meets its budgets at p50.** The R7 sanity gate in 01 predicted a TTFT miss for
  `qwen3.5:4b` (2.4 s on ~1.6k-token synthetic inputs); real dev articles after the cascade are shorter (an
  825-token `/summary` prompt at p50), so its TTFT lands at 1,128 ms.
- **Both 9B decision models miss the `/signal` budget** (659 and 1,061 ms; see the trade-off section below).
- **The tails are outside the budgets, which bind only the p50.** Streamed TTFT p95 is 1,108 ms for the 2B and
  2,469 to 2,995 ms for the 3-4B models; complete p95 passes 4 s for `/summary` 4B (4,232) and for `/analyze` on
  both 4B models (4,627 and 4,979). The tail is the long articles: in the raw samples, the slowest 10% of
  full-scope requests carry about 2,550 to 2,800 prompt tokens against 825 to 1,074 at p50, and write longer.
- In each `qwen3.5:2b` cell, 1 of 30 warm summaries hit `num_predict` and was served cut at a sentence with
  `truncated: true` (01); no other cell truncated. All 165 streamed samples, cold and warm, kept the event
  order (`meta` first, `done` last, one `sentiment` before `done` on `/analyze`).

### Where the time goes

Warm p50s from `latency.json`; per-token rates are ratios of p50s, so approximate.

| endpoint | model | prompt tokens | prompt eval ms | output tokens | eval ms | prompt eval share | decode ms/token |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| /signal lede | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | 530 | 126 | 7 | 43 | 75% | 6.1 |
| /summary SSE | `qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M` | 825 | 423 | 92 | 827 | 34% | 9.0 |
| /summary SSE | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | 825 | 1,029 | 68 | 1,075 | 49% | 15.8 |
| /analyze SSE | `ministral-3:3b` | 979 | 713 | 92 | 1,361 | 34% | 14.8 |
| /analyze SSE | `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M` | 970 | 862 | 88 | 1,236 | 41% | 14.0 |
| /analyze SSE | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | 963 | 992 | 96 | 1,539 | 39% | 16.0 |

- `/signal` is a prefill problem: 7 output tokens (label schema, `num_predict` 16), so prompt length decides
  the time. That is why the quick signal reads the lede (01, Q4).
- The summarisers differ. The 2B spends two thirds decoding; the 4B prefills at about 800 tokens/s against
  about 1,950 for the 2B, so prompt eval is half its time and almost all of its TTFT (1,029 of 1,128 ms).
  Shorter inputs move TTFT; shorter outputs move completion. Warm load is under 1 ms, and everything outside
  inference (parse, extract, input, response) is 3 to 6 ms.

### Streaming, JSON and field order

Same model, same articles: the transport does not change the total (SSE minus JSON is -2.9% to +1.1% at p50),
but SSE shows text at 38 to 54% of it (`/summary` 4B: 1,128 of 2,199 ms). The UI defaults to streaming.

**Sentiment-first field order** (R3) is what makes the streamed signal useful in `/analyze`. The incremental
scanner emits the `sentiment` event as soon as the score closes: 194 to 249 ms before the first summary text,
and 1.1 to 1.5 s before a JSON client would see it (signal 802 / 1,098 ms streamed against 2,219 / 2,580 ms JSON
for `ministral-3:3b` / `qwen3.5:4b`). `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507` ignores schema property order and writes the
entity first (01), so its signal leads the summary by only 83 ms.

### Lede against full scope

| model | lede p50 / p95 | full p50 / p95 | prompt tokens lede / full |
|---|---|---|---|
| `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | 178 / 195 | 231 / 532 | 530 / 1,074 |
| `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` | 659 / 807 | 1,893 / 4,007 | 286 / 831 |
| `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` | 1,061 / 1,182 | 2,321 / 5,242 | 448 / 1,003 |

Full scope costs the 0.8B little at the median but widens every tail: its p95 crosses 500 ms, and the 9B tails
grow 4 to 5 times. Lede keeps `/signal` predictable as well as fast.

### Cold start, parse and extract

- **Cold**: the model load adds 0.7 to 1.3 s over warm for the generative models (load p50 785 to 1,328 ms),
  0.9 to 1.2 s for `nimble` and 5.4 to 6.2 s for `clef-flash` (a 10.58 GB file); n=3, so indicative. A cold 4B
  misses TTFT (2,132 ms for `/summary`). Every call sends `keep_alive` 30m, so only the first request after a
  start or 30 idle minutes pays it.
- **Parse and extract**: 1.2 to 1.6 ms and 1.6 to 2.5 ms at p50 in every cell, under 2% of even the fastest
  `/signal`, so the parser is not a latency lever (03: every parser yields the same body; `selectolax` is
  chosen for speed and footprint). The extractor matters through tokens instead: competent extractors send
  704 to 822 `full` tokens against 2,116 for `strip-tags` (03), and prompt eval scales with that.

## Network

The suite excludes fetch on purpose. Live cost from the source probe ([02-source-probe.md](02-source-probe.md),
EU residential ISP, 2026-10-18): median of the per-source medians 148 ms, slowest 552 ms.

| source | fetch ms (median) | source | fetch ms (median) |
|---|---|---|---|
| bbc | 26 | globenewswire | 552 |
| cnbc | 161 | guardian | 116 |
| cnn | 35 | prnewswire | 34 |
| fool | 202 | sec | 135 |
| fortune | 367 | yahoo | 477 |

As a rough sum of medians (not measured end to end), a lede signal lands about 0.33 s after submit on a
typical source and about 0.73 s on the slowest; on 4 of the 10 sources the fetch takes longer than the signal.
What the service does about it:

- **One pooled HTTP/2 client** (`veritrade.fetch.client`): keep-alive connections (60 s) let a second article
  from the same publisher skip TCP and TLS setup. Deadline 8 s, connect 3 s.
- **Single-flight fetch cache** (`veritrade.fetch.cache`): split mode fires `/signal` and `/summary` at once,
  and the second request joins the first one's in-flight download (`timings.cache.fetch` is `"joined"`), so
  the page is fetched once. Pages live 10 minutes (512 entries, 200 MB); typed fetch errors live 60 s, so a
  refusing publisher is not hit per request.
- **Result cache** (`veritrade.services.cache`): finished responses keyed by (endpoint, url, model, prompt
  version, parser, extractor, scope) for 1 hour; a hit returns with zero stage timings and `meta.cached`.
- **Consent cookie**: the Yahoo reject-all form costs 857 ms once; the shared cookie jar skips it afterwards
  (about 120 ms, 02).

## Split against combined

The UI offers both, split by default. Defaults first, then the other combined candidates; each row measured
alone at concurrency 1.

| arrangement | signal | first summary text | summary complete | resident model files |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| split: `/signal` 0.8B lede + `/summary` `qwen3.5:4b` SSE | 178 | 1,128 | 2,199 | 2 (1.02 + 3.32 GB) |
| combined: `/analyze` `qwen3.5:4b` SSE (default) | 1,098 | 1,292 | 2,584 | 1 (3.32 GB) |
| combined: `/analyze` `ministral-3:3b` SSE | 802 | 1,051 | 2,242 | 1 (2.95 GB) |
| combined: `/analyze` `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507` SSE | 1,118 | 1,201 | 2,234 | 1 (2.50 GB) |

- **Split** gives the fastest signal, about 0.2 s, while the summary streams, at the cost of two prompts, two
  resident models and two prefills of the same article.
- **Combined** yields the signal at about 0.8 to 1.1 s and the summary by about 2.2 to 2.6 s, from one model
  and one prompt. Its signal is not worse: `qwen3.5:4b` scores dev300 F0.5 0.752 against 0.730 for the 0.8B,
  and 0.880 against 0.685 on the 30 dev articles (wide CIs, [selection.md](../../../evals/results/selection/selection.md)).
- **Not measured**: split mode's two requests running at once on one GPU; the split row joins two isolated
  measurements, so its summary times are a lower bound for real use.

## /signal: accuracy against latency

| model | dev300 F0.5 [95% CI] | articles dev F0.5 [95% CI] | lede p50 / p95 ms | cold p50 ms | file GB | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | 0.730 [0.651, 0.795] | 0.685 [0.473, 0.833] | 178 / 195 | 992 | 1.02 | served default |
| `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` | 0.874 [0.811, 0.937] | 0.848 [0.708, 0.963] | 659 / 807 | 6,064 | 10.58 | misses 500 ms; alone over the 10 GB bundle cap (R8) |
| `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` | 0.843 [0.773, 0.901] | 0.895 [0.771, 0.976] | 1,061 / 1,182 | 2,219 | 5.63 | misses 500 ms |

The 9B decision models are 0.11 to 0.14 F0.5 better on dev300 and neither fits the budget, so the 0.8B wins as
the only candidate inside it. The budget was reported, not moved to admit them. Both stay on the allowlist: on
native Ollama a request picks one with the `model` parameter and trades about 0.5 to 0.9 s for precision.
Whether the gap holds on unseen data is a holdout question ([04-evals.md](04-evals.md)).

## docker-cpu

Docker Desktop cannot pass Apple's GPU into a Linux container (01, Q1), so the bundled Ollama runs llama.cpp on
CPU. `latency docker-cpu` measures the bundled defaults over HTTP (`/signal` 0.8B lede JSON; `/summary` and
`/analyze` `qwen3.5:4b`, SSE and JSON), warm n=10 per cell; the app fetches live, so fetch and consent are
subtracted, and it warms up on an 11th dev article.

Two earlier passes were discarded, and neither is committed:

1. **Pass 1 found a prompt-cache bias.** The bundled Ollama has no host port, so the native unload was not
   available, and each JSON cell re-sent the prompts its SSE twin had just evaluated on the same articles;
   those rows showed prompt eval of 118 to 171 ms. Fix: a reload hook (`container_reload` in `latency.py`) runs
   `docker exec ... ollama stop <model>` before every warm phase and waits until `ollama ps` drops it,
   mirroring the native unload.
2. **Pass 2 was invalidated by host contention.** Unrelated workloads on the same Mac pushed the load average
   to 50-64 (6.9 at the native preflight). `qwen3.5:0.8b` decode went from about 31 ms/token to about
   2.8 s/token and 4 `/analyze` requests timed out. Root cause: the bundled Ollama runs llama.cpp with 14
   threads on a 14-vCPU Docker VM over a 14-core host, and its spin-barrier threads stall whenever the host
   takes cores, so CPU inference collapses instead of slowing in proportion.

Indicative only (pass-1 rows the cache bias did not touch, n=10, not committed):

| endpoint | model | transport | complete p50 | TTFT p50 | to signal p50 | x native (complete / TTFT / signal) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| /signal | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` lede | JSON | 2,657 | - | - | 14.9x |
| /summary | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | SSE | 14,405 | 8,768 | - | 6.6x / 7.8x |
| /analyze | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | SSE | 12,106 | 9,147 | 8,644 | 4.7x / 7.1x / 7.9x |

In pass 1, CPU-only Docker was roughly 5 to 15 times slower than Metal on this machine and would miss every
budget. That is why native Ollama is the macOS default and the bundled profile is for Linux and CI: a portability path, not
a latency path. `OLLAMA_CPUS` in `compose.yaml` sets a `cpus:` quota, which does not lower llama.cpp's thread
count, so a quota below the visible core count can make CPU inference slower rather than just capped; a cpuset
or `num_thread` is the fix (backlog). The re-run repeats pass 1's protocol, reload hook included, on a quiet
host, and its rows go in the `docker-cpu` section of `latency.md`.

<!-- PENDING:docker-cpu warm n=10 table from the quiet-host re-run (signal 0.8b lede JSON; summary and analyze qwen3.5:4b SSE and JSON): complete p50/p95, TTFT p50, time to signal p50, ratio to native, preflight load average -->

## Levers

Used:
- **Input and model size**: lede scope for `/signal` (half the tokens of full, p95 195 ms instead of 532); a
  cascade that sends about 720 `full` tokens where `strip-tags` sends about 2,100 (03); the smallest `/signal`
  model that clears the accuracy filters, answering in 7 tokens.
- **Perceived latency**: SSE, sentiment-first field order and an incremental JSON scanner.
- **Warm models**: `keep_alive` 30m on every call; `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS` 3 native (2 bundled) keeps both
  split-mode models resident; flash attention and a q8_0 KV cache in the Ollama env.
- **Bounded generation**: `think: false`, greedy decoding, per-endpoint `num_predict`, and the served summary
  cap of 3 sentences / 60 words (01).
- **Network and hops**: pooled HTTP/2, single-flight fetch cache, result cache, consent cookie reuse; the UI is
  served by the same FastAPI process (R1), and the fast parsers extract inline, without a thread hand-off.

Left: the latency items in [90-optional-backlog.md](90-optional-backlog.md) (progressive `/signal`, split-mode
concurrency, a GPU compose profile, CPU threads for the bundled Ollama, latency under load), plus:
- Preload the default models at app start, so the first request does not pay 0.7 to 1.3 s of load.
- Trim the 4B prompts: prompt eval is half of `/summary` and nearly all of its TTFT.
- Start the fetch when a URL is pasted, before submit, to hide part of the network cost.

## Reproduce

```bash
uv run python -m veritrade_evals latency preflight   # records the machine; fails while Docker containers run
uv run python -m veritrade_evals latency run         # native suite, resumable; writes latency.{json,md}
uv run python -m veritrade_evals latency docker-cpu --base-url http://localhost:8000   # bundled stack up first
uv run python -m veritrade_evals latency report      # re-aggregates the raw samples
```

The native run needs the private article HTML (`articles verify` passes) and an otherwise idle machine.

# 90 - Optional backlog

What we would do with more time. This is a PoC and rigor was balanced per aspect (R2 in
[01-decisions.md](01-decisions.md)), so each item below marks a place where we stopped on purpose. Every item gives
the reason and the expected payoff; items are ranked by impact within their group, highest first. Items that an
earlier doc or a results file already names as future work link back to it.

## Accuracy

1. **A DSPy-style prompt optimiser instead of the hand grid** (Q7). The lean grid tried up to 8 configs per model
   with synthetic shots. An optimiser over instructions, shot selection and the decision rule, scored on dev300 F0.5
   under the 2% inversion cap, searches far wider. The largest lever found by hand was a decision rule
   (`directional_tau`, +0.218 F0.5 for `qwen3.5:0.8b`, [grid notes](../../../evals/results/grid/notes.md)).
2. **Distil the 9B decision model into the sub-second tier.** Label a large unlabelled stream of headlines and ledes
   with `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` (dev300 F0.5 0.874), then fine-tune `qwen3.5:0.8b` or a small classifier head on its
   calls. Payoff: part of the 0.874 vs 0.730 gap at the 178 ms tier, without a 10.58 GB model
   ([selection.md](../../../evals/results/selection/selection.md)).
3. **Logprob-weighted confidence for streamed `/analyze`.** Streams already carry logprobs (undocumented, see
   [01 build-time findings](01-decisions.md#build-time-findings-that-adjusted-the-plan)), so the ordinal
   `|score| >= 1` rule could become a tunable probability threshold like `/signal`'s. It needs a sign-safe score
   encoding: the qwen3.5 tokenizer fuses the space and minus sign, which hid the sign of negative scores in the
   0.8b grid.
4. **Serve the number-grounding check.** The summary eval already checks every number against the source; running
   it on each served summary and flagging sentences with unsupported numbers needs no model call. The `/summary`
   winner still has minor slips in 50% and material errors in 10% of dev summaries
   ([summary eval](../../../evals/results/summary/summary.md)), and numbers are the slips a trader acts on.
5. **A rubric for mixed results.** Earnings and guidance tweets hold the most wrong calls for their size (13 in 46,
   against 14 in 128 for the catch-all bucket), which fits a beat alongside a cut outlook. An aspect-level output
   (results vs outlook) or an explicit mixed rule targets the content type the brief names.
6. **Decide price moves before tuning for them.** The rubrics ask for economic impact, so the generative models miss
   33-44 of 57 directional price-move tweets, while the `/analyze` models miss only 0-1 of the 5 directional
   price-move headlines in the article dev set ([articles dev notes](../../../evals/results/articles_dev/notes.md)).
   Whether a reported move is directional is a product call; the rubric sentence the error pass left out is ready
   if the answer is yes.
7. **Revisit dropped candidates when their bugs close.** Gemma 4 (think + format bug) and `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507`
   ignoring schema property order and `think:false` under a schema. Low effort, more combined-endpoint candidates.

## Latency and serving

1. **Analyse on publish, not on request.** The 10 sources already have `feeds` / `sections` in
   [`sources.toml`](../../../backend/src/veritrade/data/sources.toml), and the evals' discovery code reads them.
   Polling them and analysing new articles ahead of time turns a request into a cache hit; the cost is inference on
   articles nobody opens.
2. **Progressive `/signal`.** Return the 0.8b verdict at 178 ms, then replace it when a 9B decision model answers
   (clef-flash lede p50 659 ms, [latency.md](../../../evals/results/latency/latency.md)). On the article dev set the
   default catches 10 of 20 directional articles and clef-flash 17 of 20, with 1 inversion each
   ([articles dev](../../../evals/results/articles_dev/summary.md)).
3. **A GPU compose profile.** A `gpu` profile with a device reservation would give Linux hosts with a CUDA GPU the
   bundled path at native-like speed. CPU-only Docker measured roughly 5-15x slower than Metal on the build machine
   (indicative, [01 build-time findings](01-decisions.md#build-time-findings-that-adjusted-the-plan)).
4. **Split-mode concurrency on one Ollama.** The latency suite runs at client concurrency 1, yet split mode fires
   `/signal` and `/summary/stream` at once against two resident models on one GPU. Measure that pair, then tune
   `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` and `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS` (3 native, 2 bundled). Payoff: the split-mode TTFT a user
   actually sees.
5. **A batching server for throughput.** Beyond a handful of analysts, a server with continuous batching (vLLM, or
   llama.cpp server with parallel slots) serves many concurrent streams per GPU. Cost: a second serving stack and
   model format beside Ollama.
6. **CPU threads for the bundled Ollama.** `OLLAMA_CPUS` in [`compose.yaml`](../../../compose.yaml) sets a CPU
   quota, which does not lower llama.cpp's thread count, so a quota below the visible cores can slow inference
   rather than cap it. Pin a `cpuset` or set `num_thread` to match. Payoff: predictable CPU latency in CI and on
   shared hosts.
7. **Trim the remaining story tails.** The cascade still leaks 13-15% of tokens on Yahoo, PR Newswire and
   GlobeNewswire, mostly after the story ([03](03-extraction.md)). That costs prompt-eval time and summary focus on
   the `full` scope, not the lede.
8. **Start `/signal` on a partial body.** The lede sits early in the HTML, so parsing a streamed prefix could start
   inference before the download ends. The payoff is bounded by transfer time, so mostly on large pages (CNN
   5.7 MB).

## Data and evaluation

1. **A human-checked article set and a larger test set.** The 90 articles are labelled by Opus only (two labellers
   and an adjudicator). With 10 per class on dev a gap needs about 0.2 F0.5 to clear zero, so most article
   comparisons are ties ([articles dev](../../../evals/results/articles_dev/summary.md)). A few hundred
   human-checked articles would separate finalists that tie today.
2. **Extraction beyond the top 10.** Any public URL is accepted, but the matrix covers only profiled sources; other
   publishers fall through to JSON-LD and `density`, unmeasured. A set of other publishers would show whether
   `trafilatura-precision`, the source-agnostic candidate in [03](03-extraction.md), should back the cascade there.
3. **Entity-level and multi-entity sentiment data.** Labels are for the article's primary entity, and the public
   sets are sentence- or headline-level (FinEntity only in its single-label rows). Entity-level data would measure
   the question an analyst asks ("bullish for whom?") and back entity-targeted requests.
4. **Fresh pages for the three tuned profiles.** GlobeNewswire, PR Newswire and Yahoo were tightened on the pages
   they are scored on, so the honest cascade F1 is 0.929 and 0.959 is in-sample ([03](03-extraction.md)).
5. **Resample the threshold choice.** Grid CIs hold the operating point fixed, so they are optimistic
   ([grid summary](../../../evals/results/grid/summary.md)). A nested bootstrap or a separate threshold split would
   give honest CIs on the precision knobs.
6. **A sharper key-fact metric.** Embedding coverage agrees with hand labels on 33 of 45 facts at cosine 0.60. A
   per-fact entailment check would track the Opus judge more closely and could gate summary prompts in CI.
7. **Latency on a dedicated host and under load.** Grid and extraction timings came from a shared workstation, and
   contention invalidated a docker-cpu pass. A dedicated runner plus a 1 / 4 / 16 client sweep would give p95s fit
   for capacity planning.
8. **A label-noise pass.** 20 directional dev300 tweets get no correct call from any model
   ([grid notes](../../../evals/results/grid/notes.md)); review them before reading that recall loss as model error.
9. **A second vantage point for the source probe.** One EU residential IP chose the final 10, and datacenter IPs
   meet stricter bot management ([02](02-source-probe.md)). Probe from where the service would run.

## Product and API

1. **Entity-targeted requests.** Accept a ticker or entity and answer for it, and return per-entity calls for
   multi-entity articles, where one story can be bullish for one company and bearish for another. Depends on data
   item 3.
2. **Licensed feeds for the blocked sources.** AP News, Investing.com, Benzinga and Business Wire refuse a plain
   client at their CDN, and evasion is ruled out (Q19). Licensed APIs or feeds would add four widely read sources.
3. **A per-request precision knob.** Thresholds are frozen per model; an override of `min_p` / `directional_tau`
   within the dev300 operating curve would let a desk trade recall for precision without a redeploy.
4. **Non-HTML content.** PDF exhibits and attachments return `unsupported_content`, yet earnings decks and some
   filings arrive that way.
5. **Non-English news.** Discovery skips non-English items and every prompt is English; EU and Asian sources need
   multilingual prompts and their own labelled set.

## Operations

1. **Auth and inbound rate limiting.** The API has no authentication and no per-client limit; the only limiter is
   outbound, for EDGAR ([`client.py`](../../../backend/src/veritrade/fetch/client.py)). API keys or SSO plus per-key
   quotas come before it leaves localhost. The SSRF guard is already in place.
2. **Source DOM drift monitoring beyond the weekly live smoke.**
   [`live-smoke.yml`](../../../.github/workflows/live-smoke.yml) runs weekly and never gates. Profiles depend on selectors, and Guardian, BBC and Yahoo hash class names. A
   daily canary over fresh feed items that alerts when the cascade falls back from `profile` to `density`, body
   word counts drop, or `source_blocked` rises would catch silent degradation. No backup sources remain.
3. **Observability.** Every response already carries per-stage timings. Exported as traces and histograms
   (OpenTelemetry) with alerts on the R7 budgets, they make the latency report a live one.
4. **A shared cache (Redis) with distributed single-flight.** Fetch and result caches are in-process, so each
   replica fetches the same breaking story and a restart empties them. A shared store with a short lock keeps one
   fetch per URL across replicas.
5. **Quality monitoring.** Shadow-score a sample of served `/signal` calls with a 9B decision model and judge a
   sample of summaries offline; alert when agreement drops. It catches model, prompt or publisher drift that
   latency metrics miss.
6. **Pin models by digest and gate upgrades.** Eval manifests record model digests. Serving only digests that
   passed `freeze` and the holdout keeps served behaviour equal to measured behaviour across `ollama pull` and
   Ollama upgrades.

```
</details>

# 03 - Extraction

Question (Q10, R4): which parser and extractor recover a financial news body best and fastest, and does the
choice change what the `/signal` model decides? The answer is measured on the 90-article evaluation set with
the same `extract` function the API calls, not assumed from library benchmarks. Numbers come from
`evals/results/extraction/matrix.json` (summary tables in `evals/results/extraction/summary.md`). They are from
the second measurement, taken after the changes listed in "Changes after the first measurement". That section
also keeps the first-run numbers.

## Setup

- **Articles**: the 90 committed articles, 10 sources with 9 each (Yahoo 10, BBC 8), fetched on
  2026-10-18. The stored HTML and the gold bodies stay in `evals/data/private/`; only ids, sources
  and numbers are committed. All splits are used. The extraction code and source profiles were committed (M2)
  before the set existed (M3), and none of the 90 URLs is among the probe pages the profiles were first tuned
  on (`02-source-probe.md`). After the first measurement, however, the GlobeNewswire, PR Newswire and Yahoo
  profiles were tightened with this same set in view (see Caveats). For those three sources the set is no
  longer held out.
- **Gold body**: Opus chose line ranges from the page's visible-text lines (`evals/opus_prompts/20-gold.md`).
  The lines are the selectolax block walk (the `strip-tags` output), with very long blocks split into
  sentence chunks. The gold excludes the headline, dek, key-points boxes, captions, promos, financial tables and
  press-release boilerplate (About, forward-looking statements, contacts).
- **Rows (22)**: 4 parsers (`selectolax`, `lxml`, `bs4`, `bs4-lxml`) x 4 own strategies (`cascade`, `jsonld`,
  `profile`, `density`), plus 6 extractors that bring their own parser: `trafilatura` (default and
  `favor_precision`), `readability-lxml`, `newspaper4k`, `jusText` and the `strip-tags` baseline. Every row
  calls `veritrade.extract.registry.extract(html, final_url, parser=..., extractor=...)`. An extraction under
  40 words raises `ExtractionEmpty`, as in the API.

## Metrics

- **Tokens**: maximal runs of Python `\w` characters in the lowercased text; an extraction's text is its
  paragraphs joined by blank lines.
- **Precision, recall, F1**: bag of words with multiplicity. With `c(t)` the count of token `t`,
  `common = sum over t of min(c_extracted(t), c_gold(t))`, `P = common / |extracted|`,
  `R = common / |gold|`, `F1 = 2PR / (P + R)`. Each is a macro mean over the 90 articles, and a failed
  extraction scores 0 on all three. 95% CIs are percentile bootstraps over articles (B = 1000, same resamples
  for every row).
- **Leakage**: the share of extracted tokens that lie in no 5-token window also present, in order, in the
  gold token sequence. It is a mean over successful extractions, since a failure sends nothing. Bag-of-words
  `1 - P` is reported too. The two differ on purpose: `1 - P` credits a promo or caption that reuses the
  story's names and common words, and it penalises body text repeated twice. Order-aware coverage asks
  whether the text is part of the story. On this set the two agree within about 1 point per row, except
  `readability` (34.4% against 30.7%), where order-aware coverage flags more of the output.
- **Failure rate**: `ExtractionEmpty` or any exception, recorded by type name.
- **Time**: wall ms around one `extract` call, covering parse, strategy, JSON-LD scan and title. Each
  (row, article) gets one untimed warm-up, which is the output that gets scored, then 5 timed calls. The
  article's time is the median of the 5, and p50 / p95 are taken over the 90 articles, failures included. Rows
  are interleaved per article, so machine-load drift hits every row alike.
- **Tokens to the LLM**: `chars / 4`, the service's estimate, of `build_input(article, "full", uncapped)`
  (`TITLE:` line plus body), at p50. Served inputs are further capped at the model's `max_input_tokens`
  (2000 to 6000). The lede size is `build_input(article, "lede", 2000)`.
- **Install MB**: decimal MB of the files in each distribution's RECORD, summed over the row's dependency
  closure minus the backend core. The core is the closure of the backend's requirements with every parser and
  extractor package removed, so it is what a row adds to the app. Own strategies add nothing beyond their
  parser.
- **Downstream signal**: the `/signal` decision model `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` with its grid-best config `v4`
  (plain instructions, bare criteria) and the probability policy at the grid's operating point,
  `p >= 0.8` (abstentions become neutral, as served). The input is the serving lede,
  `build_input(article, "lede", 2000)`, built from each row's paragraphs. The title is held at the gold
  headline so that only the body varies. The reference is the same lede built from the gold body.
  Agreement is the share of the 90 articles whose verdict matches the gold-lede verdict, and a failed
  extraction counts as a miss. Calls go through the grid runner's `call_once` at concurrency 1. The
  prediction cache keys each record by (row, article) and reuses an answer when the input hash repeats.
  There were 2,070 records (1,980 rows x articles plus 90 gold ledes). The 348 failed extractions need no
  call, and the other 1,722 collapse to 375 distinct ledes. The re-measurement reused every cached answer
  and called the model only for the 9 ledes that were new.

## Results

### Quality: the parser does not matter

For every own strategy the four parsers give the same scores (F1 spread 0.0000). The shared block walker joins
text identically on every backend (`02-source-probe.md`), so the parser is purely a speed and footprint
choice. Own strategies below use `selectolax`.

| extractor | F1 [95% CI] | P | R | leakage | fail | tokens full (p50) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cascade` (served) | 0.959 [0.942, 0.973] | 0.945 | 0.981 | 5.3% | 0.0% | 718 |
| `density` | 0.953 [0.936, 0.967] | 0.936 | 0.977 | 6.1% | 0.0% | 704 |
| `profile` | 0.927 [0.888, 0.961] | 0.915 | 0.947 | 5.2% | 3.3% | 723 |
| `jsonld` | 0.100 [0.044, 0.167] | 0.100 | 0.100 | 0.0% | 90.0% | 917 |
| `trafilatura-precision` | 0.864 [0.826, 0.905] | 0.820 | 0.984 | 17.7% | 0.0% | 796 |

| `newspaper` | 0.800 [0.750, 0.853] | 0.776 | 0.911 | 21.3% | 2.2% | 742 |

### Speed and footprint

p50 / p95 ms per article; install MB is what the parser adds to the app core.

| parser (parse p50 ms) | install MB | `cascade` | `density` | `profile` | `jsonld` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `selectolax` (0.6) | 7.5 | 1.2 / 2.4 | 1.6 / 11.6 | 1.1 / 11.0 | 0.2 / 2.3 |
| `lxml` (1.3) | 20.0 | 2.1 / 3.9 | 2.8 / 25.1 | 2.1 / 24.6 | 0.2 / 2.3 |
| `bs4` (11.4) | 0.6 | 13.3 / 37.5 | 18.3 / 48.9 | 15.8 / 50.8 | 0.2 / 2.2 |
| `bs4-lxml` (8.0) | 20.5 | 10.5 / 27.5 | 14.1 / 42.8 | 10.7 / 46.9 | 0.2 / 2.2 |

| extractor | p50 ms | p95 ms | install MB | failures |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `trafilatura-precision` | 16.5 | 61.5 | 60.8 | none |
| `trafilatura` | 12.4 | 56.5 | 60.8 | none |
| `newspaper` | 71.5 | 154 | 37.1 | 2 (1 SEC, 1 Yahoo) |
| `justext` | 9.8 | 45.0 | 22.4 | 1 (BBC) |
| `readability` | 16.1 | 132 | 23.4 | 9 (all Motley Fool) |
| `strip-tags` | 2.0 | 12.9 | 7.5 | none |

`bs4` is small because `beautifulsoup4` and `soupsieve` are pure Python, and it is the slowest parser for the
same reason. The `jsonld` rows never build a tree, so all four cost 0.2 ms. They fail on 81 of 90 pages,
because only CNN ships an `articleBody`. Every row, including the unchanged third-party ones, is faster than
in the first run (cascade p50 1.6 ms and p95 3.3 ms then), mostly because the machine was less loaded (see
Caveats).

### Per source

F1 by source. The `cascade` column also names the strategy that won.

| CNBC | 1.00 (profile 9) | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.99 | 0.94 | 0.96 |
