| /analyze | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | full | JSON | 30 | 2,580 | 4,582 | - | 2,580 | 3,544 | 2 | 2 | 2,575 | 992 | 1,504 | met (complete p50 2,580/4,000) |

### What meets and what misses

- **Every generative candidate meets its budgets at p50.** The R7 sanity gate in 01 predicted a TTFT miss for
  `qwen3.5:4b` (2.4 s on ~1.6k-token synthetic inputs); real dev articles after the cascade are shorter (an
  825-token `/summary` prompt at p50), so its TTFT lands at 1,128 ms.
- **Both 9B decision models miss the `/signal` budget** (659 and 1,061 ms; see the trade-off section below).
- **The tails are outside the budgets, which bind only the p50.** Streamed TTFT p95 is 1,108 ms for the 2B and
  2,469 to 2,995 ms for the 3-4B models; complete p95 passes 4 s for `/summary` 4B (4,232) and for `/analyze` on
  both 4B models (4,627 and 4,979). The tail is the long articles: in the raw samples, the slowest 10% of
  full-scope requests carry about 2,550 to 2,800 prompt tokens against 825 to 1,074 at p50, and write longer.
- In each `qwen3.5:2b` cell, 1 of 30 warm summaries hit `num_predict` and was served cut at a sentence with
  `truncated: true` (01); no other cell truncated. All 165 streamed samples, cold and warm, kept the event
  order (`meta` first, `done` last, one `sentiment` before `done` on `/analyze`).

### Where the time goes

Warm p50s from `latency.json`; per-token rates are ratios of p50s, so approximate.

| endpoint | model | prompt tokens | prompt eval ms | output tokens | eval ms | prompt eval share | decode ms/token |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| /signal lede | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | 530 | 126 | 7 | 43 | 75% | 6.1 |
| /summary SSE | `qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M` | 825 | 423 | 92 | 827 | 34% | 9.0 |
| /summary SSE | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | 825 | 1,029 | 68 | 1,075 | 49% | 15.8 |
| /analyze SSE | `ministral-3:3b` | 979 | 713 | 92 | 1,361 | 34% | 14.8 |
| /analyze SSE | `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M` | 970 | 862 | 88 | 1,236 | 41% | 14.0 |
| /analyze SSE | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | 963 | 992 | 96 | 1,539 | 39% | 16.0 |

- `/signal` is a prefill problem: 7 output tokens (label schema, `num_predict` 16), so prompt length decides
  the time. That is why the quick signal reads the lede (01, Q4).
- The summarisers differ. The 2B spends two thirds decoding; the 4B prefills at about 800 tokens/s against
  about 1,950 for the 2B, so prompt eval is half its time and almost all of its TTFT (1,029 of 1,128 ms).
  Shorter inputs move TTFT; shorter outputs move completion. Warm load is under 1 ms, and everything outside
  inference (parse, extract, input, response) is 3 to 6 ms.

### Streaming, JSON and field order

Same model, same articles: the transport does not change the total (SSE minus JSON is -2.9% to +1.1% at p50),
but SSE shows text at 38 to 54% of it (`/summary` 4B: 1,128 of 2,199 ms). The UI defaults to streaming.

**Sentiment-first field order** (R3) is what makes the streamed signal useful in `/analyze`. The incremental
scanner emits the `sentiment` event as soon as the score closes: 194 to 249 ms before the first summary text,
and 1.1 to 1.5 s before a JSON client would see it (signal 802 / 1,098 ms streamed against 2,219 / 2,580 ms JSON
for `ministral-3:3b` / `qwen3.5:4b`). `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507` ignores schema property order and writes the
entity first (01), so its signal leads the summary by only 83 ms.

### Lede against full scope

| model | lede p50 / p95 | full p50 / p95 | prompt tokens lede / full |
|---|---|---|---|
| `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | 178 / 195 | 231 / 532 | 530 / 1,074 |
| `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` | 659 / 807 | 1,893 / 4,007 | 286 / 831 |
| `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` | 1,061 / 1,182 | 2,321 / 5,242 | 448 / 1,003 |

Full scope costs the 0.8B little at the median but widens every tail: its p95 crosses 500 ms, and the 9B tails
grow 4 to 5 times. Lede keeps `/signal` predictable as well as fast.

### Cold start, parse and extract

- **Cold**: the model load adds 0.7 to 1.3 s over warm for the generative models (load p50 785 to 1,328 ms),
  0.9 to 1.2 s for `nimble` and 5.4 to 6.2 s for `clef-flash` (a 10.58 GB file); n=3, so indicative. A cold 4B
  misses TTFT (2,132 ms for `/summary`). Every call sends `keep_alive` 30m, so only the first request after a
  start or 30 idle minutes pays it.
- **Parse and extract**: 1.2 to 1.6 ms and 1.6 to 2.5 ms at p50 in every cell, under 2% of even the fastest
  `/signal`, so the parser is not a latency lever (03: every parser yields the same body; `selectolax` is
  chosen for speed and footprint). The extractor matters through tokens instead: competent extractors send
  704 to 822 `full` tokens against 2,116 for `strip-tags` (03), and prompt eval scales with that.

## Network

The suite excludes fetch on purpose. Live cost from the source probe ([02-source-probe.md](02-source-probe.md),
EU residential ISP, 2026-10-18): median of the per-source medians 148 ms, slowest 552 ms.

| source | fetch ms (median) | source | fetch ms (median) |
|---|---|---|---|
| bbc | 26 | globenewswire | 552 |
| cnbc | 161 | guardian | 116 |
| cnn | 35 | prnewswire | 34 |
| fool | 202 | sec | 135 |
| fortune | 367 | yahoo | 477 |

As a rough sum of medians (not measured end to end), a lede signal lands about 0.33 s after submit on a
typical source and about 0.73 s on the slowest; on 4 of the 10 sources the fetch takes longer than the signal.
What the service does about it:

- **One pooled HTTP/2 client** (`veritrade.fetch.client`): keep-alive connections (60 s) let a second article
  from the same publisher skip TCP and TLS setup. Deadline 8 s, connect 3 s.
- **Single-flight fetch cache** (`veritrade.fetch.cache`): split mode fires `/signal` and `/summary` at once,
  and the second request joins the first one's in-flight download (`timings.cache.fetch` is `"joined"`), so
  the page is fetched once. Pages live 10 minutes (512 entries, 200 MB); typed fetch errors live 60 s, so a
  refusing publisher is not hit per request.
- **Result cache** (`veritrade.services.cache`): finished responses keyed by (endpoint, url, model, prompt
  version, parser, extractor, scope) for 1 hour; a hit returns with zero stage timings and `meta.cached`.
- **Consent cookie**: the Yahoo reject-all form costs 857 ms once; the shared cookie jar skips it afterwards
  (about 120 ms, 02).

## Split against combined

The UI offers both, split by default. Defaults first, then the other combined candidates; each row measured
alone at concurrency 1.

| arrangement | signal | first summary text | summary complete | resident model files |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| split: `/signal` 0.8B lede + `/summary` `qwen3.5:4b` SSE | 178 | 1,128 | 2,199 | 2 (1.02 + 3.32 GB) |
| combined: `/analyze` `qwen3.5:4b` SSE (default) | 1,098 | 1,292 | 2,584 | 1 (3.32 GB) |
| combined: `/analyze` `ministral-3:3b` SSE | 802 | 1,051 | 2,242 | 1 (2.95 GB) |
| combined: `/analyze` `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507` SSE | 1,118 | 1,201 | 2,234 | 1 (2.50 GB) |

- **Split** gives the fastest signal, about 0.2 s, while the summary streams, at the cost of two prompts, two
  resident models and two prefills of the same article.
- **Combined** yields the signal at about 0.8 to 1.1 s and the summary by about 2.2 to 2.6 s, from one model
  and one prompt. Its signal is not worse: `qwen3.5:4b` scores dev300 F0.5 0.752 against 0.730 for the 0.8B,
  and 0.880 against 0.685 on the 30 dev articles (wide CIs, [selection.md](../../../evals/results/selection/selection.md)).
- **Not measured**: split mode's two requests running at once on one GPU; the split row joins two isolated
  measurements, so its summary times are a lower bound for real use.

| model | dev300 F0.5 [95% CI] | articles dev F0.5 [95% CI] | lede p50 / p95 ms | cold p50 ms | file GB | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | 0.730 [0.651, 0.795] | 0.685 [0.473, 0.833] | 178 / 195 | 992 | 1.02 | served default |
| `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` | 0.874 [0.811, 0.937] | 0.848 [0.708, 0.963] | 659 / 807 | 6,064 | 10.58 | misses 500 ms; alone over the 10 GB bundle cap (R8) |
| `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` | 0.843 [0.773, 0.901] | 0.895 [0.771, 0.976] | 1,061 / 1,182 | 2,219 | 5.63 | misses 500 ms |

The 9B decision models are 0.11 to 0.14 F0.5 better on dev300 and neither fits the budget, so the 0.8B wins as
the only candidate inside it. The budget was reported, not moved to admit them. Both stay on the allowlist: on
native Ollama a request picks one with the `model` parameter and trades about 0.5 to 0.9 s for precision.
Whether the gap holds on unseen data is a holdout question ([04-evals.md](04-evals.md)).

## docker-cpu

Docker Desktop cannot pass Apple's GPU into a Linux container (01, Q1), so the bundled Ollama runs llama.cpp on
CPU. `latency docker-cpu` measures the bundled defaults over HTTP (`/signal` 0.8B lede JSON; `/summary` and
`/analyze` `qwen3.5:4b`, SSE and JSON), warm n=10 per cell; the app fetches live, so fetch and consent are
subtracted, and it warms up on an 11th dev article.

Two earlier passes were discarded, and neither is committed:

1. **Pass 1 found a prompt-cache bias.** The bundled Ollama has no host port, so the native unload was not
   available, and each JSON cell re-sent the prompts its SSE twin had just evaluated on the same articles;
   those rows showed prompt eval of 118 to 171 ms. Fix: a reload hook (`container_reload` in `latency.py`) runs
   `docker exec ... ollama stop <model>` before every warm phase and waits until `ollama ps` drops it,
   mirroring the native unload.
2. **Pass 2 was invalidated by host contention.** Unrelated workloads on the same Mac pushed the load average
   to 50-64 (6.9 at the native preflight). `qwen3.5:0.8b` decode went from about 31 ms/token to about
   2.8 s/token and 4 `/analyze` requests timed out. Root cause: the bundled Ollama runs llama.cpp with 14
   threads on a 14-vCPU Docker VM over a 14-core host, and its spin-barrier threads stall whenever the host
   takes cores, so CPU inference collapses instead of slowing in proportion.

Indicative only (pass-1 rows the cache bias did not touch, n=10, not committed):

| endpoint | model | transport | complete p50 | TTFT p50 | to signal p50 | x native (complete / TTFT / signal) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| /signal | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` lede | JSON | 2,657 | - | - | 14.9x |
| /summary | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | SSE | 14,405 | 8,768 | - | 6.6x / 7.8x |
| /analyze | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | SSE | 12,106 | 9,147 | 8,644 | 4.7x / 7.1x / 7.9x |

In pass 1, CPU-only Docker was roughly 5 to 15 times slower than Metal on this machine and would miss every
budget. That is why native Ollama is the macOS default and the bundled profile is for Linux and CI: a portability path, not
a latency path. `OLLAMA_CPUS` in `compose.yaml` sets a `cpus:` quota, which does not lower llama.cpp's thread
count, so a quota below the visible core count can make CPU inference slower rather than just capped; a cpuset
or `num_thread` is the fix (backlog). The re-run repeats pass 1's protocol, reload hook included, on a quiet
host, and its rows go in the `docker-cpu` section of `latency.md`.

<!-- PENDING:docker-cpu warm n=10 table from the quiet-host re-run (signal 0.8b lede JSON; summary and analyze qwen3.5:4b SSE and JSON): complete p50/p95, TTFT p50, time to signal p50, ratio to native, preflight load average -->

## Levers

Used:
- **Input and model size**: lede scope for `/signal` (half the tokens of full, p95 195 ms instead of 532); a
  cascade that sends about 720 `full` tokens where `strip-tags` sends about 2,100 (03); the smallest `/signal`
  model that clears the accuracy filters, answering in 7 tokens.
- **Perceived latency**: SSE, sentiment-first field order and an incremental JSON scanner.
- **Warm models**: `keep_alive` 30m on every call; `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS` 3 native (2 bundled) keeps both
  split-mode models resident; flash attention and a q8_0 KV cache in the Ollama env.
- **Bounded generation**: `think: false`, greedy decoding, per-endpoint `num_predict`, and the served summary
  cap of 3 sentences / 60 words (01).
- **Network and hops**: pooled HTTP/2, single-flight fetch cache, result cache, consent cookie reuse; the UI is
  served by the same FastAPI process (R1), and the fast parsers extract inline, without a thread hand-off.

Left: the latency items in [90-optional-backlog.md](90-optional-backlog.md) (progressive `/signal`, split-mode
concurrency, a GPU compose profile, CPU threads for the bundled Ollama, latency under load), plus:
- Preload the default models at app start, so the first request does not pay 0.7 to 1.3 s of load.
- Trim the 4B prompts: prompt eval is half of `/summary` and nearly all of its TTFT.
- Start the fetch when a URL is pasted, before submit, to hide part of the network cost.

## Reproduce

```bash
uv run python -m veritrade_evals latency preflight   # records the machine; fails while Docker containers run
uv run python -m veritrade_evals latency run         # native suite, resumable; writes latency.{json,md}
uv run python -m veritrade_evals latency docker-cpu --base-url http://localhost:8000   # bundled stack up first
uv run python -m veritrade_evals latency report      # re-aggregates the raw samples
```

The native run needs the private article HTML (`articles verify` passes) and an otherwise idle machine.

# 90 - Optional backlog

What we would do with more time. This is a PoC and rigor was balanced per aspect (R2 in
[01-decisions.md](01-decisions.md)), so each item below marks a place where we stopped on purpose. Every item gives
the reason and the expected payoff; items are ranked by impact within their group, highest first. Items that an
earlier doc or a results file already names as future work link back to it.

## Accuracy

1. **A DSPy-style prompt optimiser instead of the hand grid** (Q7). The lean grid tried up to 8 configs per model
   with synthetic shots. An optimiser over instructions, shot selection and the decision rule, scored on dev300 F0.5
   under the 2% inversion cap, searches far wider. The largest lever found by hand was a decision rule
   (`directional_tau`, +0.218 F0.5 for `qwen3.5:0.8b`, [grid notes](../../../evals/results/grid/notes.md)).
2. **Distil the 9B decision model into the sub-second tier.** Label a large unlabelled stream of headlines and ledes
   with `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` (dev300 F0.5 0.874), then fine-tune `qwen3.5:0.8b` or a small classifier head on its
   calls. Payoff: part of the 0.874 vs 0.730 gap at the 178 ms tier, without a 10.58 GB model
   ([selection.md](../../../evals/results/selection/selection.md)).
3. **Logprob-weighted confidence for streamed `/analyze`.** Streams already carry logprobs (undocumented, see
   [01 build-time findings](01-decisions.md#build-time-findings-that-adjusted-the-plan)), so the ordinal
   `|score| >= 1` rule could become a tunable probability threshold like `/signal`'s. It needs a sign-safe score
   encoding: the qwen3.5 tokenizer fuses the space and minus sign, which hid the sign of negative scores in the
   0.8b grid.
4. **Serve the number-grounding check.** The summary eval already checks every number against the source; running
   it on each served summary and flagging sentences with unsupported numbers needs no model call. The `/summary`
   winner still has minor slips in 50% and material errors in 10% of dev summaries
   ([summary eval](../../../evals/results/summary/summary.md)), and numbers are the slips a trader acts on.
5. **A rubric for mixed results.** Earnings and guidance tweets hold the most wrong calls for their size (13 in 46,
   against 14 in 128 for the catch-all bucket), which fits a beat alongside a cut outlook. An aspect-level output
   (results vs outlook) or an explicit mixed rule targets the content type the brief names.
6. **Decide price moves before tuning for them.** The rubrics ask for economic impact, so the generative models miss
   33-44 of 57 directional price-move tweets, while the `/analyze` models miss only 0-1 of the 5 directional
   price-move headlines in the article dev set ([articles dev notes](../../../evals/results/articles_dev/notes.md)).
   Whether a reported move is directional is a product call; the rubric sentence the error pass left out is ready
   if the answer is yes.
7. **Revisit dropped candidates when their bugs close.** Gemma 4 (think + format bug) and `qwen3:4b-instruct-2507`
   ignoring schema property order and `think:false` under a schema. Low effort, more combined-endpoint candidates.

## Latency and serving

1. **Analyse on publish, not on request.** The 10 sources already have `feeds` / `sections` in
   [`sources.toml`](../../../backend/src/veritrade/data/sources.toml), and the evals' discovery code reads them.
   Polling them and analysing new articles ahead of time turns a request into a cache hit; the cost is inference on
   articles nobody opens.
2. **Progressive `/signal`.** Return the 0.8b verdict at 178 ms, then replace it when a 9B decision model answers
   (clef-flash lede p50 659 ms, [latency.md](../../../evals/results/latency/latency.md)). On the article dev set the
   default catches 10 of 20 directional articles and clef-flash 17 of 20, with 1 inversion each
   ([articles dev](../../../evals/results/articles_dev/summary.md)).
3. **A GPU compose profile.** A `gpu` profile with a device reservation would give Linux hosts with a CUDA GPU the
   bundled path at native-like speed. CPU-only Docker measured roughly 5-15x slower than Metal on the build machine
   (indicative, [01 build-time findings](01-decisions.md#build-time-findings-that-adjusted-the-plan)).
4. **Split-mode concurrency on one Ollama.** The latency suite runs at client concurrency 1, yet split mode fires
   `/signal` and `/summary/stream` at once against two resident models on one GPU. Measure that pair, then tune
   `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` and `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS` (3 native, 2 bundled). Payoff: the split-mode TTFT a user
   actually sees.
5. **A batching server for throughput.** Beyond a handful of analysts, a server with continuous batching (vLLM, or
   llama.cpp server with parallel slots) serves many concurrent streams per GPU. Cost: a second serving stack and
   model format beside Ollama.
6. **CPU threads for the bundled Ollama.** `OLLAMA_CPUS` in [`compose.yaml`](../../../compose.yaml) sets a CPU
   quota, which does not lower llama.cpp's thread count, so a quota below the visible cores can slow inference
   rather than cap it. Pin a `cpuset` or set `num_thread` to match. Payoff: predictable CPU latency in CI and on
   shared hosts.
7. **Trim the remaining story tails.** The cascade still leaks 13-15% of tokens on Yahoo, PR Newswire and
   GlobeNewswire, mostly after the story ([03](03-extraction.md)). That costs prompt-eval time and summary focus on
   the `full` scope, not the lede.
8. **Start `/signal` on a partial body.** The lede sits early in the HTML, so parsing a streamed prefix could start
   inference before the download ends. The payoff is bounded by transfer time, so mostly on large pages (CNN
   5.7 MB).

## Data and evaluation

1. **A human-checked article set and a larger test set.** The 90 articles are labelled by Opus only (two labellers
   and an adjudicator). With 10 per class on dev a gap needs about 0.2 F0.5 to clear zero, so most article
   comparisons are ties ([articles dev](../../../evals/results/articles_dev/summary.md)). A few hundred
   human-checked articles would separate finalists that tie today.
2. **Extraction beyond the top 10.** Any public URL is accepted, but the matrix covers only profiled sources; other
   publishers fall through to JSON-LD and `density`, unmeasured. A set of other publishers would show whether
   `trafilatura-precision`, the source-agnostic candidate in [03](03-extraction.md), should back the cascade there.
3. **Entity-level and multi-entity sentiment data.** Labels are for the article's primary entity, and the public
   sets are sentence- or headline-level (FinEntity only in its single-label rows). Entity-level data would measure
   the question an analyst asks ("bullish for whom?") and back entity-targeted requests.
4. **Fresh pages for the three tuned profiles.** GlobeNewswire, PR Newswire and Yahoo were tightened on the pages
   they are scored on, so the honest cascade F1 is 0.929 and 0.959 is in-sample ([03](03-extraction.md)).
5. **Resample the threshold choice.** Grid CIs hold the operating point fixed, so they are optimistic
   ([grid summary](../../../evals/results/grid/summary.md)). A nested bootstrap or a separate threshold split would
   give honest CIs on the precision knobs.
6. **A sharper key-fact metric.** Embedding coverage agrees with hand labels on 33 of 45 facts at cosine 0.60. A
   per-fact entailment check would track the Opus judge more closely and could gate summary prompts in CI.
7. **Latency on a dedicated host and under load.** Grid and extraction timings came from a shared workstation, and
   contention invalidated a docker-cpu pass. A dedicated runner plus a 1 / 4 / 16 client sweep would give p95s fit
   for capacity planning.
8. **A label-noise pass.** 20 directional dev300 tweets get no correct call from any model
   ([grid notes](../../../evals/results/grid/notes.md)); review them before reading that recall loss as model error.
9. **A second vantage point for the source probe.** One EU residential IP chose the final 10, and datacenter IPs
   meet stricter bot management ([02](02-source-probe.md)). Probe from where the service would run.

## Product and API

1. **Entity-targeted requests.** Accept a ticker or entity and answer for it, and return per-entity calls for
   multi-entity articles, where one story can be bullish for one company and bearish for another. Depends on data
   item 3.
2. **Licensed feeds for the blocked sources.** AP News, Investing.com, Benzinga and Business Wire refuse a plain
   client at their CDN, and evasion is ruled out (Q19). Licensed APIs or feeds would add four widely read sources.
3. **A per-request precision knob.** Thresholds are frozen per model; an override of `min_p` / `directional_tau`
   within the dev300 operating curve would let a desk trade recall for precision without a redeploy.
4. **Non-HTML content.** PDF exhibits and attachments return `unsupported_content`, yet earnings decks and some
   filings arrive that way.
5. **Non-English news.** Discovery skips non-English items and every prompt is English; EU and Asian sources need
   multilingual prompts and their own labelled set.

## Operations

1. **Auth and inbound rate limiting.** The API has no authentication and no per-client limit; the only limiter is
   outbound, for EDGAR ([`client.py`](../../../backend/src/veritrade/fetch/client.py)). API keys or SSO plus per-key
   quotas come before it leaves localhost. The SSRF guard is already in place.
2. **Source DOM drift monitoring beyond the weekly live smoke.**
   [`live-smoke.yml`](../../../.github/workflows/live-smoke.yml) runs weekly and never gates. Profiles depend on selectors, and Guardian, BBC and Yahoo hash class names. A
   daily canary over fresh feed items that alerts when the cascade falls back from `profile` to `density`, body
   word counts drop, or `source_blocked` rises would catch silent degradation. No backup sources remain.
3. **Observability.** Every response already carries per-stage timings. Exported as traces and histograms
   (OpenTelemetry) with alerts on the R7 budgets, they make the latency report a live one.
4. **A shared cache (Redis) with distributed single-flight.** Fetch and result caches are in-process, so each
   replica fetches the same breaking story and a restart empties them. A shared store with a short lock keeps one
   fetch per URL across replicas.
5. **Quality monitoring.** Shadow-score a sample of served `/signal` calls with a 9B decision model and judge a
   sample of summaries offline; alert when agreement drops. It catches model, prompt or publisher drift that
   latency metrics miss.
6. **Pin models by digest and gate upgrades.** Eval manifests record model digests. Serving only digests that
   passed `freeze` and the holdout keeps served behaviour equal to measured behaviour across `ollama pull` and
   Ollama upgrades.

# Signal grid on dev300

Generated by `uv run python -m veritrade_evals.grid analyze` from the local prediction cache; no dataset text is stored here.

- Data: dev300, 300 Twitter Financial News train tweets, 100 per class; every rate is weighted back to the train prior (bullish 20.2%, bearish 15.1%, neutral 64.7%). Confusion and error counts are raw.
- Selection: F0.5 macro over bullish/bearish; operating point = best F0.5 with bullish<->bearish inversions <= 2% of directional calls; below the threshold the call abstains to neutral.
- Policies: decision models threshold native class probabilities (min_p); generative /signal thresholds first-token label probabilities (label schema) or the |score| of an ordinal -2..2 schema (t in {1, 2}); both probability policies are also swept with the served `directional_tau` rule (min_p 0, see below); /analyze is streamed sentiment-first and always uses |score|.
- Decoding: Ollama options temperature=0, seed=0, presence_penalty=0, frequency_penalty=0, repeat_penalty=1 on every generative call (greedy; overrides the penalties some Modelfiles ship).
- CIs: 95% stratified bootstrap (B=1000) at the chosen threshold; the threshold choice itself is not resampled, so these are optimistic.
- Latency: per-call wall ms during the grid run (Ollama 0.40.6 native-metal, warm, client concurrency 1); /analyze is time to the score with the stream stopped there. Indicative only: the latency suite runs separately.

## directional_tau vs the plain rule

The plain rule calls the argmax class and abstains below min_p, so a model that keeps most of its mass on neutral is never pushed into a call. The served `directional_tau` rule (min_p 0) calls the likelier directional class when neutral leads and that class holds p >= tau; a leading directional class is always called, and below tau the row is a served neutral, not an abstention. Both rules are tuned on these 300 tweets; the gap is a paired bootstrap.

## Notes from the error-analysis read

Hand-written after reading the tables above; counts and my own descriptions only, no dataset text. These are
tweets, not articles: the thresholds and latencies here are a starting point for the article dev set, not a
substitute for it.

**A decoding fix came out of this grid.** The qwen3.5 Modelfiles ship `presence_penalty 1.5`, and the client
only pinned temperature and seed, so "greedy" qwen3.5 output was pushed away from any token in the recent
context. With four shots whose last answer is neutral (or score 0), the generated qwen3.5:0.8b label disagreed
with its own first-token argmax on 84/300 (v2) and 62/300 (v4) tweets, and v2-ordinal emitted -2 for 104/300.
`FIXED_OPTIONS` now neutralises the penalties; every number on this page comes from the greedy re-run. The
label-logprob cells were identical before and after (logprobs are reported before the penalty is applied), and
seven cells re-run to replace contended timings reproduced their predictions exactly, so the cache and decoding
are deterministic.

**Decision models lead on precision.** clef-flash v4 (plain question, bare labels) reaches F0.5 0.874 at
min_p 0.80 with no inversions, answering 73% of tweets and calling 33% directional against a 35% directional
prior. nimble over-calls: with no threshold it calls 65-74% of tweets directional, and it only becomes precise
at min_p 0.97-0.98, where it answers about a quarter of the tweets (F0.5 0.843 for v1). The served
`directional_tau` rule runs at min_p 0, so for these peaked models it only removes their abstention: it loses
to the plain rule by 0.046 (clef-flash) and 0.303 (nimble) F0.5, both significant, and is not served for them.

**qwen3.5:0.8b is neutral-leaning, which caps the served label policy.** Its first-token argmax is neutral on
most directional tweets (0.3-7% signal rate across label configs), so a min_p threshold can only remove calls:
the plain rule (v2-label, no abstention) misses 162 of 200 directional tweets at F0.5 0.512. The served
`directional_tau` rule calls the likelier directional class when neutral leads and that class reaches tau;
at tau 0.28 it gives F0.5 0.730 [0.651, 0.795] with precision 0.91 / 0.92 and no inversions (+0.218
[+0.141, +0.307] paired). It is the largest single lever found here, it is now the model's best config, and it
is frozen (min_p 0, directional_tau 0.28).

**Knob verdict for qwen3.5:0.8b.** As served (argmax + min_p on label tokens vs |score| >= t on the ordinal

## Notes from the error-analysis read

Hand-written after reading the tables above; counts and my own descriptions only, no dataset text. These are
tweets, not articles: the thresholds and latencies here are a starting point for the article dev set, not a
substitute for it.

**A decoding fix came out of this grid.** The qwen3.5 Modelfiles ship `presence_penalty 1.5`, and the client
only pinned temperature and seed, so "greedy" qwen3.5 output was pushed away from any token in the recent
context. With four shots whose last answer is neutral (or score 0), the generated qwen3.5:0.8b label disagreed
with its own first-token argmax on 84/300 (v2) and 62/300 (v4) tweets, and v2-ordinal emitted -2 for 104/300.
`FIXED_OPTIONS` now neutralises the penalties; every number on this page comes from the greedy re-run. The
label-logprob cells were identical before and after (logprobs are reported before the penalty is applied), and
seven cells re-run to replace contended timings reproduced their predictions exactly, so the cache and decoding
are deterministic.

**Decision models lead on precision.** clef-flash v4 (plain question, bare labels) reaches F0.5 0.874 at
min_p 0.80 with no inversions, answering 73% of tweets and calling 33% directional against a 35% directional
prior. nimble over-calls: with no threshold it calls 65-74% of tweets directional, and it only becomes precise
at min_p 0.97-0.98, where it answers about a quarter of the tweets (F0.5 0.843 for v1). The served
`directional_tau` rule runs at min_p 0, so for these peaked models it only removes their abstention: it loses
to the plain rule by 0.046 (clef-flash) and 0.303 (nimble) F0.5, both significant, and is not served for them.

**qwen3.5:0.8b is neutral-leaning, which caps the served label policy.** Its first-token argmax is neutral on
most directional tweets (0.3-7% signal rate across label configs), so a min_p threshold can only remove calls:
the plain rule (v2-label, no abstention) misses 162 of 200 directional tweets at F0.5 0.512. The served
`directional_tau` rule calls the likelier directional class when neutral leads and that class reaches tau;
at tau 0.28 it gives F0.5 0.730 [0.651, 0.795] with precision 0.91 / 0.92 and no inversions (+0.218
[+0.141, +0.307] paired). It is the largest single lever found here, it is now the model's best config, and it
is frozen (min_p 0, directional_tau 0.28).

**Knob verdict for qwen3.5:0.8b.** As served (argmax + min_p on label tokens vs |score| >= t on the ordinal
schema), the best label config beats the best ordinal config by +0.059 F0.5 [-0.068, +0.187]: not significant
at n=300. With the `directional_tau` rule the logprob knob wins clearly. The ordinal schema cannot borrow that
rule: this tokenizer fuses the space and the minus sign (" -") while the bare-space alternative keeps about a
quarter of the mass, so the sign is unobservable for negative scores. `score_sign_probabilities` used to read
those as bearish 1.0 (and miss the " -" mass behind positive scores). It now returns None for every negative
score in these cells (48, 32, 17 and 8 of 300), and serving falls back to the ordinal policy there.

**Prompt dimensions.**
- Rubric A (definitions) beats rubric B (impact questions) for every generative model. B's "is the change
  clear and material" framing makes the small models answer neutral: qwen3.5:0.8b v3-label calls 0.3% of
  tweets directional, and ministral drops from 0.660 to 0.440.
- Four synthetic shots help qwen3.5:0.8b on the label schema (0.365 to 0.512) but hurt every /analyze model:
  qwen3.5:4b 0.752 to 0.655, ministral 0.660 to 0.494, and qwen3-instruct v2 breaks the inversion cap. Shots
  also roughly double qwen3.5:4b's time to score.
- For the decision models the spread across prompts is small (clef 0.83-0.87, nimble 0.81-0.84). Bare labels
  with the short question are also the fastest variant (clef 468 vs 710 ms, nimble 751 vs 975 ms).

**Where the calls go wrong.**
- Inversions are nearly absent: one bullish tweet called bearish across all six best configs.
- Wrong calls are mostly gold-neutral tweets called directional (1-8 per model). Relative to its size, the
  earnings and guidance bucket holds the most of them (13 across the six models in 46 tweets, against 14 in
  128 for the catch-all bucket), which fits mixed results (a beat alongside a cut outlook) being the hard case.
- The real loss is recall: 34 (clef-flash) to 162 (qwen3.5:0.8b) directional tweets missed.
- The biggest miss bucket for every generative model is the price-move tweet: 33-44 of 57 directional ones
  missed, against 10 for clef-flash. The rubrics ask for economic impact, not tone, and the small models read
  a reported share-price move as not material, while the dataset labels such moves as directional. Whether to
  close that gap is a product question: on articles the impact reading is the intended behaviour.
- Analyst actions (upgrades, price targets) are handled well by the larger models (qwen3.5:4b catches 21 of
  22, clef-flash 19 of 22, with no wrong calls).
- 20 directional tweets get no correct call from any model; they are the first place to look for label noise
  or genuinely ambiguous items.

**Follow-ups after the grid (analyze).** Two cells per model, each paired against v1 on the same tweets
and never eligible as the best config.
- v5 = v1 with the summary rule tightened after the summary eval (2 to 3 sentences, at most 50 words, entity
  first). Only the summary line changes, yet the score moves: ministral +0.025 [+0.002, +0.052], qwen3-instruct
  -0.011 [-0.047, +0.023], qwen3.5:4b -0.021 [-0.054, +0.007]. On the article dev set qwen3.5:4b loses more
  (0.800 vs 0.880, gap -0.080 [-0.178, -0.014]: two more bullish articles missed), so the freeze keeps v1 for
  qwen3.5:4b /analyze and serves v5 to ministral and qwen3-instruct.
- `v1-summary-first` (the field-order check) is never better: ministral -0.017 [-0.088, +0.059], qwen3.5:4b
  -0.061 [-0.122, +0.003], and its time to the score is 1.0-1.5 s against 0.15-0.6 s, because the whole
  summary decodes first. Every /analyze model stays sentiment-first.

**The one manual revision.** Few-shot is dropped for /analyze (every frozen /analyze prompt is zero-shot).
The price-move / analyst-action sentence was not added: on the article dev set the /analyze models miss 0-1
of the 5 directional price-move headlines and no headline falls in the analyst-action bucket, so the tweet
misses do not carry over (see `evals/results/articles_dev/summary.md`). qwen3.5:0.8b keeps its four shots: they
help the label schema (0.365 to 0.512 plain).

**Timing provenance.** Wall times are per call at client concurrency 1, warm. Concurrent load on the shared
machine (mostly the Docker Desktop VM saturating the CPU) inflated some tails, so clef-flash v2 and nimble v2/v3
were re-run at 19:28-19:47 and all eight qwen3.5:0.8b cells at 20:11-20:25, each with identical predictions.
The tables show the re-run timings. The qwen3.5:0.8b re-run still shared the machine (load about 30): on a
quiet machine earlier the same calls measured p50 155-200 ms with p95 near 210-300 ms, against 209-276 ms and
up to 1.06 s here. nimble v3's tail is also somewhat elevated. The analyze follow-ups (v5, summary-first)
ran later at concurrency 1 on an Ollama shared with two other eval runs, so their timings are indicative only.

# Grid finalists on the articles dev set

Generated by `uv run python -m veritrade_evals finalists analyze` from the local prediction cache; counts and rates only, no article text.

- Data: the articles dev split, n=30 news articles labelled for their primary entity (bullish 10, bearish 10, neutral 10). Balanced and unweighted: unlike dev300, rates are not reweighted to a class prior.
- Inputs: the serving path. `cascade` extraction with `selectolax` on the stored HTML at the fetch's final URL, then the endpoint scope (headline + lede, or the full body) cut to each model's `max_input_tokens`. Extraction failures: 0 (no call; scored as abstentions).
- Thresholds: each config's dev300 operating point (max F0.5 with inversions <= 2%), never re-tuned here. A rule counts as clearly failing only when the whole 95% CI of its inversion rate is above the cap, or the whole coverage CI is below 50% of its dev300 coverage.
- CIs: 95% stratified bootstrap (B=1000). With 10 articles per class they are wide: a gap needs roughly 0.2 F0.5 to clear zero, so most comparisons below are ties.
- Latency: wall ms per call on an Ollama 0.40.6 native-metal shared with other eval runs (client concurrency 1); indicative only.

Filters: dev300 inversion rate <= 2% at the frozen operating point (n=300); the articles dev set must not fail the cap, meaning the 95% CI of its inversion rate reaches down to 2% (the freeze's clear-failure rule: at n=30 one inversion is about 5% of the calls); warm native p50 excluding fetch <= 500 ms at lede. Rank: dev300 F0.5 macro (primary, n=300), then articles dev F0.5, then lower latency.
8:- **analyze**: Candidates: the frozen /analyze configs (full scope, ordinal |score| >= t, sentiment-first). Filters: the same inversion rules as /signal; streamed TTFT p50 <= 1.5 s and complete p50 <= 4 s (warm, native, excluding fetch). Rank: dev300 F0.5 macro, then articles dev F0.5, then lower latency.

```python
"""Print the slowest warm samples per full-scope cell with prompt / eval tokens, plus the cell p50 tokens."""

import json
import statistics
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

path = Path(sys.argv[1])
cells = defaultdict(list)
for line in path.read_text().splitlines():
    row = json.loads(line)
    if row["phase"] == "warm" and row["ok"]:
        cells[row["cell"]].append(row)

for cell, rows in sorted(cells.items()):
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["total_ms"])
    slow = rows[-3:]
    p50_prompt = statistics.median(r["prompt_tokens"] or 0 for r in rows)
    p50_eval = statistics.median(r["eval_tokens"] or 0 for r in rows)
    desc = " | ".join(
        f"{r['total_ms']:.0f} ms p={r['prompt_tokens']} e={r['eval_tokens']}" for r in slow
    )
    print(f"{cell} n={len(rows)} p50 prompt={p50_prompt} eval={p50_eval} :: {desc}")

```markdown

## Execution phases (Workflows; every agent `model: 'opus'`; main loop commits after each gate)

| Phase | Work | Gate -> commit to main |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | Main loop: record + `docker stop` running containers; `brew install ollama`, `brew services start`, `launchctl setenv OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS`; background model pulls; `git init`, repo-local identity, `.gitignore`, MIT, `gh repo create cleverjobs/veritrade-analytics --public`, SSH-alias remote; workspace + all deps declared and locked; contracts (`contracts.py`, protocols, `openapi.json`), `models.toml`/`sources.toml` skeletons; `ci.yml` backend + frontend jobs; design docs 00/01 | `check.py --fast`, CI green, M0 push |
| P1 | Probe agent: `probe_sources.py` over 14 sources -> `02-source-probe.md`, final 10 + profile hints | 10 usable sources, M1 |
| P2 | 5 parallel file-disjoint agents: fetch/, extract/ + skeleton capture, inference/ + scanner, frontend (MSW against contract), evals loaders/metrics | `check.py --fast`; M3-style probe on real Ollama (logprobs in stream? schema order honoured? systemone shape?) + baseline dev300 + latency probe; **R7 sanity gate: if budgets look unrealistic, stop and ask Kris** -> M2 |
| P3 | (a) api/services/caches/SSE + integration tests; (b) Opus article sub-workflow: discover -> gold + key facts -> labellers A/B -> adjudicate -> finalize | `check.py --full`; one analyze per source on native Ollama; M3 |
| P4 | (a) Docker, compose, e2e, Playwright (iterate on main); (b) accuracy grid, knobs, scope, field order, error pass, freeze, extraction matrix (background); (c) summary eval + Opus judge on finalists | CI incl. e2e green (`gh run watch`), M4 |
| P5 | Exclusive (no builds/agents): re-stop containers, latency suite, select --write, holdout once, docker-cpu pass, report, design docs 03-05 + 90, README | budgets reported, M5 |
| P6 | Verification checklist, fresh-clone smoke, transcript export + gate | M6 push; final message with `docker start ...` command |

Ad-hoc scripts live in `.temp/<slug>/` and run via `uv run python`; no inline Python; terse WHY-only comments; no
em-dashes; no git stash.

## Verification

1. `uv run python scripts/check.py --full` passes (ruff, format, mypy, BE unit + integration, evals tests, FE lint/
   typecheck/prettier/vitest/build, openapi + type drift).
2. Native path: `brew services list` shows ollama; `docker compose up -d`; `/api/health` reports `native-metal`;
   one `/api/analyze` (JSON + stream) succeeds per source; blocked/paywalled cases return typed errors.
3. Bundled path: `docker compose --profile bundled --env-file env/bundled.env up -d` healthy; one analyze succeeds.
4. UI: split and combined modes, streaming toggle, model/parser/extractor/scope switches, Benchmarks page.
5. Latency report vs R7 budgets printed and committed; holdout run recorded once.
6. GitHub Actions `ci.yml` green on HEAD incl. e2e; `live-smoke.yml` dispatched once and noted.
7. `git ls-files` contains nothing from `evals/data/private/`; skeleton purity test passes; every commit authored by
   Kristiyan Dimitrov with the Co-Authored-By trailer.
8. Fresh clone into `.temp/fresh-clone/` builds and serves one analyze without private data.
9. Transcript gate passes with zero hits; rendered HTML skimmed; README links resolve.

## Risks

- Label-token logprobs may be ambiguous or masked by grammar -> score-sign fallback or ordinal only (probe decides).
- Ollama may ignore schema property order -> field-order dimension dropped, documented.
- 9B decision models may miss the 500 ms lede budget -> Pareto knee, stated.
- 30/60 article sets give wide CIs; Opus-only labels may inflate agreement; thresholds from tweets may not transfer.
- Publisher DOMs, Yahoo consent forms and blocking change; runner IPs get blocked differently than Kris's IP.
- Docker Desktop restart can revive stopped containers -> re-stop before P5.
- Brew Ollama 0.40.4 vs container 0.40.5 version drift -> versions recorded with every benchmark.

The 9B decision models are 0.11 to 0.14 F0.5 better on dev300 and neither fits the budget, so the 0.8B wins as
the only candidate inside it. The budget was reported, not moved to admit them. Both stay on the allowlist: on
native Ollama a request picks one with the `model` parameter and trades about 0.5 to 0.9 s for a higher F0.5, mostly recall.
Whether the gap holds on unseen data is a holdout question ([04-evals.md](04-evals.md)).

````
"""Report relative markdown links in the given files whose targets do not exist."""

import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

LINK = re.compile(r"\]\(([^)#\s]+)(?:#[^)]*)?\)")

missing = 0
for name in sys.argv[1:]:
    doc = Path(name).resolve()
    for target in LINK.findall(doc.read_text(encoding="utf-8")):
        if "://" in target:
            continue
        path = (doc.parent / target).resolve()
        status = "ok" if path.exists() else "MISSING"
        missing += status == "MISSING"
        print(f"{status:7s} {target}")
sys.exit(1 if missing else 0)
----
"""Check every relative link and #anchor in a markdown file against GitHub-style heading slugs."""

import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

LINK = re.compile(r"\]\(([^)\s]*)\)")
FENCE = re.compile(r"^```")


def slugs(path: Path) -> set[str]:
    out: set[str] = set()
    in_code = False
    for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        if FENCE.match(line):
            in_code = not in_code
            continue
        if in_code or not line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        text = line.lstrip("#").strip().lower()
````

```
**Errors** share one envelope, `{"error": {"code", "message", "hint", "retryable", "upstream_status"}}`
([`errors.py`](backend/src/veritrade/errors.py), [`contracts.py`](backend/src/veritrade/api/contracts.py)); other
request-body validation errors, such as an unknown `parser`, `extractor` or `scope` or an extra field, return
FastAPI's standard 422 `{"detail": [...]}`.

| HTTP | Codes | When |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `invalid_url`, `blocked_destination`, `model_not_allowed` | Malformed URL; SSRF guard (private or reserved address, a port other than 80/443); model not on the allowlist or disabled by `VT_MODELS`, or not served on that endpoint |
----
- **Precision first** (Q2): a wrong directional call costs a trade, a missed one little, so selection uses F0.5 macro
  over bullish and bearish with inversions capped at 2% ([04](.context/docs/design/04-evals.md#1-objective-and-metrics)).
- **Abstain rather than guess** (Q3): thresholds on decision-model class probabilities, on label-token probabilities
  (`/signal`, plus `directional_tau`) or on an ordinal -2..+2 score (`/analyze`, works mid-stream); every signal
  reports `abstained`. The frozen defaults never abstain (dev300 coverage 100%): the 0.8B runs at `min_p` 0 with
  tau 0.28 and `/analyze` at \|s\| >= 1 on integer scores, so they hold back by answering neutral; only the 9B
  decision models abstain (dev300 coverage 72.9% and 26.3%).
- **Split and combined, both served** (Q8): a fast signal model next to a summariser, or one model for score, entity
  and summary; the UI switches and both were measured ([05](.context/docs/design/05-latency.md#split-against-combined)).
----
- **Prompt grid**: 33 prompt cells on dev300 (prompt version x output schema or field order per model), each swept
  over confidence policy and threshold; one error-analysis pass, then a freeze into [`frozen.json`](evals/results/frozen.json) and `models.toml`. The largest lever was a decision
  rule, not a prompt: `directional_tau` lifts the 0.8B by +0.218 [+0.141, +0.307] F0.5
  ([grid notes](evals/results/grid/notes.md)). On `/analyze`, `qwen3.5:4b` leads dev300 with 0.752 against 0.685
  (`ministral-3:3b`) and 0.647 (`qwen3:4b-instruct-2507`).
- **Summaries**: deterministic checks (length, every number grounded in the source, entity named), key-fact
  coverage with `qwen3-embedding:0.6b` at cosine 0.60, and blind Opus judges (faithfulness, coverage,
  hallucinations, lead) on the 30 dev articles ([`summary.md`](evals/results/summary/summary.md)). Extraction is
  scored separately against Opus gold bodies ([`summary.md`](evals/results/extraction/summary.md)).
- **Reproducing**: `uv run python -m veritrade_evals --help` lists every step; `datasets fetch` re-downloads the
----

| Layer | Where | What it guards |
|---|---|---|
| Backend unit | `backend/tests/unit` | Extractors on skeleton fixtures under all four parsers, the SSRF guard (address classes, DNS rebinding, ports), block / consent / paywall detection, prompts, confidence policies, the stream scanner split at every byte offset, the Ollama client, the API contract |
| Backend integration | `backend/tests/integration` | The ASGI app against fake publishers (skeleton pages) and a scripted Ollama: every endpoint in JSON and SSE, event order, single-flight and result caches, the error table, failures mid-stream, client disconnects |
| Evals and scripts | `evals/tests/unit`, `scripts/tests` | Metrics, splits, grid, freeze, selection, the holdout guard, latency aggregation, the report, transcript redaction |
| Frontend | `frontend/tests` | Vitest + Testing Library: SSE parser, components, and MSW integration (signal before the summary completes, JSON fallback, errors, abort on resubmit, benchmarks page) |
```

````markdown
# VeriTrade Analytics - real-time financial news analysis (PoC)

Paste a public financial-news URL and get a Bullish / Bearish / Neutral signal in about 0.2 s and a 2-3 sentence
summary that starts streaming in about 1.1 s (native Metal, warm models, fetch excluded). A FastAPI service fetches
and extracts the article and runs open-weight models locally through Ollama, tuned for **precision of directional
calls**, with every model, prompt and threshold chosen by a committed evaluation.

> **This is a proof of concept, and rigor is balanced per aspect.** The signal metric, the data splits, the latency
> budgets and the one-time holdout are strict; the prompt grid is deliberately lean; article labels and summary
> judgements come from Claude Opus subagents with no human check. The limits are listed
> [at the end](#limitations-and-next-steps).

| The brief asks for | Where |
|---|---|
| Design decisions | [Design decisions](#design-decisions), [`01-decisions.md`](.context/docs/design/01-decisions.md) |
| Latency trade-offs | [Latency trade-offs](#latency-trade-offs), [`05-latency.md`](.context/docs/design/05-latency.md) |
| How to run | [Quickstart](#quickstart), [Using it](#using-it) |
| How to test | [Testing](#testing) |
| AI tools and the conversation log | [AI tools used](#ai-tools-used), [`.context/transcript/`](.context/transcript/) |

The design docs read in order from [`00-overview.md`](.context/docs/design/00-overview.md); each number below links
to the committed result it comes from.

## Results at a glance

Per-endpoint defaults, picked by the rules in [`selection.md`](evals/results/selection/selection.md). Latency is
native Metal on an Apple M4 Pro, warm, concurrency 1, excluding fetch ([`latency.md`](evals/results/latency/latency.md)).

| Endpoint | Default model | Quality on dev | Warm p50 latency | Budget (p50) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/api/signal` (lede) | `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | dev300 F0.5 0.730 [0.651, 0.795], 0.0% inversions | 178 ms (p95 195) | <= 500 ms: met |
| `/api/summary` | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | Opus judge faithfulness 4.40 [4.17, 4.60] of 5, material errors 10% [0%, 20%] | TTFT 1,128 ms, complete 2,199 ms | TTFT <= 1,500 ms, complete <= 4,000 ms: met |
| `/api/analyze` | `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | dev300 F0.5 0.752 [0.664, 0.834], 0.0% inversions; faithfulness 4.47 | signal 1,098 ms, TTFT 1,292 ms, complete 2,584 ms | as `/summary`: met |

- Two model files serve all three endpoints: 4.34 GB against the 10 GB bundle cap.
- Extraction (`selectolax` + `cascade`, [03](.context/docs/design/03-extraction.md)): body F1 0.959 [0.942, 0.973]
  on 90 articles (0.929 before three profiles were tuned on the same set, the honest estimate), p50 1.2 ms.
- Live fetch, outside the budgets: median of the per-source medians 148 ms, slowest source 552 ms.
- The higher-scoring 9B decision models miss the 500 ms `/signal` budget ([the trade-off](#the-signal-trade-off)).

These are dev numbers. The frozen configs then run once on unseen test splits
([`04-evals.md`](.context/docs/design/04-evals.md#8-holdout)).

## Quickstart

Requirements: Docker with Compose 2.20 or later (the `docker compose` plugin), Homebrew for the macOS default, and
for local development [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) plus Node 24 with pnpm (via corepack).

### 1. macOS (default): native Ollama plus the app container

Docker Desktop cannot pass the Apple GPU into a Linux container, so Ollama runs on the host with Metal.

```bash
brew install ollama && brew services start ollama
ollama pull qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0 && ollama pull qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M   # the two defaults, 4.34 GB
docker compose up -d                                              # builds the app image on the first run
open http://localhost:8000
```

- `scripts/dev_setup.py native` installs Ollama and sets the measured service env (`OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1`,
  `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0`, `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=30m`, `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=3`; see
  [`preflight.json`](evals/results/latency/preflight.json)); `scripts/dev_setup.py pull --set eval` pulls the whole
  eval roster ([`models-eval.txt`](deploy/models-eval.txt), about 36 GB). Run both with `uv run python`.
- On Linux with a native Ollama, start it with `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` so the container reaches it through
  `host.docker.internal`.

### 2. Bundled CPU Ollama (Linux, CI, no native install)

```bash
docker compose --profile bundled --env-file deploy/bundled.env up -d
```

An `ollama/ollama` container pulls the two defaults listed in [`bundled.env`](deploy/bundled.env) (written by
`veritrade_evals select --write`) into a named volume on the first start, and the app waits for the pull. CPU-only
inference was roughly 5-15x slower than Metal on the build machine ([indicative](#native-vs-docker-cpu)), so this is
a portability path, not a latency path. Leave `OLLAMA_CPUS` unset: it is a CPU quota, not a thread count, and a
quota below the visible cores can slow llama.cpp down rather than just cap it.

### 3. Local development without Docker

```bash
uv sync --all-packages
VT_CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:3000 uv run uvicorn veritrade.api.app:create_app --factory --port 8000 --reload
cd frontend && pnpm install && NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE=http://localhost:8000 pnpm dev   # second shell, port 3000
# or serve the built UI from FastAPI: pnpm build in frontend/, then start uvicorn with VT_STATIC_DIR=frontend/out
```

### Where it answers, and how to stop

- **UI**: http://localhost:8000 (Analyze) and http://localhost:8000/benchmarks/ (the eval tables from
  `evals/results/benchmarks.json`, written by `veritrade_evals report`; a labelled sample shows when it is absent).
- **API**: `http://localhost:8000/api/...`, interactive docs at `/docs`, contract in
  [`backend/openapi.json`](backend/openapi.json). Health: `curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/health`.
- **Stop**: `docker compose down`; for the bundled stack `docker compose --profile bundled --env-file
  deploy/bundled.env down` (add `-v` to delete the pulled models); `brew services stop ollama` for native Ollama.
- **Settings** are environment variables ([`config.py`](backend/src/veritrade/config.py),
  [`compose.yaml`](compose.yaml)): `VT_PORT` (host port, 8000), `VT_OLLAMA_BASE_URL`, `VT_MODELS` (restricts the
  allowlist in [`models.toml`](backend/src/veritrade/data/models.toml)), `VT_DEFAULT_MODEL_SIGNAL` / `_SUMMARY` /
  `_ANALYZE`, and `SEC_USER_AGENT` (the declared contact for SEC EDGAR's fair-access policy; set your own).

## Using it

### The UI

- Paste any public HTML article URL (the 10 tested sources are listed under the input) and press **Analyze**.
  *Split* mode (default) fires `/api/signal` and `/api/summary` together, so the signal card renders first;
  *Combined* makes one `/api/analyze` call. **Streaming** (on by default) uses the SSE endpoints, off the JSON ones.
- Pickers filled from `GET /api/models` choose a model per endpoint (models not pulled are disabled), the extractor
  (10), the parser (4) and, in split mode, the scope.
- Results: the signal card (label, abstention with the direction the model leaned, policy, confidence), the
  streamed summary, the article line (source, extraction method) and a latency bar that puts each request's server
  stage timings on one client time axis, with time-to-signal and first-token marks.

### The API

| Method and path | Request body | Response |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/signal` | `url`, `model`, `parser`, `extractor`, `scope` (default `lede`), `no_cache` | `meta`, `signal`, `timings` |
| `POST /api/summary` | `url`, `model`, `parser`, `extractor`, `no_cache` (scope is always `full`) | `meta`, `summary`, `truncated`, `timings` |
| `POST /api/summary/stream` | as `/api/summary` | SSE: `meta -> summary_delta* -> done` |
| `POST /api/analyze` | as `/api/signal`, `scope` default `full` | `meta`, `signal`, `entity`, `summary`, `truncated`, `timings` |
| `POST /api/analyze/stream` | as `/api/analyze` | SSE: `meta -> sentiment -> summary_delta* -> done` |
| `GET /api/models` | - | Allowlist (kind, endpoints, installed, size), per-endpoint defaults, parsers, extractors, scopes |
| `GET /api/health` | - | `ok` / `degraded`, Ollama reachability and version, backend label (`native-metal` / `docker-cpu`) |

Only `url` is required; `model` must be on the allowlist; `parser` and `extractor` default to `selectolax` and
`cascade` (`GET /api/models` lists the 4 parsers and 10 extractors); `no_cache: true` bypasses both caches.
`signal` holds `sentiment`, `abstained`, `policy` and, by policy, `confidence`, `score` (-2..2) or `probabilities`.
`timings` splits each request into fetch, consent, parse, extract and inference (wall, TTFT, load, prompt eval,
eval, tokens) and reports both cache outcomes.

```bash
URL='https://...'   # any public article URL
curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/signal -H 'content-type: application/json' -d "{\"url\": \"$URL\"}"
curl -sN http://localhost:8000/api/analyze/stream -H 'content-type: application/json' -d "{\"url\": \"$URL\"}"
```

**SSE order.** `meta` (article meta, fetch / parse / extract timings) once extraction is done; on `/analyze/stream`
one `sentiment` event as soon as the score closes (served field order: sentiment-first); `summary_delta` text
chunks; `done` with the full JSON response. A failure before the stream opens is a JSON error with its HTTP status,
after that one `error` event; a closed connection stops the upstream generation.

**Errors** share one envelope, `{"error": {"code", "message", "hint", "retryable", "upstream_status"}}`
([`errors.py`](backend/src/veritrade/errors.py), [`contracts.py`](backend/src/veritrade/api/contracts.py)); other
request-body validation errors, such as an unknown `parser`, `extractor` or `scope` or an extra field, return
FastAPI's standard 422 `{"detail": [...]}`.

| HTTP | Codes | When |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `invalid_url`, `blocked_destination`, `model_not_allowed` | Malformed URL; SSRF guard (private or reserved address, a port other than 80/443); model not on the allowlist or disabled by `VT_MODELS`, or not served on that endpoint |
| 422 | `paywalled`, `consent_required`, `extraction_empty`, `unsupported_content`, `too_large` | Fetched, but no usable article: paywall, consent wall, under 40 words, not HTML (PDF, feed), over 10 MB |
| 502 | `source_blocked`, `upstream_http`, `schema_violation` | Publisher refused (CDN bot wall, 401/403/429/451, with a hint to a syndicated copy); other upstream HTTP error; malformed model output |
| 503 | `model_unavailable`, `llm_unreachable` | Model not pulled (the hint gives the `ollama pull` command); Ollama down |
| 504 | `upstream_timeout`, `inference_timeout` | Fetch deadline (8 s); inference timeout (90 s) |

## Architecture

```
browser ──► FastAPI (same origin: /api + static Next.js export)
              │ fetch (httpx, HTTP/2, SSRF guard, consent/paywall/block detection, single-flight cache)
              │ extract (parser x extractor registry, lede/full scope, token cap)
              ├─► /api/signal   decision model (/v1/systemone, class probabilities) or tiny LLM
              ├─► /api/summary  small LLM, JSON or SSE stream
              └─► /api/analyze  one small LLM -> {score, entity, summary}, JSON or SSE stream
                         ▼
                      Ollama (native Metal on macOS, or the bundled container)
```

A request is checked against the model allowlist; one pooled HTTP/2 client fetches the page behind an SSRF guard
that vets every resolved address and redirect hop, and bot walls, consent walls and paywalls become typed errors.
Extraction (default `selectolax` + `cascade`: JSON-LD `articleBody`, then the per-source profile in
[`sources.toml`](backend/src/veritrade/data/sources.toml), then a text-density fallback) cuts the `lede` or `full`
input. Ollama gets the model's frozen prompt with a JSON schema, greedy decoding and `think: false`, and the
model's confidence policy turns the answer into a label or an abstention (`backend/src/veritrade/`).

## Design decisions

Every decision was settled in an interview before any code was written; the full table, with the question each one
answers, is in [`01-decisions.md`](.context/docs/design/01-decisions.md).

- **Open-weight models on a local Ollama** ([Q1](.context/docs/design/01-decisions.md#round-1)): everything runs and
  reproduces with no API key or paid service. Native Metal is the macOS default because Docker Desktop cannot reach
  the Apple GPU; a `bundled` CPU profile covers Linux and CI.
- **Precision first** (Q2): a wrong directional call costs a trade, a missed one little, so selection uses F0.5 macro
  over bullish and bearish with inversions capped at 2% ([04](.context/docs/design/04-evals.md#1-objective-and-metrics)).
- **Abstain rather than guess** (Q3): thresholds on decision-model class probabilities, on label-token probabilities
  (`/signal`, plus `directional_tau`) or on an ordinal -2..+2 score (`/analyze`, works mid-stream); every signal
  reports `abstained`. The frozen defaults never abstain (dev300 coverage 100%): the 0.8B runs at `min_p` 0 with
  tau 0.28 and `/analyze` at \|s\| >= 1 on integer scores, so they hold back by answering neutral; only the 9B
  decision models abstain (dev300 coverage 72.9% and 26.3%).
- **Split and combined, both served** (Q8): a fast signal model next to a summariser, or one model for score, entity
  and summary; the UI switches and both were measured ([05](.context/docs/design/05-latency.md#split-against-combined)).
- **The quick signal reads the lede** (Q4): headline plus opening paragraphs, body capped at 200 tokens; `/signal`
  answers in about 7 tokens, so prompt length is its latency.
- **Stream, sentiment first** (R3): the schema puts the score first and an incremental scanner emits it as it closes.
- **One origin** ([R1](.context/docs/design/01-decisions.md#round-2)): FastAPI serves the static Next.js export; no
  proxy hop, no Node at runtime.
- **Extraction measured, not assumed** (Q10, R4): 22 parser x extractor rows on 90 real articles; the served
  `selectolax` + `cascade` is best or tied on quality and has the lowest tail of any row that finds bodies (p95
  2.4 ms, [03](.context/docs/design/03-extraction.md)).
- **Fetch like a browser, never evade** (Q18-Q20): standard headers, Yahoo consent answered with reject-all, typed
  errors; four CDN-blocked publishers were replaced, not evaded ([02](.context/docs/design/02-source-probe.md)).
- **Budgets before measurements** (R7): set first (see [the table](#latency-trade-offs)); a miss is reported, never moved.
- **Select by rules in code, test once** (Q6, Q7, R5-R8): lean grid, one error pass, freeze; `select` writes the
  defaults; the holdout runs once behind a guard keyed by the frozen config's hash ([04](.context/docs/design/04-evals.md)).
- **Publisher rights in a public repo** (Q11): skeleton test fixtures (real DOM, synthetic text); no article or
  dataset text is committed, only ids, URLs, hashes, labels and numbers.

## Latency trade-offs

Full analysis: [`05-latency.md`](.context/docs/design/05-latency.md). Native suite: 528 samples, 0 errors, cold n=3
and warm n=30 per cell on the 30 dev articles served from memory.

| Endpoint (default) | Budget, p50 | Measured p50 | Measured p95 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/signal` lede, `qwen3.5:0.8b` | <= 500 ms | 178 ms | 195 ms |
| `/summary` SSE, `qwen3.5:4b` | TTFT <= 1,500 ms, complete <= 4,000 ms | TTFT 1,128 ms, complete 2,199 ms | complete 4,232 ms |
| `/analyze` SSE, `qwen3.5:4b` | TTFT <= 1,500 ms, complete <= 4,000 ms | signal 1,098 ms, TTFT 1,292 ms, complete 2,584 ms | complete 4,627 ms |

The budgets bind the p50 and every default meets them. The tails do not: the slowest requests are the long articles;
in every full-scope cell the two slowest of 30 carry about 2,550-2,980 prompt tokens (1,990-2,200 for `clef-flash`,
whose article input is capped at 2,000 tokens) against 825-1,074 at p50.

- **Split or combined.** Split delivers the signal at 178 ms while the summary streams (first text 1,128 ms);
  combined delivers it at 1,098 ms, six times later, but from one model and one prompt instead of two resident models
  (1.02 + 3.32 GB) and two prefills, and it scores higher on the article dev set (0.880 vs 0.685, overlapping CIs at
  n=30; dev300 0.752 vs 0.730). Split's two concurrent requests on one GPU were not measured, so its times are a lower bound.
- **Streaming.** SSE does not change the total (-2.9% to +1.1% against JSON at p50) but shows text at 38-54% of it.
  Sentiment-first, the streamed score lands 194-249 ms before the first summary text and 1.4-1.5 s before a JSON
  client would see it.
- **Lede scope.** The 0.8B answers in 178 / 195 ms (p50 / p95) on the lede against 231 / 532 ms on the full
  article, and the 9B tails grow 4-5x at full scope: lede keeps `/signal` predictable as well as fast.
- **Where the time goes.** `/signal` is prefill: the 0.8B spends 126 ms on prompt eval and 43 ms writing a 7-token
  answer. The 4B summariser prefills at about 800 tokens/s, so prompt eval is 1,029 of its 1,128 ms TTFT. Parse and
  extract take 1.2-1.6 and 1.6-2.5 ms, under 2% of the fastest `/signal`; the extractor matters through tokens
  instead (704-822 `full` tokens for competent extractors, 2,116 for `strip-tags`). A cold model load adds 0.7-1.3 s,
  paid only after a start or 30 idle minutes (`keep_alive` 30m).
- **Network and caches.** Fetch adds a median of the per-source medians of 148 ms, slowest 552 ms (GlobeNewswire),
  so a lede signal lands about 0.33 s after submit on a typical source (a rough sum of medians). A pooled HTTP/2
  client keeps connections alive for 60 s; the single-flight fetch cache (10 min, 512 entries, 200 MB; errors 60 s)
  downloads a page once for split mode's two requests; results are cached for an hour; Yahoo's consent cookie is
  reused (857 ms once, then about 120 ms).

### The `/signal` trade-off

| Model | dev300 F0.5 [95% CI] | Articles dev F0.5 | Lede p50 / p95 | File | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` | 0.730 [0.651, 0.795] | 0.685 | 178 / 195 ms | 1.02 GB | served default |
| `clef-flash:9b-q8_0` | 0.874 [0.811, 0.937] | 0.848 | 659 / 807 ms | 10.58 GB | misses 500 ms; alone over the 10 GB bundle cap |
| `nimble:9b-q4_K_M` | 0.843 [0.773, 0.901] | 0.895 | 1,061 / 1,182 ms | 5.63 GB | misses 500 ms |

The 9B models score 0.11-0.14 higher on dev300, mostly through recall, but neither fits the budget and clef-flash
alone exceeds the bundle cap. The 0.8B is precise when it calls (dev300 precision 0.91 / 0.92) but cautious: on the
article dev set it catches 10 of 20 directional articles against 17 for clef-flash, one inversion each. The budget
was reported, never moved; both 9B models stay selectable per request (`model`, native Ollama) for 0.5-0.9 s more.

### Native vs docker-cpu

The bundled Ollama runs llama.cpp on CPU, measured through the bundled app over HTTP (warm n=10 per cell, fetch
subtracted). Two passes were discarded, and neither is committed:

- **Pass 1**: the JSON rows were biased by Ollama's prompt cache (prompt eval 118-171 ms), because each JSON cell
  re-sent prompts its SSE twin had just evaluated. Fix: a reload hook (`container_reload` in
  [`latency.py`](evals/src/veritrade_evals/latency.py)) runs `docker exec ... ollama stop` before every warm phase.
- **Pass 2**: invalidated by unrelated workloads on the same Mac (load average 50-64 against 6.9 at the native
  preflight): `qwen3.5:0.8b` decode went from about 31 ms to about 2.8 s per token and 4 `/analyze` requests timed
  out, because llama.cpp's 14 spin-barrier threads on a 14-vCPU Docker VM over a 14-core host stall whenever the
  host takes cores.

Pass 1's valid rows, indicative only (n=10, not committed): CPU-only Docker is roughly 5-15x slower than Metal on
this machine and would miss every budget, so the bundled profile is for Linux and CI.

| Endpoint | Transport | docker-cpu p50 | x native |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/signal` 0.8B lede | JSON | 2,657 ms | 14.9x |
| `/summary` 4B | SSE | TTFT 8,768 ms, complete 14,405 ms | 7.8x / 6.6x |
| `/analyze` 4B | SSE | signal 8,644 ms, TTFT 9,147 ms, complete 12,106 ms | 7.9x / 7.1x / 4.7x |

The quiet-host re-run uses the same protocol, reload hook included, and its rows go to the `docker-cpu` section of
[`latency.md`](evals/results/latency/latency.md).

## Evaluation

Full method and results: [`04-evals.md`](.context/docs/design/04-evals.md). The harness imports the serving code, so
what is measured is what is served.

- **Metric**: F0.5 macro over bullish and bearish, a 2% inversion cap, and an operating point at the best F0.5
  under the cap; 95% stratified bootstrap CIs (B = 1,000) on the headline metrics.
- **Tweets and sentences** ([`splits/`](evals/data/splits/), ids, hashes and labels only): `dev300` for tuning (100
  per class from Twitter Financial News train, reweighted to its 20.2 / 15.1 / 64.7% prior); Twitter FNS validation
  (2,388), Financial PhraseBank AllAgree (2,259) and FinEntity single-label paragraphs (851) held out.
- **Articles**: 90 recent articles from the 10 sources, 3 per class per source (Yahoo 4 bearish and BBC 2, keeping
  30 per class), split 30 dev / 60 test, labelled by
  two independent Opus labellers plus an adjudicator. On the 157 double-labelled pool articles they agree on 96.2%
  (kappa 0.943); 24 ambiguous articles were replaced ([`stats.json`](evals/data/articles/stats.json)).
- **Prompt grid**: 33 prompt cells on dev300 (prompt version x output schema or field order per model), each swept
  over confidence policy and threshold; one error-analysis pass, then a freeze into
  [`frozen.json`](evals/results/frozen.json) and `models.toml`. The largest lever was a decision rule, not a prompt:
  `directional_tau` lifts the 0.8B by +0.218 [+0.141, +0.307] F0.5 ([grid notes](evals/results/grid/notes.md)). On `/analyze`, `qwen3.5:4b` leads dev300 with 0.752 against 0.685
  (`ministral-3:3b`) and 0.647 (`qwen3:4b-instruct-2507`).
- **Summaries**: deterministic checks (length, every number grounded in the source, entity named), key-fact
  coverage with `qwen3-embedding:0.6b` at cosine 0.60, and blind Opus judges (faithfulness, coverage,
  hallucinations, lead) on the 30 dev articles ([`summary.md`](evals/results/summary/summary.md)). Extraction is
  scored separately against Opus gold bodies ([`summary.md`](evals/results/extraction/summary.md)).
- **Reproducing**: `uv run python -m veritrade_evals --help` lists every step; `datasets fetch` re-downloads the
  pinned public datasets behind the tweet, sentence and paragraph splits, but the article-level runs (signal on
  articles, extraction, summaries, latency) need the stored HTML and Opus gold bodies in the gitignored
  `evals/data/private/`, which publisher rights keep out of the repo, so for those a clone can only read the
  committed results.

Summary quality of the served pair on the dev articles (n = 30):

| Endpoint, model | Checks pass | Numbers grounded | Key facts (0.60) | Opus faithfulness [95% CI] | Coverage | Hallucination flag | Material errors [95% CI] |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|--:|--:|---|
| `/summary`, `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | 90% | 93% | 47% | 4.40 [4.17, 4.60] | 4.57 | 50% | 10% [0%, 20%] |
| `/analyze`, `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` | 93% | 97% | 57% | 4.47 [4.20, 4.70] | 4.63 | 40% | 10% [0%, 20%] |

The hallucination flag counts any unsupported detail, minor slips included; a material error is faithfulness <= 3
(a wrong key number, an unsupported claim that matters). The `/summary` runner-up, `qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M`, is faster
(TTFT 484 ms) but scores 3.97 with 30% material errors, so the 4B serves both summary endpoints.

**Holdout.** The frozen configs run once on the test splits (`articles_test`, `tfns_val`, `fpb_allagree`,
`finentity_single`), with `qwen3.5:9b-q4_K_M` as an untuned quality ceiling, and Opus judges the winners' summaries
on the 60 test articles. Nothing is re-tuned on these numbers ([protocol](.context/docs/design/04-evals.md#8-holdout)).
The one-time run is in progress; its results are added here when it completes.

## Testing

| Layer | Where | What it guards |
|---|---|---|
| Backend unit | `backend/tests/unit` | Extractors on skeleton fixtures under all four parsers, the SSRF guard (address classes, DNS rebinding, ports), block / consent / paywall detection, prompts, confidence policies, the stream scanner split at every byte offset, the Ollama client, the API contract |
| Backend integration | `backend/tests/integration` | The ASGI app against fake publishers (skeleton pages) and a scripted Ollama: every endpoint in JSON and SSE, event order, single-flight and result caches, the error table, failures mid-stream, client disconnects |
| Evals and scripts | `evals/tests/unit`, `scripts/tests` | Metrics, splits, grid, freeze, selection, the holdout guard, latency aggregation, the report, transcript redaction |
| Frontend | `frontend/tests` | Vitest + Testing Library: SSE parser, components, and MSW integration (signal before the summary completes, JSON fallback, errors, abort on resubmit, benchmarks page) |
| End to end | `frontend/e2e` | Playwright on the compose stack: bundled CPU Ollama with the CI models, an nginx fixture site answering for the 10 publisher hostnames, split and combined streaming, a decision model with a switched extractor, a signal check per source profile, the benchmarks page |
| Live smoke | `backend/tests/live` | One real article per source; informational, never gates |

```bash
uv sync --all-packages
(cd frontend && pnpm install)            # frontend deps for check.py
uv run python scripts/check.py --fast    # ruff, format, mypy, OpenAPI drift, backend unit + evals + scripts tests, frontend lint/format/typecheck/test
uv run python scripts/check.py --full    # adds backend integration tests with a 75% coverage floor, and the frontend build
uv run pytest -m live backend/tests/live -rA   # live publishers, opt-in
```

End to end on the CI stack, which pulls `qwen3.5:0.8b-q8_0` and `tev1:0.8b-q8_0` (a CI-only decision model that
exercises the decision-model path and is never evaluated); CPU inference is slow, so test timeouts are 300 s.

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.e2e.yaml up -d --wait
(cd frontend && pnpm install && pnpm exec playwright install chromium && pnpm exec playwright test)
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.e2e.yaml down
```

**CI** ([`ci.yml`](.github/workflows/ci.yml), on push to `main` and pull requests): `backend` runs
`scripts/check.py --backend --full`; `frontend` checks the generated API types against `backend/openapi.json`, then
lint, format, typecheck, tests and the build; `e2e` builds the image, restores the cached Ollama models, starts the
stack, warms both models and runs Playwright, uploading logs on failure. [`live-smoke.yml`](.github/workflows/live-smoke.yml)
fetches the real publishers weekly and never gates, because publishers change markup and block datacenter IPs.

## AI tools used

- **Claude Code CLI** (2.1.30x) with **Claude Opus 5.5** (`claude-opus-5-5`) as the main loop, high reasoning effort
  and plan mode.
- **`/grill-me` skill**: Claude interviewed Kris until every decision was settled, before any code (Q1-Q20, R1-R10
  and follow-ups in [`01-decisions.md`](.context/docs/design/01-decisions.md)). The approach was handpicked from
  [`.context/openai-research.md`](.context/openai-research.md), a research and architecture proposal Kris provided.
- **Workflow tool** (multi-agent orchestration, "ultracode") and **Claude Code subagents**, every one pinned to Opus
  5.5, each owning a disjoint set of files. Opus subagents also produced the eval data that needs judgment: article
  discovery, gold bodies and key facts, two independent labellers, an adjudicator and blind summary judges (prompts
  in [`evals/opus_prompts/`](evals/opus_prompts/00-README.md)).
- **No API keys or paid services** anywhere. Serving uses only open-weight local models through Ollama.

Kris set the direction and settled every decision; Claude Code planned, wrote the code, tests, eval harness and docs,
and ran the evaluations. The full, redacted conversation (main loop, subagents, workflows) is in
[`.context/transcript/`](.context/transcript/): rendered HTML and Markdown, raw JSONL, and `meta.json` with the
harness, model, effort, subagents and token usage.

## Limitations and next steps

- **One model family labels and judges.** Article labels, gold bodies, key facts and summary judgements all come
  from Claude Opus with no human check, and with 30 dev articles the served rules' CIs span about 0.2-0.5 F0.5.
- **Precision costs recall.** The `/signal` default caught 10 of 20 directional dev articles, so users will see many
  neutrals; the 9B decision models catch more but miss the latency budget.
- **The inversion cap is unproven on articles.** On the 30 dev articles the `/signal` default inverts 1 of its 14
  directional calls (7.1% against the 2% cap); selection passes it only because the 95% CI at n=30 reaches 0%, so
  the holdout is the real check ([`selection.md`](evals/results/selection/selection.md)).
- **Tuned on tweets.** Prompts and thresholds were tuned on 300 tweets and checked on balanced article sets; real
  traffic is likely neutral-heavy, so served precision is likely lower ([threats](.context/docs/design/04-evals.md#9-threats-to-validity)).
- **Summaries still slip.** The `/summary` default has an unsupported detail (minor slips included) in 50% of dev
  summaries and a material error in 10% [0%, 20%]; numbers are not re-checked against the source at serve time.
- **Latency is one machine at concurrency 1.** Tails exceed the budgets, split mode's concurrent pair and multi-user
  load were not measured, and the docker-cpu figures are indicative.
- **Coverage and hardening.** 10 profiled English sources (others fall back to JSON-LD and density, unmeasured),
  no PDFs; no authentication or inbound rate limiting, and the caches are in-process (per replica).

Next, from [`90-optional-backlog.md`](.context/docs/design/90-optional-backlog.md): a DSPy-style prompt optimiser;
distilling the 9B decision model into the sub-second tier; a progressive `/signal` that upgrades the 0.8B verdict
when a 9B model answers; analysing articles on publish; serving the number-grounding check; a GPU compose profile.

## Layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `backend/` | FastAPI service (`veritrade` package): fetch, extract, inference, API; serving config in `src/veritrade/data/` |
| `evals/` | Evaluation and benchmarking harness (`veritrade_evals` package), committed splits and results, Opus prompts |
| `frontend/` | Next.js 16 static export, served by FastAPI |
| `scripts/` | Setup, quality gate, probes, exports |
| `docker/`, `deploy/`, `compose.yaml`, `compose.e2e.yaml` | App image, bundled Ollama pull, e2e fixture site, model lists |
| `.github/workflows/` | CI and the weekly live smoke |
| `.context/` | Brief, research, design docs, AI conversation transcript |
